tests.request: Create a venue-screening checklist for the Redwood Ridge team offsite before we choose a venue.

input.body:
Redwood Ridge team offsite — venue-screening checklist

Use this checklist for every candidate venue before selecting a finalist. Record evidence, owner, date checked, open questions, and decision (pass / follow-up / reject). Sarah Kim coordinates the process; HR owns the budget.

1. Hard gates — reject or escalate if any apply

- [ ] Business-grade internet is available throughout the working areas, with reliable upload/download performance and sufficient capacity for the full group.
- [ ] Venue can support the required dates, arrival/departure window, room setup, and overall program schedule.
- [ ] Total cost is within the approved budget, including taxes, service charges, meeting-room fees, food and beverage minimums, AV, transportation, activities, and cancellation exposure.
- [ ] No undisclosed deposit, resort, destination, cleaning, service, or other mandatory fee creates an unacceptable cost or contracting risk.
- [ ] Venue can accommodate the group’s accessibility, dietary, mobility, medical, and other stated needs.
- [ ] Contract terms are reviewable before commitment and include clear cancellation, attrition, force-majeure, payment, liability, insurance, and damage provisions.
- [ ] Venue is not Sonoma Lodge.

2. Workability and meeting infrastructure

- [ ] Main meeting room fits the group comfortably in the intended layout, with adequate ceiling height, acoustics, lighting, temperature control, and ventilation.
- [ ] Breakout rooms and quiet spaces meet the agenda’s needs and are available for the full required periods.
- [ ] Tables, chairs, whiteboards, screens, microphones, speakers, adapters, power, and charging capacity are available or can be sourced at a known price.
- [ ] Internet access is dedicated or appropriately segmented for attendees; obtain written details on bandwidth, redundancy, outages, support response, and any device or content restrictions.
- [ ] Mobile coverage and backup connectivity are adequate for operational needs.
- [ ] Venue provides an on-site event contact and clear escalation path during the offsite.
- [ ] Noise, construction, weddings, public events, and other simultaneous bookings will not materially disrupt work.
- [ ] Check-in, luggage storage, deliveries, printing, package handling, and after-hours access are workable.

3. Lodging and attendee experience

- [ ] Room block has enough rooms, suitable bed configurations, and a clear release date.
- [ ] Rooms and shared spaces are clean, secure, climate-controlled, and suitable for the intended stay.
- [ ] Arrival and departure logistics are practical, including airport/rail access, parking, shuttles, rideshare, and late-arrival handling.
- [ ] Food service supports the schedule, dietary restrictions, allergies, nonalcoholic options, and reasonable break timing.
- [ ] Venue has comfortable, low-friction spaces for informal connection without compromising quiet time.
- [ ] Wellness, safety, and privacy expectations are documented, including emergency procedures, first aid, security, and incident contacts.
- [ ] Local activities are optional, accessible, weather-appropriate, and priced transparently.

4. Accessibility, inclusion, and safety

- [ ] Confirm step-free routes from arrival through lodging, meeting rooms, dining, restrooms, and any planned activities.
- [ ] Confirm accessible rooms, bathrooms, parking/drop-off, elevators, seating, signage, and emergency evacuation support.
- [ ] Venue can accommodate dietary, religious, sensory, and other inclusion requirements without singling people out.
- [ ] Review lighting, sound, crowding, temperature, and quiet-room options for sensory and health needs.
- [ ] Obtain current fire, evacuation, security, and severe-weather procedures and identify responsible venue staff.
- [ ] Confirm appropriate alcohol-service controls and a safe transportation plan if alcohol is offered.

5. Cost and commercial review

- [ ] Collect an itemized proposal with room rates, meeting-space charges, F&B pricing, AV, internet, staffing, taxes, gratuities, transportation, activities, and all mandatory fees.
- [ ] Calculate the all-in per-person and total cost under realistic attendance scenarios.
- [ ] Identify optional versus mandatory spend and any minimums, surcharges, commissions, or price-escalation clauses.
- [ ] Confirm payment schedule, deposit amount, approved payment method, refundability, and currency/tax treatment.
- [ ] Compare at least two viable alternatives using the same cost assumptions.
- [ ] Document the budget owner’s approval and any exception requiring escalation.

6. Contract and risk review

- [ ] Request the full contract, addenda, banquet/event order, room-block terms, and venue policies before selection.
- [ ] Review cancellation, rebooking, attrition, substitution, force majeure, service failure, and refund language.
- [ ] Confirm liability, indemnification, insurance, alcohol, damage, data/privacy, and confidentiality obligations.
- [ ] Confirm who may sign and whether procurement, HR, finance, legal, or security review is required.
- [ ] Ensure verbal promises and negotiated concessions are written into the contract or event order.
- [ ] Record all open legal or operational issues and their owners; do not treat an unresolved issue as approved.

7. Evidence and decision record

- [ ] Save the proposal, floor plans, connectivity details, accessibility answers, sample menus, policies, references, and site-visit notes.
- [ ] Verify important claims with dated written evidence or a documented site inspection; label unverified statements as open questions.
- [ ] Assign an owner and due date to every follow-up item.
- [ ] Score each venue consistently on hard gates, workability, attendee experience, accessibility/safety, cost, and contract risk.
- [ ] Prepare a short finalist comparison showing strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, unresolved risks, and total cost.

document.body:
Redwood Ridge team offsite — venue-screening checklist

Use this checklist for every candidate venue before selecting a finalist. Record evidence, owner, date checked, open questions, and decision (pass / follow-up / reject). Sarah Kim coordinates the process; HR owns the budget.

1. Hard gates — reject or escalate if any apply

- [ ] Business-grade internet is available throughout the working areas, with reliable upload/download performance and sufficient capacity for the full group.
- [ ] Venue can support the required dates, arrival/departure window, room setup, and overall program schedule.
- [ ] Total cost is within the approved budget, including taxes, service charges, meeting-room fees, food and beverage minimums, AV, transportation, activities, and cancellation exposure.
- [ ] No undisclosed deposit, resort, destination, cleaning, service, or other mandatory fee creates an unacceptable cost or contracting risk.
- [ ] Venue can accommodate the group’s accessibility, dietary, mobility, medical, and other stated needs.
- [ ] Contract terms are reviewable before commitment and include clear cancellation, attrition, force-majeure, payment, liability, insurance, and damage provisions.
- [ ] Venue is not Sonoma Lodge.

2. Workability and meeting infrastructure

- [ ] Main meeting room fits the group comfortably in the intended layout, with adequate ceiling height, acoustics, lighting, temperature control, and ventilation.
- [ ] Breakout rooms and quiet spaces meet the agenda’s needs and are available for the full required periods.
- [ ] Tables, chairs, whiteboards, screens, microphones, speakers, adapters, power, and charging capacity are available or can be sourced at a known price.
- [ ] Internet access is dedicated or appropriately segmented for attendees; obtain written details on bandwidth, redundancy, outages, support response, and any device or content restrictions.
- [ ] Mobile coverage and backup connectivity are adequate for operational needs.
- [ ] Venue provides an on-site event contact and clear escalation path during the offsite.
- [ ] Noise, construction, weddings, public events, and other simultaneous bookings will not materially disrupt work.
- [ ] Check-in, luggage storage, deliveries, printing, package handling, and after-hours access are workable.

3. Lodging and attendee experience

- [ ] Room block has enough rooms, suitable bed configurations, and a clear release date.
- [ ] Rooms and shared spaces are clean, secure, climate-controlled, and suitable for the intended stay.
- [ ] Arrival and departure logistics are practical, including airport/rail access, parking, shuttles, rideshare, and late-arrival handling.
- [ ] Food service supports the schedule, dietary restrictions, allergies, nonalcoholic options, and reasonable break timing.
- [ ] Venue has comfortable, low-friction spaces for informal connection without compromising quiet time.
- [ ] Wellness, safety, and privacy expectations are documented, including emergency procedures, first aid, security, and incident contacts.
- [ ] Local activities are optional, accessible, weather-appropriate, and priced transparently.

4. Accessibility, inclusion, and safety

- [ ] Confirm step-free routes from arrival through lodging, meeting rooms, dining, restrooms, and any planned activities.
- [ ] Confirm accessible rooms, bathrooms, parking/drop-off, elevators, seating, signage, and emergency evacuation support.
- [ ] Venue can accommodate dietary, religious, sensory, and other inclusion requirements without singling people out.
- [ ] Review lighting, sound, crowding, temperature, and quiet-room options for sensory and health needs.
- [ ] Obtain current fire, evacuation, security, and severe-weather procedures and identify responsible venue staff.
- [ ] Confirm appropriate alcohol-service controls and a safe transportation plan if alcohol is offered.

5. Cost and commercial review

- [ ] Collect an itemized proposal with room rates, meeting-space charges, F&B pricing, AV, internet, staffing, taxes, gratuities, transportation, activities, and all mandatory fees.
- [ ] Calculate the all-in per-person and total cost under realistic attendance scenarios.
- [ ] Identify optional versus mandatory spend and any minimums, surcharges, commissions, or price-escalation clauses.
- [ ] Confirm payment schedule, deposit amount, approved payment method, refundability, and currency/tax treatment.
- [ ] Compare at least two viable alternatives using the same cost assumptions.
- [ ] Document the budget owner’s approval and any exception requiring escalation.

6. Contract and risk review

- [ ] Request the full contract, addenda, banquet/event order, room-block terms, and venue policies before selection.
- [ ] Review cancellation, rebooking, attrition, substitution, force majeure, service failure, and refund language.
- [ ] Confirm liability, indemnification, insurance, alcohol, damage, data/privacy, and confidentiality obligations.
- [ ] Confirm who may sign and whether procurement, HR, finance, legal, or security review is required.
- [ ] Ensure verbal promises and negotiated concessions are written into the contract or event order.
- [ ] Record all open legal or operational issues and their owners; do not treat an unresolved issue as approved.

7. Evidence and decision record

- [ ] Save the proposal, floor plans, connectivity details, accessibility answers, sample menus, policies, references, and site-visit notes.
- [ ] Verify important claims with dated written evidence or a documented site inspection; label unverified statements as open questions.
- [ ] Assign an owner and due date to every follow-up item.
- [ ] Score each venue consistently on hard gates, workability, attendee experience, accessibility/safety, cost, and contract risk.
- [ ] Prepare a short finalist comparison showing strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, unresolved risks, and total cost.
- [ ] Obtain Sarah Kim’s coordination sign-off and HR’s budget approval before commitment.
- [ ] Obtain any required legal, finance, procurement, or security approval before signing.
- [ ] Record the final decision, rationale, approvers, selected package, and backup plan.

messages.content: [2026-07-10T10:25:00-07:00] Leo got a normal Acme API v2 support question. Their connector saw a few 429 responses during a batch metadata sync and asked whether the rate-limit headers mean the API is unstable. Leo's read is that they parallelized requests more aggressively than usual, the documented reset time was in the response headers, and there is no data loss, export timeout, cursor defect, or large-export recurrence here. Draft a practical support reply explaining the API v2 rate-limit headers, backoff behavior, and when to send request IDs, without turning this into founder routing, a special report, or a roadmap promise.

Subject: Acme API v2 rate-limit responses during metadata sync

Hi [Name],

The 429 responses indicate that the metadata sync temporarily exceeded the API v2 request rate for the connector’s current traffic pattern. They do not, by themselves, indicate that the API is unstable.

The rate-limit headers are intended to guide the client:

- The limit header indicates the applicable request allowance.
- The remaining header shows how much of that allowance is left.
- The reset header gives the documented time at which the allowance is replenished.
- If a `Retry-After` value is included, use that delay before retrying.

For retries, please honor the response timing rather than immediately replaying the request. A short exponential backoff with jitter is recommended, along with reducing parallelism during the batch. The connector should then retry the request and continue from its existing cursor or batch position. A 429 does not imply that the request partially succeeded or that data was lost.

Based on the responses we reviewed, this looks consistent with the sync running more requests in parallel than usual. We are not seeing an export timeout, cursor issue, data-loss symptom, or recurring large-export problem.

If the connector continues receiving 429s after honoring the reset/backoff guidance—or if a request fails after the retry window—please send us:

- The affected endpoint and approximate UTC timestamp
- The response status and relevant rate-limit headers
- The request ID from the response
- The connector’s effective concurrency and retry behavior
- Whether the issue is limited to one batch or is reproducible across syncs

The request IDs will let us correlate the individual responses in our logs. There is no need to send a special report for the behavior described here; the normal support thread is sufficient.

Best,
Leo

Hi {{customer_name}},

It looks like the OAuth authorization was canceled before {{source_name}} finished connecting to Mercury. Because authorization was not completed, Mercury did not create the source connection and no source data was imported.

You can retry at any time:

1. Return to Mercury and start the {{source_name}} connection again.
2. Select the correct account or workspace when prompted.
3. Complete the OAuth authorization and select Allow/Authorize.
4. Wait for Mercury to return you to the connection screen and confirm that the source shows as connected.

If the authorization window was closed accidentally, or you selected Cancel or Deny, simply start the connection again and complete the authorization. If you still cannot connect, please reply with the approximate time of the attempt and a screenshot of any error message. Please do not send passwords, access tokens, or other credentials.

Best,
{{agent_name}}
Mercury Support

arguments.title: May 3 Quarterly All-Hands — Speaker Sheet
arguments.body:
MAY 3 QUARTERLY ALL-HANDS — SPEAKER SHEET
Live Q&A answers | Keep answers short and factual

1. Nadia cc’d on Evergreen — is customer ownership moving from Sarah?
Answer: No ownership change is being announced here. Sarah remains the continuity owner for customer work. Nadia is included to capture customer-growth patterns; she is not taking over product, roadmap, or enterprise/customer-thread ownership.
Boundary: Do not frame the cc as an org change or a transfer of account ownership.

2. Mercury support evidence — what belongs in launch evidence?
Answer: Keep the boundary tight: a ticket, screenshot, or one-off customer note is normal support signal unless it is part of the defined Mercury truth check and has the required verification context. The weekly check should use Leo’s risk, evidence, and readout standard—not promote every support artifact into launch evidence.
Boundary: Support signals can inform review; they do not by themselves establish launch readiness or feature timing.

3. Kestrel Mercury newsletter — launch marker, funding announcement, or broader go-to-market push?
Answer: Treat it as an external communications item, not as a launch, funding, or broader go-to-market announcement. The newsletter does not change Mercury’s release status or establish feature timing.
Boundary: Do not infer launch positioning, funding, or enterprise-readiness dates from the newsletter.

4. Atlas backup notes — outside technical conversations or standard continuity work?
Answer: They are standard continuity and backup-coverage work. Keep the discussion at the coverage-discipline level; do not speculate about or discuss anyone’s outside conversations.
Boundary: Rishi remains the Atlas owner. This does not change ownership or create a personnel discussion.

Not for live answer
- Mercury feature timing and broader enterprise-readiness dates: route asynchronously when confirmed.
- Individual manager/process and people/comp questions: follow up separately.

Live-answer rule
Answer the question asked, state the boundary, and avoid upgrading a signal into an ownership change, launch claim, funding claim, readiness date, or personnel discussion.

messages.content:
Assessment: this is not evidence of a verifier defect. The customer copied the documentation’s example `nbf` value, so the token’s validity window can begin in the future relative to the verifier. Deployment-time clock skew can make that more apparent.

Suggested customer response:

“Your token verifiers are behaving as expected. The `nbf` value in the documentation is illustrative and must not be copied into production tokens. Generate `nbf` from the current issuance time for each token, ensure the issuer and verifier clocks are synchronized, and allow up to five minutes of clock skew as documented. If freshly generated tokens still fail after those checks, please provide the redacted `nbf`, `iat`, and `exp` claims along with the approximate issuance and verification times so we can investigate further.”

The current internal search also shows the updated documentation covering the five-minute allowance and warning against reusing sample timestamps.

arguments.title: Compass June closeout packet — June 4 evidence read
arguments.body:
# Compass June closeout packet
## June 4 evidence read

**Prepared / owner-fill cutoff:** June 2, 2025  
**Evidence read:** June 4, 2025  
**Audience:** Internal operating review only  
**Scope:** Compass remains an experiment and operating input. This packet is not a customer-facing launch, dashboard rebuild, product/GTM proof, hiring trigger, or Series C narrative.

## 1. Decision status

**Final cut/keep decision: PENDING the June 4 evidence read.**

This packet consolidates the evidence and decision boundaries; it does not pre-commit the final disposition. The June 4 discussion should decide whether to keep a narrowly bounded internal prompt practice, cut it, or retain only specific controls/scripts with a defined follow-up evidence bar.

**Working evidence conclusion:** Compass shows limited internal operating learning—better account-team preparation and more specific follow-up questions—but the evidence does not establish Compass-caused customer behavior change or a repeatable expansion motion.

## 2. Evidence question

Did Compass produce a meaningful, repeatable change in owner behavior or customer/account behavior, sufficient to justify keeping or expanding the work?

Separate these claims:

- Internal preparation or conversation quality.
- Named owner follow-up and operating discipline.
- Customer behavior, adoption, expansion, or revenue impact.
- Repeatable account-source quality across more than one account.

## 3. Behavior-change evidence

| Signal | Before / baseline | After / observation | Source and date | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Account-team conversation preparation | No standardized or quantified Compass baseline supplied. | Nadia’s scripts helped owners prepare better questions for Evergreen and Acme conversations. | Direct internal review, Apr. 25; Friday wrap, May 30. | Qualitative internal improvement; no customer-action attribution. |
| Renewal-risk / admin-friction follow-up | No dated baseline for follow-up quality supplied. | Owners identified specific follow-up work and asked better questions about the underlying friction. | Direct internal review, Apr. 25; Friday wrap, May 30. | Limited internal learning; not customer behavior change. |
| Post-first-live-sync expansion follow-up | No repeatability baseline supplied. | Prompt was legible to internal account owners, but did not produce a repeatable expansion motion. | Direct internal review, Apr. 25; Friday wrap, May 30. | Legibility only; growth impact not evidenced. |
| Customer/account behavior attributable to Compass | No customer-side before/after measure supplied. | No customer behavior change attributable to Compass established. | May Board Cycle evidence grid, May 12; Friday wrap, May 30. | Not established. |
| Enterprise-readiness intake routing | No completion or outcome-rate baseline supplied. | Routing expectations became clearer by function; completed handoffs and outcomes were not supplied. | May Board Cycle evidence grid, May 12; hiring-hold decision record, May 13. | Operating rule retained; behavior change not evidenced. |

**Summary:** The strongest observed change is internal preparation and follow-up quality. There is no controlled before/after measure, multi-account corroboration, or customer-side action record tying behavior causally to a Compass prompt.

## 4. Prompt evidence and boundaries

| Signal / intervention | Observed response | Source quality / confidence | Question for June 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Renewal-risk / admin-friction prompt with a named owner action, source, date, and caveat | Owners identified specific follow-up work and asked better questions. | Medium for internal preparation; low for customer causality. Evidence outside Evergreen remains uneven. | Is this bounded internal utility sufficient to keep the script? |
| Post-first-live-sync prompt separating teammate-invite/admin-role state from inferred readiness | Legible to account owners; no repeatable expansion motion. | Medium for legibility; low for growth impact. | Keep as a narrow prompt, or cut generic expansion framing? |
| Evidence/source-quality guardrail: definitions, provenance, dates, and caveats attached to each signal | Improved discipline for owner-group use. | Medium/high as a process control; not proof of customer value. | Retain as a control regardless of the script decision? |
| Acme export/full-account-health path | Smaller scoped replay completed; Atlas/API v2 export/full-account-health path timed out. | High confidence this is a separate technical/support issue; no Compass behavior evidence. | Exclude from Compass decision evidence; track separately. |

## 5. Account-source quality

| Account / source | Date / owner | What it supports | Gaps and caveats |
|---|---|---|---|
| Evergreen account thread / current-state packet | Apr. 25; May 5; May 12–13 / Sarah Kim | Clean, traceable current-state account evidence and bounded follow-up context. | One account only; does not establish repeatability, growth motion, or staffing logic. |
| Accounts beyond Evergreen | May 12–30 / Nadia and Sarah | Open question for repeatability review. | Comparable corroborated evidence is mixed/uneven; no denominator, consistent rubric, or negative-case set supplied. |
| Acme live-only review | May 20–21 / Sarah, Nadia, Jake | Account-specific live review using Acme’s own signals. | No Evergreen-derived written materials; Atlas/API v2 export timeout is separate technical/support context, not Compass evidence. |

**Source-quality conclusion:** Evergreen is strong for narrow current-state use. Evidence beyond that thread is insufficient to support a repeatable account pattern or broader product/GTM conclusion.

## 6. Owner-routed intake

| Intake area | Owner | Bounded next step | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Customer-thread continuity and account evidence | Sarah Kim | Maintain provenance, recency, and separation of customer statement, observed usage, support fact, procurement context, and internal interpretation. | Keep bounded. |
| Commercial / procurement framing | Devon Hayes | Classify commercial questions without turning current-state evidence into a commitment. | Owner-routed; no commitment. |
| Pattern capture across accounts | Nadia Singh | Record whether a prompt produces a named owner action; separate repeatable patterns from account-specific observations. | Repeatability unproven. |
| Product / workflow input | Jake | Keep Compass lightweight; prevent dashboard, analytics-surface, or bespoke roadmap drift. | Bounded input only. |
| Data/platform seam and event provenance | Leo Park | Validate event path and source recency before any broader exposure; do not create a separate scoring/platform layer. | Bounded input only. |

Routing volume is not evidence of product value, GTM traction, hiring need, or roadmap priority.

## 7. Cut/keep decision frame for June 4

### Candidate keep

- Renewal-risk/admin-friction and post-first-live-sync prompts only as small internal owner-group scripts.
- A named owner, specific next action, dated source, provenance, and caveat attached to every prompt.
- Source-quality discipline and separation of customer fact from internal interpretation.
- Owner-routed intake with the bounded roles above.

### Candidate cut or explicitly exclude

- Claims that Compass caused customer behavior change, adoption, expansion, revenue, or a repeatable customer-growth motion.
- Generic renewal-risk scores, generic upsell language, and prompts without a named action.
- Dashboard rebuilds, broader customer analytics surfaces, scoring services, and bespoke product/roadmap commitments.
- Unattributed, stale, single-source, or inferred account claims used as decision evidence.
- Customer-facing launch language, GTM proof, hiring-trigger language, and Series C narrative.
- The Acme Atlas/API v2 export timeout as Compass evidence; retain it only as a separate technical/support record.

### Decision criteria

The June 4 decision should explicitly record:

1. What, if anything, is being kept.
2. What is being cut or parked.
3. The named owner for any retained practice.
4. The minimum dated, source-attributable evidence required before reconsideration or expansion.
5. Confirmation that no broader product, GTM, staffing, financing, or customer-facing implication follows.

## 8. Source register

- April 25, 2025 — Compass April Prompt Trial Closeout.
- May 12, 2025 — May Board Cycle: Evidence Grid (Compass / Evergreen).
- May 13, 2025 — Spring customer-growth hiring-hold decision record.
- May 20–21, 2025 — Acme Atlas/API v2 export issue classification; separate from Compass behavior evidence.
- May 30, 2025 — Friday wrap and owner-action read.
- June 2, 2025 — Owner-fill deadline and evidence-only closeout preparation.

## 9. Explicit exclusions

- No customer-facing launch.
- No dashboard rebuild.
- No GTM proof claim.
- No staffing trigger.
- No Series C narrative.
- No claim that Evergreen alone proves repeatability.
- No claim that Acme’s export issue shows Compass-driven behavior.

**Final cut/keep decision:** **PENDING June 4, 2025 evidence read.**

# Compass June closeout — narrow evidence read

**Evidence cutoff / owner-fill date:** June 2, 2025  
**Closeout review:** June 4, 2025  
**Prepared for:** narrow internal evidence read only  
**Scope:** Compass remains an experiment and operating input—not a customer-facing launch, product/GTM proof, dashboard rebuild, hiring trigger, or Series C narrative.

## 1. Closeout decision

**Overall status:** **Inconclusive for customer behavior change; limited internal operating learning evidenced.**

**One-sentence conclusion:** Compass improved account-team preparation and follow-up questions in a small internal owner-group trial, but the evidence does not show Compass-caused customer behavior change or a repeatable expansion motion.

**Decision / disposition:** **Keep as bounded internal prompt evidence work; do not expand the surface.** Revisit only with a defined evidence question and dated, source-attributable before/after evidence.

**Rationale:**
- The April 25 review recorded better internal questions and more specific follow-up work, not customer behavior change.
- The May 12–13 evidence gate retained the same conclusion: a few account-team follow-ups, uneven account-source quality outside Sarah’s Evergreen thread, and owner-routed intake—but no basis for broader claims.
- The May 30 wrap confirmed the post-first-live-sync prompt had not produced a repeatable expansion motion; scripts remain useful only when tied to a named owner action and evidence caveats.

## 2. Behavior-change evidence

**Question:** Did Compass change owner behavior or operating practice?

| Signal / behavior | Before | After | Evidence / source | Owner | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Renewal-risk / admin-friction follow-up | No dated baseline for follow-up quality supplied. | Owners noticed specific follow-up work and asked better questions about the underlying friction. | Direct internal review record, April 25, 2025; Friday wrap, May 30, 2025. | Nadia / account owner | **Changed, limited internal learning.** Do not call this customer behavior change or a sales wedge. |
| Post-first-live-sync expansion follow-up | No repeatability baseline supplied. | Prompt was legible to internal account owners after first live sync, but did not create a repeatable expansion motion. | Direct internal review record, April 25, 2025; Friday wrap, May 30, 2025. | Nadia / Jake / Leo | **Unclear for behavior change; repeatable motion not evidenced.** |
| Customer or account behavior attributable to Compass | No customer-side before/after measure supplied. | No customer behavior change attributable to Compass established. | May Board Cycle evidence grid, May 12, 2025; Friday wrap, May 30, 2025. | Product owner / Jake as needed | **Not established.** Internal follow-up must not be relabeled as customer adoption, product proof, GTM proof, or revenue impact. |
| Enterprise-readiness intake routing | Intake risked becoming an unowned customer-growth sink; no baseline count or completion measure supplied. | Routing standard is explicit and bounded by function; completed handoffs or outcome rate were not supplied. | May Board Cycle evidence grid, May 12, 2025; May 13 hiring-hold decision record. | Sarah / Devon / Nadia / Jake / Leo | **Operating rule retained; behavior change not evidenced.** |

**Behavior-change summary:**
- **Observed change:** better internal account-team preparation, more specific follow-up questions, and clearer owner-oriented discussion.
- **No change observed:** no customer behavior change attributable to Compass; no repeatable customer-growth or expansion motion.
- **Evidence gap:** no controlled before/after measure, multi-account corroboration, or customer-side action record tied causally to a Compass prompt.

## 3. Prompt evidence by signal

Record only evidence tied to a named signal; separate observation from interpretation.

| Signal | Prompt / intervention used | Response or action observed | Source quality | Confidence | Keep / drop |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Renewal-risk / admin-friction | Owner-group prompt and Nadia script asking what concrete follow-up the signal should trigger; definitions, dates, sources, and caveats attached. | Owners identified specific follow-up work and asked better questions. Customers were not shown to act because Compass surfaced the signal. | Direct internal review; dated April 25 and May 30; account-source quality still uneven outside Evergreen. | Medium for internal prep; low for customer causality. | **Keep, narrowly:** only with named owner action, provenance, and caveat. |
| Post-first-live-sync expansion | Prompt after first live sync, with teammate-invite/admin-role state and observed usage kept distinct from inferred readiness. | Legible to internal account owners; no repeatable expansion motion. | Direct internal review; dated April 25 and May 30; no repeatable multi-account outcome supplied. | Medium for legibility; low for growth impact. | **Keep only as a bounded internal prompt; cut generic expansion/upsell framing.** |
| Evidence/caveat and source-quality guardrail | Attach definitions, evidence sources, dates, caveats, and provenance to each prompt; separate customer statement, observed usage, support fact, and internal interpretation. | Improved discipline for owner-group use; broader exposure not supported. | Direct internal review, April 25; May evidence grid, May 12; source-recency handling acceptable for owner-group use only. | Medium/high for process guardrail; not a behavior-change claim. | **Keep.** This is a control, not proof of customer value. |
| Acme renewal-risk/export path | Acme live review of Acme’s own signals only; large Atlas/API v2 export/full-account-health plus renewal-risk path timed out. | Smaller scoped replay completed; no corrupt data indicated. The timeout is a technical/support issue, not Compass-driven behavior. | Direct technical record, May 20–21; Acme remains live-only and receives no Evergreen-derived written materials. | High for issue classification; none for Compass behavior. | **Drop as Compass proof.** Keep only as a separate support/technical record. |

## 4. Account-source quality

**Question:** Is there account-source evidence beyond Sarah’s Evergreen thread?

| Account / source | Source owner | Date | Direct customer/account evidence? | What it supports | Gaps / caveats |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evergreen account thread / current-state packet | Sarah Kim | April 25; May 5; May 12–13, 2025 | Yes; clean and traceable current-state account evidence. | Annual-customer and enterprise-readiness current-state context; evidence that the account can support bounded follow-up. | One account only. Does not establish repeatable account-source quality, growth motion, or staffing logic. |
| Accounts beyond Evergreen | Nadia / Sarah | May 12–30, 2025 | Mixed/uneven; comparable corroborated evidence not supplied. | Open question for repeatability review only. | No denominator, consistent rubric, or negative-case set supplied; do not generalize beyond evidence. |
| Acme live-only review | Sarah / Nadia / Jake | May 20–21, 2025 | Acme’s own signals may be reviewed live; no written cross-account material. | Account-specific live review and boundary discipline. | Atlas/API v2 export timeout is not evidence of Compass-driven behavior; no Evergreen-derived examples or materials for Acme. |

**Source-quality conclusion:** **Mixed / insufficient for repeatability.** Evergreen is high-quality for narrow current-state use; evidence outside that thread remains uneven or account-specific. No broader product, GTM, staffing, or financing conclusion follows.

## 5. Owner-routed enterprise-readiness intake

Capture intake with a clear owner and next step; logging intake is not a product or roadmap commitment.

| Intake / request | Routed owner | Next step | Due date | Status | Evidence/source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Customer-thread continuity and account evidence | Sarah Kim | Maintain provenance, recency, and separation of customer statement, observed usage, support fact, procurement context, and internal interpretation. | Ongoing | Keep bounded | May Board Cycle evidence grid, May 12, 2025; May 13 decision record |
| Commercial / procurement framing | Devon Hayes | Classify procurement or commercial questions and preserve the boundary between current-state evidence and any future request. | Ongoing / per item | Owner-routed; no commitment | May Board Cycle evidence grid, May 12, 2025; May 13 decision record |
| Pattern capture across accounts | Nadia Singh | Record whether a prompt produces a named owner action; separate repeatable pattern from account-specific observation. | Ongoing | Owner-routed; repeatability unproven | May 13 decision record; May 30 Friday wrap |
| Product or workflow input | Jake | Keep Compass lightweight; prevent dashboard, analytics-surface, or bespoke roadmap drift. | As needed | Bounded input only | April 25 trial closeout; May 13 decision record |
| Data/platform seam and event provenance | Leo Park | Validate event path and source recency before any broader exposure; do not create a separate scoring/platform layer. | As needed | Bounded input only | April 25 trial closeout; May 13 decision record |

**Routing conclusion:** Intake is owner-routed as an operating rule, but the closeout does not contain a dated, decision-grade inventory of completed enterprise-readiness requests or outcomes. Do not convert routing volume into a product, GTM, hiring, or roadmap commitment.

## 6. Cut / keep recommendation

### Keep

- The renewal-risk/admin-friction and post-first-live-sync prompts only as small internal owner-group scripts.
- A named owner, specific next action, source provenance, date, and caveat attached to every prompt.
- Sarah’s reliable/mixed/too-thin source-quality discipline and the separation of customer fact from internal interpretation.

### Cut

- Dashboard rebuilds, broader customer analytics surfaces, scoring services, and bespoke product/roadmap commitments.
- Unattributed, stale, single-source, or inferred account claims used as decision evidence.
- Customer-facing launch language, GTM proof, hiring-trigger language, and Series C narrative.

**Recommended disposition:** **Keep the bounded internal scripts and evidence/source controls; cut expansion of the surface and park further prompt work unless a new, defined question has dated multi-account evidence.**

## 7. Explicit exclusions / claims not made

Subject: Friday dry-run — Jan. 11 Northstar readout

Devon and Anna—

Before everyone disappears for the weekend, let’s use Friday’s dry run to rehearse the talk track—not restructure the deck. The structure is locked. Please focus on clean speaker transitions and how we’ll handle likely objections.

Suggested run-through:

1. Cohort definition
- Open by stating exactly who is included, who is excluded, the time window, and why that definition is appropriate for this readout.
- Handoff: “With that cohort defined, Anna will walk through what the results do—and do not—tell us.”
- Likely objections: selection bias, sample size, comparability to the broader population, and whether the cutoff changes the conclusion.
- Keep the answer anchored to the stated scope; don’t overclaim generalizability.

2. Evergreen caveats
- Make the caveat explicit without letting it sound like the result is being withdrawn.
- Handoff: “The Evergreen caveat affects how we interpret the result, so Devon will separate the observed signal from the broader implication.”
- Likely objections: Does Evergreen invalidate the readout? Can we apply this finding elsewhere? What remains unknown?
- Distinguish clearly between what we observed, what Evergreen may explain, and what still needs validation.

3. Pricing
- Transition from evidence to decision: “Given those boundaries, here is how we’re thinking about pricing.”
- Likely objections: What is the pricing based on? How sensitive is the recommendation to the cohort or Evergreen caveat? What would cause us to change it?
- Keep the explanation tied to the readout; avoid opening a broader pricing-framework discussion unless necessary.

4. Close
- End with the decision or takeaway we want the audience to leave with, plus the specific next step.
- Handoff should make ownership clear: who answers follow-up questions and who captures open items.
- Likely objections: What are we asking Northstar to approve? What happens next? What would change our recommendation?
- Avoid reopening the deck structure or introducing new analysis in the close.

For Friday, let’s practice the handoffs verbatim, pressure-test the objections above, and note any places where the narrative needs a tighter sentence—not a new slide.

arguments.title: Mercury auth — open questions for Friday decision window
arguments.body:
# Mercury auth — open questions for Friday decision window

**Readout basis:** Thu Jun 8, 2023 — Morgan, Jake, Rishi

## Current baseline (not a decision)

- Clerk's sandbox session path worked end to end in the happy path.
- The magic-link path is also working at demo level.
- Org-invite behavior still has edge cases, especially the existing-user vs. new-user accept flow and the landing/org-context behavior after acceptance.
- SSO and admin depth remain unresolved; we do not yet have a clean answer for how much admin surface we would need to build around the provider.
- No provider call is being made from this readout. Clerk has the faster sandbox path right now, but the invite and SSO/admin questions remain open.

## Questions to answer Friday

### 1. Session path

- Does the full session lifecycle behave correctly in staging, including sign-in, refresh/expiry, logout, and return to the intended destination?
- What happens on interrupted, expired, duplicated, or otherwise invalid sessions?
- Are multi-tab and browser refresh behaviors acceptable?
- What telemetry and user-facing failure state do we have when session establishment fails?

### 2. Magic-link path

- Are link expiry, one-time use, replay, resend, and invalid-link behavior defined and verified?
- Does the flow work across devices and browsers without creating ambiguous account state?
- How are existing users and new users handled, including an already-authenticated user who opens a link?
- Are delivery, failure, and support/recovery paths clear enough for a staged release?

### 3. Organization invites

- What is the intended accept flow for an existing user versus a new user?
- After acceptance, does the user land in the correct organization context every time?
- How do we handle expired, revoked, duplicated, or already-accepted invites?
- Are membership creation, role assignment, and authorization boundaries explicit and tested?
- What should happen when the invite email does not match an existing account or the user is signed into the wrong account?

### 4. SSO and admin surface

- Which SSO capabilities are required for the near-term product, and which can be deferred?
- What admin controls do we need to build around the provider rather than receive from it?
- Are domain management, role/group mapping, provisioning/deprovisioning, auditability, and recovery requirements known?
- What is the minimum acceptable depth for the first release, and what would remain on the follow-up path?

### 5. Provider baseline

- Is the faster Clerk sandbox path enough to justify proceeding, given the unresolved invite and SSO/admin work?
- What evidence is required before choosing a provider baseline?
- If the open questions remain unresolved, what is the explicit decision rule: defer the provider call, run a focused spike, or proceed with documented risk?

**Status:** Leave the provider baseline unsettled. This note is for closing the questions, not recording a provider selection.

### 6. Deploy and prod posture

- What exactly must pass in staging before any production discussion?
- What signoff is required, and who owns each remaining gap?
- What rollback, monitoring, and support readiness are required if the staging pass is successful?
- If staging exposes a gap, what is the stop/defer rule?

**Status:** Leave deploy/prod unsettled. No production conversation should proceed until the required staging pass is clean.

## Staging-discipline checks

- Use the standard staging pipeline only. No shortcut path, direct production change, or staging bypass.
- Run the session path, magic-link path, and org-invite matrix in staging—not only in the sandbox/demo environment.
- Include both existing-user and new-user invite acceptance, correct org context after acceptance, and negative/expired/replayed cases.
- Record test results, known failures, owners, and explicit signoff before discussing production.
- Confirm that logs/telemetry are sufficient to diagnose auth failures without exposing sensitive tokens or link contents.
- Confirm rollback and recovery procedures are documented and exercised at the appropriate staging level.
- Treat any temptation to shortcut staging as a release-process blocker, not as an acceptable exception.

## Friday decision-window output

By the end of the window, capture:

1. Answers and evidence for each open question.
2. Remaining risks and the owner/date for each one.
3. The minimum staging acceptance bar.
4. A separate, explicit disposition for the provider baseline.
5. A separate, explicit disposition for deploy/prod readiness.

Until those are recorded, auth remains in investigation: demo-level paths are encouraging, but not a staging or production readiness signal.

arguments.body:
# Friday May 10 customer-growth read

## Caveat page: proof versus pressure

Use this page as a caveat to Nadia’s taxonomy, not as the center of the meeting. The examples below help distinguish reusable current-product truth from customer heat, procurement vocabulary, pricing/package concern, or roadmap gravity. None of the Acme or Pinecone examples is Mercury activation proof.

### Working distinction

- **Proof** = a repeatable interpretation or adoption problem we can state in current-product truth.
- **Pressure** = customer heat, procurement vocabulary, pricing/package concern, or roadmap gravity that feels important but is not yet reusable proof.

| Example | What it is evidence of | Useful internal use | What it is not evidence of | Current lane | Guardrail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Evergreen admin-control clarity** | Buyer-readiness friction around wording, visible state, and role clarity inside the current Mercury flow | Valid repeated signal for the Friday read, especially alongside visible-state/admin-role examples | Enterprise-readiness proof; launch proof; SSO timing; audit-history capability; admin-model commitment | Sarah live-thread continuity + existing product-truth lane; Devon only for caveat | Keep present-state wording. Do not let a wording example become a capability claim. |
| **Acme visible-number trust** | Finance-confidence context from a live NDA-constrained thread | Narrow contrast row only if the read needs a non-Evergreen example | Mercury activation proof; generalized expansion pattern; safe external example | Devon/Sarah caveat lane under the active NDA boundary | Do not externalize. Do not let it read like cross-customer proof. No new Acme materials. |
| **Pinecone retry semantics** | Support/process clarity on the current API v2 path and retry explanation lane | Useful only if the read needs one support/process comparison row | Enterprise-readiness proof; broader connector-market story; reason to reopen docs scope | Support + current product-facts lane | Keep it on the current path only. No broader connector narrative. |

### Pricing/package caveat

If a row starts sounding like pricing architecture, procurement sequencing, or package design, stop and annotate rather than upgrade it. That caveat stays in Devon’s lane even when the underlying customer signal is useful.

### Practical test for Friday

- If the point can be stated in current-product truth and survives a caveat, it is closer to proof.
- If the point becomes interesting only once we imply a date, promise, or package story, it is pressure and should stay marked that way.

### Meeting-use note

Keep the main read centered on current-product truth and repeatable adoption or interpretation problems. Use this page only to prevent over-reading the examples: Acme is NDA-constrained context, Pinecone is a current API v2 support/process comparison, and neither should be presented as evidence of Mercury activation.

Review: the structure is strong and the lifecycle boundaries are mostly clear. The main risk is that “customer-growth” becomes the default owner because every bucket is framed as a signal. I’d make the taxonomy explicitly separate:

- Signal synthesizer: customer-growth
- Account-specific responder: support, account owner, or procurement/security
- Product decision owner: product/engineering
- Evidence contributor: whoever observed the issue

I would not leave the owner-route cells blank for Friday. Fill them with functional routes, even if named owners are decided live.

Proposed owner routes

| Bucket | Primary route | Supporting route | Customer-growth role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Activation friction | Activation/onboarding owner | Support for live account reply; product/engineering for repeated setup failures | Aggregate patterns; do not own remediation |
| Admin handoff and role confusion | Support for account-specific interpretation | Product/UX for copy or visible-state confusion; engineering only for confirmed backend permission defects | Identify recurring confusion |
| Procurement/security packaging | Account/commercial owner or procurement/security enablement | Product for current-capability validation; legal/security as needed | Track buyer friction, not buyer response |
| Expansion stalls after first live sync | Account owner/customer-success or implementation owner | Product only when a repeated capability barrier is evidenced | Surface cross-account patterns |
| True product gaps | Product owner | Engineering for feasibility; support/account teams for evidence | Escalate and quantify, not own the product fix |

Suggested clarifications

1. Rename the admin bucket

“Admin handoff and role confusion” does not fully cover stale counts and visible admin state. Consider:

“Admin role and state clarity”

That better includes:
- authority and role interpretation
- resend/remove behavior
- source/workspace wording
- stale or misleading visible state

2. Tighten the activation rule

The current definition could be read ambiguously. Since either event qualifies as activation, use wording such as:

“Activation friction applies when neither `real_source_connected` nor `first_live_sync_completed` occurs within seven days of the relevant setup signal.”

Also specify what happens when:
- source connection occurs on day 3 but first sync occurs on day 10
- first sync occurs but the source connection event is missing
- instrumentation is incomplete

Those should be marked as instrumentation caveats, not automatically treated as customer friction.

3. Define the expansion observation window

“Do not broaden” and “no second admin motion” need a fixed observation period. Pick one before Friday—for example, 14 or 30 days after first live sync—and apply it consistently. Otherwise normal adoption timing may be mislabeled as an expansion stall.

4. Separate packaging from product gaps by remediation

A useful test:

- If better wording, a support explanation, configuration guidance, or a procurement artifact could resolve it, keep it in Procurement/security packaging or Admin role and state clarity.
- If the current product cannot perform the required capability after the explanation and workaround are tested, it may become a True product gap.
- A request for a future date, roadmap commitment, or account-specific exception remains out of band, even if commercially important.

The “SSO timing question” example should be rewritten. A timing question alone is a roadmap/date request. A better example would be:

“Current SSO configuration or availability wording causes a security review because the supported boundary is unclear.”

5. Strengthen the true-product-gap gate

“More than one clean example” is not enough on its own. I recommend requiring all of the following:

- At least two independent accounts, or one independently reproduced high-severity case
- A clear current-product behavior, not an inferred expectation
- Copy, training, config…

results.snippet: ...For Atlas, we’ll stay focused on API v2, >>>authentication<<<, >>>webhook<<< reliability, clear support contracts, and documentation that prevents repeat support issues. Support closures are inputs to reliability work, but they are not a hidden roadmap or an automatic commitment...

messages.content: [2026-06-30T11:18:00-07:00] Jake and Leo asked how I want to open the Q3 planning session for the Mercury and Atlas owner lanes. Jake is worried the team will hear `activation` and over-optimize for top-line workspace-created numbers. Leo is worried Atlas support closures will get treated like a hidden reliability roadmap. I want a short opening agenda and prompts that keep both teams in their lanes: Mercury should focus on setup/support-quality friction around workspace creation, first source, first live sync, teammate invitations, admin roles, and supported-source docs; Atlas should focus on API v2/auth/webhook owner-lane reliability, clear support contracts, and docs that reduce repeat support. Compass can consume internal owner-action evidence, but this is not a customer-facing Compass push or staffing justification. Draft something I can use to open the session.

Q3 Planning Opening

“Let’s use this session to clarify owner lanes and remove repeat friction—not to maximize a single activation number.

For Mercury, we’ll look at setup and support-quality friction across the path from workspace creation to first value: first source, first live sync, teammate invitations, admin roles, and supported-source documentation. Workspace creation is an entry point, not the outcome. We should leave with specific owner actions and evidence about where customers get stuck.

For Atlas, we’ll stay focused on API v2, authentication, webhook reliability, clear support contracts, and documentation that prevents repeat support issues. Support closures are inputs to reliability work, but they are not a hidden roadmap or an automatic commitment to build every requested fix.

Compass may consume dated internal owner-action evidence where useful. This is not a customer-facing Compass push, and it should not be used as staffing or headcount justification.

Let’s organize the discussion around four questions:
1. What customer or internal friction are we addressing?
2. What is explicitly in the Mercury or Atlas owner lane?
3. What evidence would show that the issue improved?
4. What is out of scope—including top-line activation optimization, uncommitted reliability work, customer-facing Compass positioning, or staffing conclusions?

We’ll close with named owners, next actions, evidence sources and dates, caveats, and a clear status for each item.”

Prompts for the discussion

Mercury
- Where does setup or support friction occur after workspace creation?
- Which issues delay first source, first live sync, teammate invitations, or admin-role setup?
- Which supported-source docs could prevent repeat tickets?
- What metric or dated owner follow-up would demonstrate improvement without reducing the goal to workspace-created volume?
- What is a support-quality or setup issue versus a broader product request?

Atlas
- Which API v2, auth, or webhook issues are recurring and actionable within the current owner lane?
- Which support closures indicate a reliability pattern, and which are isolated cases or customer configuration issues?
- What support contract should be made clearer?
- Which documentation changes would reduce repeat support without implying a roadmap commitment?
- What evidence is strong enough to prioritize work, and what remains a caveated signal?

Close
- What is the one owner-action each team will take in Q3?
- What evidence will be recorded—type, account or owner, source/date, caveat, action/status, and outcome?
- What should Compass consume internally, and what must not be presented externally?
- What conclusions are we explicitly not drawing about staffing, roadmap commitments, or customer-facing positioning?

arguments.body:
# May 13, 2025 — Spring customer-growth hiring hold decision record

## Final decision

The review is complete. Keep the spring customer-growth hiring hold in place through the rest of Q2, through June 30, 2025. Sofia is aligned with this decision.

This supersedes the prior **PENDING REVIEW** status in the May review materials. It is a hold, not an invitation to preserve hiring optionality or begin preparatory recruiting motion.

## Evidence basis

- **Compass:** generated a few account-team follow-ups and better internal questions, but no customer behavior change. This remains limited internal learning, not product proof, GTM proof, or a hiring trigger.
- **Evergreen:** clean, validated single-account customer/enterprise proof. It is not repeatable growth proof by itself and does not justify staffing on its own.
- **Account-source quality:** strongest in Sarah Kim’s Evergreen thread; uneven outside that thread. No broader repeatability claim is authorized.
- **Enterprise-readiness intake:** remains owner-routed and bounded—Sarah for customer-thread continuity, Devon for commercial/procurement framing, Nadia for pattern capture, and Jake/Leo for product and seam input as needed.

## Staffing guardrail through Q2

Keep the following closed through June 30, 2025:

- RevOps
- CS
- SDR
- Field sales
- Customer-growth support
- Second Mercury engineering requisition

Do not open requisitions, sourcing, placeholders, or preparatory hiring language during the hold.

Nadia Singh’s weekly cadence and Sarah Kim’s account-note hygiene remain the complete spring support plan.

## Next decision boundary

Revisit in the July 2025 / Q3 planning review. A staffing change requires, at minimum:

1. Corroborated customer behavior change across multiple customers.
2. Repeatable account-source quality beyond Evergreen Bank.
3. Owner-routed enterprise-readiness intake with clear ownership.
4. An explicit staffing decision and approval path.

## Artifact update instruction

The headcount plan and May 2025 Board Review evidence-gate slide should state the final Q2 hold directly. Do not retain “pending review” language or soften the decision into an implied future hiring option.

messages.content:
[2024-10-18T10:24:00-07:00] Can you review HR’s October all-hands run-of-show and suggest tighter edits for my opener? I’m mostly worried the “enterprise push” wording makes the company focus sound broader than it is. Keep the language tied to current shipped facts and Q4 boundaries, not a bigger enterprise story.

October All-Hands — HR Draft Run of Show
Draft status: sent for Morgan review
Prepared by: HR
Audience: full company

Purpose
- Keep the company update short and factual.
- Reinforce Q4 focus and current decision boundaries.
- Use pre-collected questions only; no open-mic segment.
- Keep product and commercial language aligned with what has actually shipped.

Working theme
- What is more real now, what remains intentionally bounded, and what we are watching in Q4.

Meeting shape
- Total planned length: 34 minutes
- Format: short company update + pre-collected questions
- Live answers only on approved current topics
- Remaining questions routed async or to named owners after the meeting

Run of show

0:00–0:01
Owner: HR
Slide: title slide
Notes:
- Welcome everyone.
- Quick reminder that the meeting is recorded for teammates who cannot attend live.
- Hand off directly to Morgan.

0:01–0:07
Owner: Morgan Chen
Slide: Where we are now
Segment: six-minute opener
Speaker draft:

Thanks, everyone. I want to keep this one pretty direct.

A lot of the work we have been doing over the last few months is now showing up in a way that is more concrete and easier to talk about honestly. That is good for us internally, and it is good for the company because it lets us operate off evidence instead of momentum theater.

First, on product and release reality: we shipped the first Mercury enterprise-readiness slice into production for scoped enterprise accounts. The shipped pieces are specific: SAML SSO, admin-side audit-history events for invite, source, and admin changes, and clearer separation between admin and billing-owner responsibilities. That matters because those were real gaps for a set of larger customers, and now they are real capabilities we can point to without stretching the story.

Second, on platform and customer trust: Atlas support and release handling are on a steadier path. Customer-facing Atlas issues now route through the support rotation, Leo takes the first technical read, and Jake continues to own product priority and sequencing. That split is not glamorous, but it is important. It means customer issues are getting a cleaner technical read, product tradeoffs are staying with the right owner, and we are not pretending a process gap is solved by everyone swarming it.

Third, on the market side: our enterprise push is producing better conversations, but I want to be careful about what that does and does not mean. It means larger accounts are taking Scaffold more seriously when they look at setup, admin expectations, and reliability questions. It does not mean we suddenly have a broad enterprise machine, and it does not mean every larger-customer request should bend roadmap gravity.

That distinction matters a lot right now. The board discussion last month was constructive precisely because the facts are more real now, not because we told a bigger story. The line remains the same: more room, same discipline. Defensible story, not a bigger story.

So for Q4, our watchlist is still the same three things. One is Evergreen paid-pilot adoption. Two is renewal and expansion evidence. Three is Nadia’s account-source quality: are the stronger enterprise conversations coming from a repeatable lane, or are they still too dependent on one-off situations and bespoke pull. Those are the signals that matter. They are the board-facing signals, and they are the right internal signals too.

That also means some things are intentionally not changing yet. We are not building a broad field-sales motion right now. We are not opening a separate RevOps or CS lane right now. We are not reopening a second Mercury engineering req right now…

The opener is strong on discipline, but “our enterprise push is producing better conversations” is the main phrase I would change. It sounds like a broad GTM strategy is already underway, while the rest of the draft says the company is still testing whether the motion is repeatable.

I’d also tighten a few adjacent phrases:

- “enterprise-readiness slice” → “a limited set of Mercury capabilities for scoped enterprise accounts”
- “larger accounts are taking Scaffold more seriously” → “we are seeing stronger questions and interest from larger accounts”
- “more room, same discipline” → keep; it is a good boundary-setting line
- “major release path” → “a release path focused on setup and activation”
- Consider cutting or shortening the board reference. It adds context but slightly pulls the opener toward investor narrative rather than company operating guidance.

Suggested revised opener:

Thanks, everyone. I want to keep this one direct.

Some of the work from the last few months is now concrete enough to evaluate against facts rather than expectations. That is useful progress, but it does not change our Q4 boundaries.

First, on product and release reality: we shipped a limited set of Mercury capabilities for scoped enterprise accounts on the normal release path. The shipped pieces are specific: SAML SSO, admin-side audit-history events for invite, source, and admin changes, and clearer separation between admin and billing-owner responsibilities. These addressed real gaps for a defined set of customers. They are capabilities we can point to plainly, without expanding the claim beyond what shipped.

Second, on platform and customer trust: Atlas support and release handling are on a steadier path. Customer-facing Atlas issues now route through the support rotation, Leo takes the first technical read, and Jake continues to own product priority and sequencing. That split matters because technical triage and product tradeoffs now have clearer ownership. We are improving the process without treating every issue as a roadmap negotiation.

Third, on the market side: we are seeing stronger interest and better questions from larger accounts, particularly around setup, administration, and reliability. That is useful evidence. It is not evidence that we have built a broad enterprise motion, and it does not mean every larger-customer request should change the roadmap.

Our Q4 focus is disciplined follow-through, not a broader company story. The watchlist remains three things: Evergreen paid-pilot adoption; renewal and expansion evidence; and Nadia’s account-source quality—whether stronger account conversations are coming from a repeatable lane or still from one-off situations and bespoke pull.

That means some things are intentionally not changing yet. We are not building a broad field-sales motion. We are not opening a separate RevOps or CS lane. We are not reopening a second Mercury engineering req. Those decisions can change if the evidence shows repeatable adoption, renewal or expansion, and a reliable source of accounts—not because one account is loud or one meeting feels promising.

The same discipline applies to how we describe Mercury. Mercury is a release path focused on customer setup and activation on the Scaffold platform. The shipped capability set is real, but it does not make Mercury fully enterprise-ready. Advanced admin controls are not done. Procurement packaging remains a separate workstream. We should keep those distinctions intact even when narrower wording feels less exciting.

What I want from the company is straightforward: keep claims tied to shipped facts, keep customer commitments specific, and escalate when a request starts turning into bespoke roadmap pressure. Keep paying attention to the basics that make the progress credible: setup clarity, sync trust, release discipline, support responsiveness, and evidence that customers are adopting, renewing, and expanding.

We have more concrete evidence than we did earli…

messages.content: [2026-02-05T08:18:00-08:00] Priya and Jake have the staging copy/config diff ready for the Mercury empty source-list work. QA is seeing three distinct states: canceled authorization returns to an empty source list with the title `No connected sources yet` and the body `Authorization was canceled before Scaffold connected a source. No data was synced. Choose a source to continue setup.`; a provider that drops connector context after OAuth uses the same title with `We couldn't preserve the provider context. Choose a source to continue setup.`; and a brand-new workspace with no source uses `Connect your first source to start syncing.` Support wants a rollout checklist before this gets wider exposure. Give me a compact rollout checklist and acceptance criteria for those three states, with the out-of-scope line explicit: this stays activation-quality explanation and does not reopen invite-link status, admin roles, granular roles, or activation-metric claims.

Mercury empty source-list rollout checklist

1. Staging verification
   - Confirm the copy/config diff is deployed to staging.
   - Exercise all three entry paths:
     - Canceled authorization
     - OAuth provider context lost
     - Brand-new workspace with no source
   - Verify the empty source list, title, body, and source-selection action.

2. QA regression
   - Confirm canceled authorization does not imply a source was connected or data synced.
   - Confirm provider-context loss is distinguishable from cancellation.
   - Confirm a genuinely new workspace does not show an error or recovery message.
   - Verify refresh, retry, and return-to-setup behavior.

3. Support readiness
   - Add the three states and expected customer guidance to the support runbook.
   - Include escalation guidance for incorrect state classification or unexpected synced data.

4. Controlled rollout
   - Release behind the existing rollout control/configuration.
   - Start with a limited exposure group and review QA/support signals before widening.
   - Keep the prior copy/config available for rollback.

5. Scope check
   - Confirm this release changes only empty-source-list explanation and related copy/config.
   - Confirm no invite-link, role, permission, or activation-metric behavior changed.

Acceptance criteria

1. Canceled authorization
   - Empty source list displays:
     - Title: `No connected sources yet`
     - Body: `Authorization was canceled before Scaffold connected a source. No data was synced. Choose a source to continue setup.`
   - The state appears only when authorization was canceled before a source connected.
   - No source or synced-data success state is shown.

2. Provider context lost after OAuth
   - Empty source list displays:
     - Title: `No connected sources yet`
     - Body: `We couldn't preserve the provider context. Choose a source to continue setup.`
   - The state appears when OAuth completes or returns but connector/provider context is unavailable.
   - The user can choose a source and continue setup without an incorrect provider-specific claim.

3. Brand-new workspace
   - Empty source list displays:
     - `Connect your first source to start syncing.`
   - No cancellation or provider-context-loss explanation is shown.
   - The source-selection action starts normal first-source setup.

4. Common behavior
   - All three states render correctly on staging-supported viewport/device combinations.
   - Copy is stable across refresh and normal navigation.
   - The source-selection action is available and functional in each state.
   - No invite-link status, admin-role, granular-role, or activation-metric claims are added or changed.

Out of scope: This remains an activation-quality explanation and does not reopen invite-link status, admin roles, granular roles, or activation-metric claims.

messages.content:
Director-ready answer:

“We should warm the Series C market in April—but as a durability test, not as a signal that the case is fully proven.

The current evidence clears the bar for quiet, relationship-building conversations: Evergreen renewed on standard Growth, Acme is back on the normal support path, February margin is clean, and Mercury’s activation friction appears to be improving.

What is still missing is evidence that these are repeatable operating conditions rather than three favorable point-in-time events:

- Evergreen: finance validation of the February usage/margin row and confirmation that the margin holds without one-off concessions or accounting effects.
- Acme: a demonstrated normal-support period through the API v2 path, without escalation or exceptional founder routing.
- Mercury: completed retention-funnel data showing that lower activation friction produces durable activation and retained usage across a meaningful cohort—not just improved onboarding activity.
- Company-wide: enough consecutive evidence to support a credible forward forecast, rather than a backward-looking recovery narrative.

So the April move would be to warm a small set of high-quality investors, test whether the story resonates, and learn what diligence they would require—without launching a formal process or pricing the company around these improvements yet. arguments.title: Board review evidence grid — 2025-06-24
arguments.body:
# Board review evidence grid

Date: 2025-06-24
Purpose: one working grid for the next board review. Keep the operating story restrained: distinguish observed evidence, interpretation, and open proof; do not turn one-off wins into repeatable growth claims.

## Executive operating story

- Lead with retention, renewals, and improving operating reliability.
- Mercury is a credible Growth pilot / win, not yet proof of repeatable growth.
- Atlas is a reliable operating workstream; the Acme timeout belongs in the support/Atlas reliability lane, not as a broad product or market signal.
- Compass stays internal-only. Present the narrowed learning and what we changed, not a GTM success story.
- Do not introduce a Series C narrative or create an investor-coffee loop from this review.

## Evidence grid

| Board topic | Observed evidence / input | What it supports | What it does not support | Confidence / gap | Owner / next proof |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Retention and renewals | Retention and renewals are the intended Q2/board anchor; customer/account continuity is being kept close to the customer thread. | We are prioritizing durable customer value and renewal execution. | It does not establish a generalized retention trend without cohort, renewal, and timing data. | Directionally supported; quantitative cohort and renewal schedule still required. | Sarah: reconcile customer-thread/account hygiene and continuity. Anna: validate evidence quality. |
| Mercury | Growth pilot pricing: $7,500/month for up to 200 active developers, then $1,000 per additional 50; SAML and admin audit included; no bespoke roadmap. | A concrete, bounded Growth offer with clear packaging and enterprise controls. | One Growth win is not repeatable growth proof; no bespoke roadmap should be implied. | Supported for offer design; need active-developer usage, adoption, renewal/expansion, and margin evidence. | Sarah: customer continuity / renewal evidence. Jake: sequencing implications. |
| Evergreen | Evergreen is one Growth win. | There is at least one credible Growth outcome to discuss. | It is not evidence of a repeatable Growth motion or forecastable pipeline. | Supported as a single case; need comparison set and repeatability evidence. | Anna: separate case evidence from broader claim. Sarah: confirm account status and customer language. |
| Atlas reliability | Atlas remains a reliable operating workstream. | We can speak to dependable execution and platform/support progress. | Avoid claiming all customer-impacting reliability questions are closed. | Directionally supported; bring incident, support, latency, and resolution evidence if available. | Leo: technical read on platform seams. Sarah: customer-impact check. |
| Acme timeout | The Acme timeout is categorized as Atlas/support. | Shows a bounded reliability/support issue with an accountable operating lane. | Does not justify a broad product failure, market weakness, or retention conclusion on its own. | Event-level evidence; need timeline, impact, root cause, and prevention/follow-up status. | Leo: technical read and prevention. Sarah: account impact and continuity. |
| Compass | Compass stays internal-only; the useful result is narrowed learning. | We learned enough to narrow the work and avoid overextending the thesis. | Do not present Compass as a GTM proof point, behavior-change proof, or external growth narrative. | Supported as an operating decision; need concise evidence for what was tested and what was ruled out. | Jake: sequencing / stop-or-narrow decision. Anna: evidence quality and wording. |
| Operating focus | Current Q2/board framing: retention, renewals, narrowed Compass learning, reliable Mercury/Atlas. | A restrained narrative centered on execution and learning. | No Series C narrative; no investor-coffee loop this week. | High confidence as framing; supporting metrics need final reconciliation. | Morgan: board/customer narrative. All owners: close only material gaps. |

## Board-safe draft language

“Q2 is about durable execution rather than broad claims: protecting retention and renewals, converting a bounded Mercury Growth pilot into evidence we can learn from, keeping Atlas reliable, and narrowing Compass based on what the evidence supports. Evergreen is a positive Growth case, but we are not treating one win as a repeatable motion. The Acme timeout is being handled as a bounded Atlas/support issue with follow-through on customer impact and prevention.”

## Do not say yet

- “We have repeatable Growth” based on Mercury or Evergreen alone.
- “Compass proved the market” or “Compass proved behavior change.”
- “The Acme timeout shows a broad product or market problem.”
- “We are building a Series C narrative.”
- Any retention, renewal, adoption, or reliability percentage until the underlying cohort/event evidence is reconciled.

## Pre-review closeout checklist

1. Anna: mark each row as sourced, corroborated, or still directional; remove unsupported adjectives.
2. Sarah: reconcile account status, renewal timing, customer impact, and continuity for Mercury, Evergreen, and Acme.
3. Jake: confirm the sequencing / narrowing decisions and the next operating checkpoint; do not start a replacement-search loop.
4. Leo: provide the concise technical read for Atlas seams and the Acme timeout, including prevention status.
5. Morgan: use the draft language above as the narrative spine; add numbers only after the owners close the evidence gaps.

Hi Evergreen team,

Ahead of our July 16 current-state/admin review, we’d like to focus the discussion on how the shipped product is working for your administrators today.

Proposed discussion:

- SAML login: confirm the current sign-in experience and any questions about using the shipped configuration.
- Invite and source visibility: review where administrators can see invitations and source-related activity.
- Admin audit lookup: walk through the available audit information and how to locate relevant activity.
- Workspace-admin support: discuss the current administrator workflow and any questions about using workspace-admin support.
- Standard Growth usage: confirm that final June usage is the reference point for standard Growth usage mechanics.
- Current-state admin controls: answer questions about the controls and workflows available today, and capture any areas where the existing experience needs clarification.

The goal is to make sure your team has a clear understanding of the current admin experience and standard Growth usage. We’ll keep the session focused on shipped functionality and current-state questions.

Best,
Sarah
