- Company-wide: enough consecutive evidence to support a credible forward forecast, rather than a backward-looking...

bookend_start.content: [2026-03-27T07:42:00-07:00] Director comment: “If Evergreen renewed on standard Growth, Acme is back in normal support, February margin is clean, and Mercury activation friction is down, why are we not at least warming the Series C market in April? What evidence is missing?” Sofia's note: “Answer as a durability test, not a defensive no.”

arguments.query: Evergreen Acme February margin Mercury activation Series C durability evidence missing April

messages.content:
Director-ready answer:

“We should warm the Series C market in April—but as a durability test, not as a signal that the case is fully proven.

The current evidence clears the bar for quiet, relationship-building conversations: Evergreen renewed on standard Growth, Acme is back on the normal support path, February margin is clean, and Mercury’s activation friction appears to be improving.

What is still missing is evidence that these are repeatable operating conditions rather than three favorable point-in-time events:

- Evergreen: finance validation of the February usage/margin row and confirmation that the margin holds without one-off concessions or accounting effects.
- Acme: a demonstrated normal-support period through the API v2 path, without escalation or exceptional founder routing.
- Mercury: completed retention-funnel data showing that lower activation friction produces durable activation and retained usage across a meaningful cohort—not just improved onboarding activity.
- Company-wide: enough consecutive evidence to support a credible forward forecast, rather than a backward-looking recovery narrative.

So the April move would be to warm a small set of high-quality investors, test whether the story resonates, and learn what diligence they would require—without launching a formal process or pricing the company around these improvements yet. If the next evidence shows repeatability across customers, cohorts, and months, we can convert that warming into a real Series C process. Guardrail:
- Record the failure mode, source, date, and owner.

- 0–5: Set the redline: evidence tests, no implied commitments, no unsupported conclusions.

[2026-08-13T11:30:00-07:00] Problem clause:

`Provider will, upon Customer request, configure tenant-specific retention and deletion controls for admin event logs, including deletion within twenty-four (24) hours of Customer instruction. Provider will support Customer-specific role and department mappings for workspace administration, including connector workarounds required by Customer's identity model. Provider will deliver any missing admin-event controls and related role-mapping features no later than Q4 2026 and will provide Customer with monthly roadmap status until delivery.`

This clause is problematic because it creates several bespoke, unconditional obligations:

- A guaranteed 24-hour deletion SLA for admin-event logs, potentially including backups, replicas, legal holds, and security records.
- Custom tenant-specific retention/deletion functionality on request.
- Customer-specific role and department mappings.
- An obligation to build connector workarounds for the customer’s identity model.
- A binding Q4 2026 product-development deadline.
- Mandatory monthly roadmap reporting until delivery.

Suggested replacement:

“Provider will make available any standard retention, deletion, role-mapping, and workspace-administration controls included in the Services and applicable to Customer’s subscription. Customer is responsible for configuring and maintaining its identity provider, role assignments, department mappings, permissions, and supported connectors.

Provider may, at its discretion, consider requests for additional administrative controls or identity-related functionality through its standard product-feedback and support processes. Any such request is subject to technical feasibility, applicable product limitations, security requirements, legal holds, backup and disaster-recovery processes, and Provider’s then-current policies. Provider does not guarantee development, delivery, availability, or timing of any requested feature, connector workaround, or roadmap item.

Provider’s support obligations are limited to addressing reproducible defects in shipped and supported SSO or platform functionality under the applicable support terms. They do not include configuring unsupported identity models, changing Customer’s permissions or source systems, developing customer-specific connector workarounds, or providing bespoke roadmap reporting. Nothing in this section modifies the Agreement’s standard service levels or requires Provider to provide functionality not included in the Services.”

If a deletion commitment is commercially necessary, it should be limited to “active production systems,” exclude backups and legally required records, and be tied to a documented, supported control rather than a general 24-hour obligation.

messages.content: [2026-08-05T10:42:00-07:00] Legal forwarded a customer security addendum that sales wants to turn this week. I am comfortable confirming shipped product behavior, documented connector behavior, ordinary platform-defect support, and normal account and product feedback capture. The problem is one clause that would make us commit to customer-configurable log retention and deletion, a 90-day roadmap delivery window for missing admin-event controls, and standard-support custom connector workarounds for the customer's identity model. I want cooperative redline language that preserves current product and documented support, but rejects the roadmap SLA, customer-specific retention and deletion configuration, custom connector workaround, and any commitment to absorb future identity or admin model changes.

Proposed cooperative replacement language:

“Provider will support the Services in accordance with the applicable Documentation and the Agreement. Provider may confirm the operation of features that are generally available and the behavior of documented connectors as described in the Documentation. Provider will provide its standard support for reproducible defects in the generally available Services and will reasonably receive and evaluate Customer’s ordinary account, product, and feature feedback through its normal support and product-feedback processes.

For clarity, Provider does not commit under this Addendum to:

(a) provide customer-configurable log-retention or log-deletion settings, or retain or delete logs for a period or in a manner different from the controls and retention practices generally available for the Services;

(b) deliver any feature, enhancement, administrative event control, or other product capability by a specified date or within a specified period, including any ninety (90)-day delivery window;

(c) develop, maintain, or provide a customer-specific connector, connector modification, integration, workaround, or other customization to accommodate Customer’s identity, authorization, provisioning, administrative, or other environment-specific model; or

(d) modify the Services, support processes, or Documentation, or absorb costs, to address future changes to Customer’s identity, access-control, administrative, regulatory, or related model.

Any request for a feature, enhancement, connector capability, or change to the Services will be handled through Provider’s standard product-feedback, support, and roadmap processes, with no obligation to implement the request or to do so by a particular date. Nothing in this Addendum limits Provider’s obligation to provide the generally available Services and standard support expressly described in the Agreement and applicable Documentation.”

If you want a shorter redline-style version targeted specifically at the problematic clause:

“Provider will provide [commercially reasonable assistance with the generally available Services, documented connector behavior, reproducible platform defects, and Customer’s ordinary account and product feedback through Provider’s standard support and product-feedback processes]. Provider will not be required to provide customer-specific log-retention or log-deletion configuration, deliver missing administrative-event controls or other roadmap items within ninety (90) days or any other specified period, develop or maintain custom connector workarounds for Customer’s identity model, or modify or support the Services to accommodate future changes to Customer’s identity, authorization, provisioning, or administrative model. Any such request will be subject to Provider’s standard support and product-roadmap processes and will not constitute a commitment to implement the request or to do so by a specified date. [Provider’s obligations remain limited to the generally available functionality and documented support expressly provided under the Agreement and applicable Documentation.]”

Suggested cover note to Sales/Legal:

“We narrowed the language to confirm what we can support today—shipped functionality, documented connector behavior, reproducible platform defects, and normal feedback capture—while avoiding commitments that would create a roadmap delivery SLA, customer-specific retention/deletion controls, custom connector work, or an obligation to absorb future identity and administrative-model changes. This should preserve a cooperative posture without expanding the Agreement or Support scope.”

messages.content: [2026-07-22T12:40:00-07:00] Legal just forwarded a customer security addendum that sales wants to accept by end of day. I'm fine reaffirming shipped SSO, documented connector behavior, normal support for platform defects, and normal account/product feedback capture, but I am not taking a roadmap SLA, customer-specific retention or deletion configuration, a custom connector workaround, or a commitment to absorb future identity or admin-model changes. Redline this into language we can accept without making the answer sound evasive.

Below is a customer-facing replacement that preserves the commitments you’re comfortable making without sounding evasive.

Proposed redline / replacement language

“Provider will:

1. Maintain and support the generally available SSO functionality described in the applicable product documentation, including addressing reproducible defects in shipped SSO functionality in accordance with Provider’s standard support terms.

2. Support the documented behavior of Provider’s generally available connectors. Provider will address reproducible defects in supported, shipped connector functionality in accordance with its standard support terms. Connector behavior may change where reasonably necessary to reflect changes to the relevant third-party service, security requirements, or supported product architecture.

3. Provide standard support for reproducible defects in the Provider platform in accordance with Provider’s standard support terms.

4. Receive and evaluate account and product feedback through Provider’s normal feedback and product-management processes. Feedback may inform future product decisions but does not create an obligation to implement the requested functionality or provide a particular roadmap, delivery date, or service level.

5. Process customer data in accordance with the applicable agreement, data-processing terms, and Provider’s generally available product functionality and documentation. Any retention or deletion request will be handled through those existing terms and generally available controls; Provider is not obligated to create or maintain customer-specific retention or deletion configurations.

6. Support the generally available identity, access, and administrative functionality documented for the applicable product. Customer remains responsible for configuring its users, permissions, identity provider, and administrative settings. Provider is not obligated to modify its product or provide a workaround to accommodate changes to Customer’s identity provider, permissions, source systems, or administrative model that are not supported by the generally available product.

For clarity, this Addendum does not create: (a) a roadmap commitment, feature-delivery deadline, or customer-specific service level; (b) an obligation to develop a custom connector or workaround; (c) an obligation to provide customer-specific retention or deletion functionality; or (d) an obligation to absorb, implement, or remediate future changes to Customer’s identity, permissions, source systems, or administrative model beyond Provider’s standard support for shipped, supported functionality.”

If the addendum uses a broad “commercially reasonable efforts” or “will support” obligation, I’d replace it with this narrower formulation:

“Provider’s obligations under this section are limited to standard support for reproducible defects in shipped, generally available, and supported functionality, together with Provider’s normal process for receiving and evaluating account and product feedback. Nothing in this section requires Provider to provide roadmap commitments, custom development, customer-specific configuration, or remediation of unsupported changes to Customer-controlled identity, permission, connector, source-system, retention, deletion, or administrative requirements.”

I would not accept language requiring Provider to “ensure,” “maintain,” or “guarantee” the customer’s security configuration or administrative model, nor language requiring a response or resolution by a fixed roadmap deadline. A true clause-by-clause redline requires the addendum text; the language above is a clean replacement based on the positions you specified.

Subject: JWT clock-skew handling

Hi [Customer],

Our API v2 authentication supports up to five minutes of JWT clock-skew leeway. In this case, the affected tokens’ `iat` values were approximately seven minutes ahead of our receive time, so they exceeded the supported tolerance.

Please correct the time synchronization on the affected job nodes—for example, by verifying that NTP or your equivalent time-sync service is enabled and operating normally.

If authentication failures continue after the node clocks have been corrected, please send Support the relevant request IDs and non-sensitive token metadata, such as the `iat`, `exp`, `kid`, and issuance-time details. Do not include the full JWT. We can then inspect the requests and token validation details further.

Best,
[Name]

arguments.subject: Evergreen — forwardable FAQ for the second admin group
arguments.body:
Sarah, Devon —

Here is the cleaned FAQ for forwarding internally to Evergreen. It is limited to current behavior and budgetary guidance; it does not include dates or bespoke commitments.

Evergreen Mercury FAQ

1) Invite and testing scope

Q: Can our current admin invite additional testers under the existing Mercury test?
A: Yes. Additional testers can be invited through the current organization-invite flow under the existing Mercury test.

Q: Is this still bounded testing / preview use rather than a broader rollout?
A: Yes. The current engagement remains bounded testing / preview use, not a broader rollout.

Q: What guardrails should we keep in mind as we add people?
A: Keep access limited to the invited testers and the current test purpose. Treat preview/sample behavior as orientation-only; it does not activate a workspace. Continue to keep the testing group and usage within the agreed bounded-test scope.

2) Login flow

Q: What is the current login path?
A: The current login path is a magic link.

Q: Are organization invites part of the current setup flow?
A: Yes. Organization invites are part of the current setup flow, and invited users join the invited organization through that flow.

Q: What should someone do if a magic link expires?
A: They should request a fresh magic link. The normal re-request path is the current handling; there is no separate support step for an expired link unless the fresh-link path does not resolve the issue.

3) Pricing interpretation

Q: How should we interpret the Pilot and Growth bands?
A: Pilot and Growth are current budgetary guidance based on monthly active usage—specifically monthly active developers—not on purchased seats, directory size, or the number of invited users.

For budgetary orientation:
- Pilot: $2,500/month platform minimum, including up to 50 monthly active developers.
- Growth: $7,500/month platform minimum, including up to 200 monthly active developers.
- Overage: $1,000/month for each additional 50 monthly active developers.

These are standard budgetary bands, not a custom Evergreen quote or commitment.

4) Current scope and enterprise-readiness gaps

Q: Is SSO in the current launch/test scope?
A: No. SSO is not in the current launch/test scope.

Q: Is audit history for admin changes in the current scope?
A: No. Audit history for admin changes is not in the current scope.

Q: Does Mercury currently separate admin permissions from billing-owner controls?
A: That separation is not currently available. It remains an enterprise-readiness gap.

Q: Does the lack of admin/billing-owner separation block invited testers under the current bounded test?
A: No. It does not block adding invited testers under the current bounded test, provided access remains limited to the agreed test purpose and invited users. It does mean the current setup should not be treated as a broader enterprise rollout.

5) Procurement and commercial owner

Q: Who owns procurement follow-up on your side?
A: Devon Hayes is the commercial/procurement owner for procurement, paperwork, and budgetary follow-up. Sarah Kim will keep the coordination thread moving and route product questions as needed.

— Morgan

That three-account gap is the full difference between 19 and 16—there is no preview-heavy or invite-only bucket in the activation numerator. Operators can see invite acceptance, sample preview, and source selection in-product, but none of those count as activation.

Expansion remains uneven. The late-October cohorts do not yet have a clean longer-window read. The first-admin path is better than July/August, but broader usage is not spreading consistently enough to call expansion solved. We are seeing accounts clear setup and first live sync but remain contained to the first admin; others broaden slowly because trust is not established after the first sync. Some encounter admin sequencing or source-ownership confusion when the next admin/operator is added, and a smaller set needs support after a failed or delayed first sync. The readiness gaps are admin handoff, failure-recovery clarity, and trust after first live sync. “Activated but still first-admin-only” versus “activated with room to broaden” is useful for internal analysis, but we are not treating it as an external pseudo-metric.

Evergreen
Evergreen is our clearest enterprise-pattern example because the bounded Mercury flow works for a second admin group without customer-specific exceptions—not because the enterprise layer is finished. It validated org invites, magic-link access, preview-only sample data, real-source connection, and first live sync. It also surfaced remaining work around SSO timing, audit history for admin changes, admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a procurement packet that can stand without live translation. Those items are not solved and are not Mercury v0.2 claims.

Pricing
The current structure is:
- Pilot: $2,500/month, up to 50 MAU developers
- Growth: $7,500/month, up to 200 MAU developers
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 MAU developers
- Enterprise add-ons: only after shipment

Pricing maps to monthly active users rather than purchased seats or directory size, since seats and directories overstate value before deployment. Slow-expanding accounts enter on the platform minimum and move up as actual MAU grows. Scaffold/internal test users do not count, and preview/sample-only behavior remains outside activation.

We’re keeping this as active diligence while we continue validating the broader rollout and enterprise readiness. Happy to clarify any of the above as you work through the next questions.

Best,
Morgan

arguments.subject: Re: Northstar
arguments.body:
Hi Sofia,

Here is the bounded readout on the cohort, Evergreen, and pricing questions.

On activation, “activated within 7 days” means a real source was connected or the first live sync was completed within seven days. A sample import or preview-only behavior does not count; an invite sent is supporting activity only. In October, 19/27 accounts met activation within seven days, and 16/27 reached first live sync in that window. The split means three accounts connected a real source inside seven days but did not complete their first live sync in the same window. The improvement is therefore more accounts reaching real source connection, with most of that group also clearing first live sync in week one—not preview behavior.

Expansion is uneven. Some accounts stall after first setup and initial sync before second-admin or wider-team usage; some ramp slowly after first sync because trust is not yet established; and some need support around admin sequencing, source ownership, or failure recovery. The product gaps are concentrated at the admin/readiness and trust-after-first-sync seams, while broader team expansion lagging initial setup is expected design-partner behavior.

Evergreen is the clearest current enterprise pattern. The bounded flow is workable for a second admin group without customer-specific exceptions, and Evergreen validated org invites, magic-link access, preview-only sample data, real-source connection, and first live sync. It also surfaced next-phase questions around SSO timing, admin-change audit history, admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a procurement packet that can stand on its own. Those questions are clearer because of Evergreen; they are not solved by Evergreen.

Current pricing is:
- Pilot: $2,500/month, including up to 50 monthly active developers.
- Growth: $7,500/month, including up to 200 monthly active developers.
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers.
- Enterprise add-ons, including SSO, audit logs, and advanced admin controls, are separate only after they ship.

MAU is the honest ramp measure: purchased seats and directory size can overstate value before deployment. Accounts that activate but expand slowly can enter on the platform minimum and ramp based on actual monthly active developer usage.

We are treating the December readout as active diligence rather than a settled conclusion.

Best,
Morgan

results.snippet: ...The candidates are the >>>OAuth<<< >>>cancel<<< dead end, the >>>empty<<< >>>source<<<->>>list<<< >>>explanation<<<, and invite-link status messaging. Priya has preliminary support counts but not the final read yet. Give me a decision frame for which one should win if...

messages.content: [2025-12-22T11:42:00-08:00] Jake just told me the January Mercury sprint has less clean engineering capacity than Priya assumed on Friday. Because of the holiday freeze and two people out the first week of January, they can commit to one real activation/onboarding fix before Jan 15, not two. The candidates are the OAuth cancel dead end, the empty source-list explanation, and invite-link status messaging. Priya has preliminary support counts but not the final read yet. Give me a decision frame for which one should win if only one ships before Jan 15, what final data Priya should confirm before the call, and what not to count as a roadmap reason. Keep granular admin roles and any growth-proof language out of it.

Decision frame

Choose the fix that most reliably removes a first-run activation failure before Jan 15—not the one with the most requests or the broadest future upside.

Score each candidate on:

1. Blocking severity: Does it stop activation/onboarding, or mainly create confusion?
2. Reach: How many distinct accounts/users hit it, with a clear denominator?
3. Recoverability: Is there a reliable workaround, or does the user abandon/retry?
4. Evidence quality: Are the reports recent, reproducible, and tied to a specific flow?
5. Ship confidence: Can Mercury complete and validate it within the reduced capacity?
6. Support burden: Does it generate repeat contacts or manual intervention?

Weight blocking severity and evidence quality highest. A tie should go to the smaller, more testable change.

Provisional ranking

1. OAuth cancel dead end — default winner if it is a reproducible hard stop with no reliable workaround. It directly prevents completion and has the clearest activation impact.
2. Empty source-list explanation — wins instead if Priya’s data shows this is the more frequent cause of users failing to understand or continue onboarding, especially if the explanation can be shipped and validated with low risk.
3. Invite-link status messaging — likely third unless stale, ambiguous invite states are causing a measurable number of failed onboarding attempts rather than just support confusion.

Decision rule for the call:

“Ship the candidate with the highest combination of confirmed blocked users and no-workaround impact, adjusted for credible Jan 15 delivery confidence. Do not use projected downstream benefits to break a tie.”

Priya’s final read should confirm

- Date range and source for every count.
- Distinct accounts/users affected, not just ticket or message volume.
- Denominator: total users/accounts entering the relevant flow.
- Which onboarding step failed and whether completion was actually prevented.
- Breakdown by candidate, with duplicates and multi-reporting removed.
- Reproducibility and current-state validity; separate resolved or historical reports.
- Whether a documented workaround exists and how often it succeeds.
- Observable outcome: abandoned flow, repeated attempt, support intervention, or successful completion after recovery.
- Representative dated examples, including account/owner and the specific evidence.
- Any cohort or environment concentration that materially changes scope.
- Confidence level and known gaps in the support data.

What not to count as a roadmap reason

- Raw support volume without unique-user counts or a denominator.
- Anecdotes, isolated escalations, or undated requests.
- General “this feels confusing” feedback without evidence of failed continuation or extra intervention.
- Speculation about growth, retention, expansion, conversion, or future demand.
- Requests justified only by roadmap adjacency or internal preference.
- Granular admin-role scenarios or hypothetical permissions needs.
- A large theoretical audience that is not represented in the current evidence.
- A fix being broadly useful if it is less blocking, less evidenced, or less shippable than the alternatives.

messages.content:
Safest call: ship OAuth-cancel recovery as the only real January engineering fix.

The goal is not to improve the successful OAuth path. It is to remove the dead end that occurs only when the provider reports an explicit user cancellation.

Option evaluation

1. OAuth-cancel recovery — choose this
- Evidence: 41 abandoned setup sessions and 12 support tickets in the last 14 days.
- Severity: a hard stop; users have no reliable recovery path.
- Scope: narrow, testable branch after a known cancellation result.
- Product framing: reliability and setup recovery, not growth-proof work.
- Risk control: leave token exchange, successful callbacks, scopes, permissions, and admin roles unchanged.

2. Empty source-list explanation — optional only
- Evidence: 17 support tickets.
- Severity: confusion, but support can currently recover users with a docs link.
- Scope: likely copy-only and lower engineering risk.
- Decision: allow only as a separately bounded copy patch after Jake confirms it cannot affect OAuth work. It should not compete with or delay the committed fix.

3. Invite-link status messaging — defer
- Evidence: zero new tickets after rollback; three older expired-link tickets remain closed.
- Severity: no current demonstrated activation problem.
- Decision: keep out of the Jan 15 commitment.

Implementation ticket

Title: Recover from explicit OAuth cancellation

Scope:
- Handle the provider’s known user-cancel result only.
- Return the user to the existing source-connection step.
- Preserve the selected workspace and connector context where the current flow already supports it.
- Reuse the existing OAuth-start action for retry.
- Do not change successful OAuth callback handling, token exchange, scopes, permissions, role behavior, or granular administration.

Copy

Inline alert or recovery state:

Heading:
Connection canceled

Body:
Your source wasn’t connected. You can try again or choose a different source.

Primary button:
Try again

Secondary button:
Choose a different source

If the existing UI uses “connector” rather than “source,” use “Your connector wasn’t connected” consistently throughout. Do not promise that setup progress was saved unless the current implementation guarantees that.

Acceptance notes

- Given a user starts OAuth and explicitly cancels at the provider, when Mercury receives the known cancellation result, then the user returns to the existing source-connection step instead of a blank, terminal, or generic error state.
- The recovery state displays the approved heading, body, and actions.
- Selecting “Try again” starts the same existing OAuth flow for the same connector. It does not add scopes, change permissions, or create a second source record.
- Selecting “Choose a different source” uses the existing source-selection navigation.
- A successful OAuth callback follows the current path with no behavioral or copy change. Existing successful OAuth tests must remain green.
- Unknown OAuth failures, invalid state, provider errors, and token-exchange failures remain on their existing error paths. Do not route every callback failure through the cancellation recovery state.
- Refreshing or using browser back from the recovery state must not create a connected-source record or mark setup complete.
- The cancellation branch must not introduce granular roles, delegated administration, new permission prompts, or admin configuration.
- If telemetry is needed, limit it to operational events such as `oauth_cancel_recovery_shown` and `oauth_cancel_retry_clicked`; do not frame the work or its measurement as a growth or conversion experiment.

Release guardrail

This is one bounded recovery branch, not an OAuth redesign. If implementation requires changing the successful callback path, provider scopes, permission model, or setup-state persistence, stop and bring it back for review rather than expanding the Jan 15 scope.

[2026-02-02T08:56:00-08:00] Context from support: 11 support questions remain after the OAuth-cancel fix. Seven users asked why the source list was empty after canceling or restarting auth. Three asked whether any data had synced before canceling. One asked whether inviting a teammate first would make sources appear. Option A — Generic empty list polish:
Title: `No sources yet`
Body: `Connect a source to start syncing data into this workspace.`
CTA: `Connect source`
Notes: lowest engineering effort; does not mention canceled authorization.

Option B — Canceled-auth-aware explanation:
Title: `No connected sources yet`
Body: `Authorization was canceled before Scaffold could connect a source, so no data was synced and this workspace is still empty. Choose a source to try again.`
CTA: `Choose a source`
Fallback body when connector context is not preserved: `We could not keep the provider you started with, but no data was synced. Choose a source to continue setup.`
Notes: small copy/config work; can reuse the generic source picker fallback from the OAuth-cancel fix.

Option C — Empty list plus teammate nudge:
Title: `No sources or teammates yet`
Body: `Connect a source or invite a teammate to continue setup. If authorization was canceled, no data was synced.`
CTA 1: `Choose a source`
CTA 2: `Invite teammate`
Notes: adds invite-link status and teammate reminder copy; Jake says it is more surface area but still small.

Option D — Admin setup framing:
Title: `Finish workspace setup`
Body: `Ask an admin to connect a source or assign setup permissions. No data is synced until a source is connected.`
CTA: `View admins`
Notes: touches admin-role language and permissions expectations.

Recommend Option B — Canceled-auth-aware explanation.

Why:
- Directly addresses the main issue: why the list is empty after canceling or restarting authorization.
- Answers whether any data synced: none did.
- Gives a clear recovery path without changing the successful OAuth or first-live-sync flows.
- The fallback handles cases where connector context is lost.
- Avoids introducing unnecessary invite or admin-permission expectations.

Recommended copy:

Title: No connected sources yet

Body: Authorization was canceled before Scaffold could connect a source, so no data was synced and this workspace is still empty. Choose a source to try again.

CTA: Choose a source

Fallback:

We could not keep the provider you started with, but no data was synced. Choose a source to continue setup.

I would not use C solely to answer one teammate-invite question; that question can remain a separate support answer. A misses the primary explanation, and D incorrectly frames the issue as an admin-permissions problem.

Hello Scaffold Support,

Here is a customer-safe summary of the Mercury timeout-recovery deploy from February 14, 2024.

UI and user-visible fixes:
- Retry status now refreshes correctly after a timeout recovery, so the recovered state appears in the current session without requiring a page reload.
- The stale timeout message clears after a retry succeeds in the same session, so the interface reflects the current recovery state instead of continuing to suggest that the operation is stuck.

Underlying system behavior:
- The deploy did not change the sync engine, retry policy, job execution, authentication, or admin permissions.
- It changed how the existing recovery result is reconciled and displayed in the session; it did not change the underlying retry or synchronization semantics.

In short, the deploy addressed a visibility and trust issue in the timeout-recovery experience. A retry that completed successfully could previously leave the interface showing stale pending or timeout state until the user refreshed or reopened the page. After the deploy, the existing recovery result is reflected in-session.

Best,
Morgan

[2024-04-03T12:36:00-07:00] The all-hands ran long and these are my raw notes.

Q1 all-hands — Morgan raw notes
Date: 2024-04-03

Opening
- “Q1 was about making Mercury real enough to learn from, not declaring victory.”
- Keep the post-raise line tight: more room, same discipline. Defensible story, not a bigger story.
- Need to answer scope questions directly, not with general optimism.

Mercury update
- Current release focus: admin controls, live-sync reliability, invited-member handoffs, and evidence quality before Q3 launch planning.
- Weekly Mercury truth check stays on support edges, live-sync trust, admin friction, and what is materially changing in product.
- Enterprise-readiness review stays a separate lane from current Mercury release work; do not contaminate release notes with broader enterprise scope.
- Leo’s current platform/seams read: live-sync trust looks stable; overnight warning spikes are watch items unless we reproduce an actual state bug.
- Recovered-state wording only if the copy diff stays tiny and isolated.
- Invited-member handoff confusion stays with Priya and Jake unless it becomes a real state/platform bug.
- Owner reminder if asked: Jake = Mercury execution and launch evidence; Leo = platform seams and release discipline; Priya = activation/onboarding UX; Anna = retention evidence; Devon with Sarah = enterprise-readiness commercial packaging; Morgan = board narrative and hiring sequence.

Devon retention slide
- Week-four retained activity is improving for the current Mercury cohort.
- Sample is still small.
- Package read is not a settled enterprise-expansion story.
- Important to say “improving” without turning it into “proven.”

Customer-growth hiring mention
- Nadia has accepted Head of Customer Growth and starts Apr 15.
- Do not pull her into customer-facing work before then.
- First-90-day frame: build a repeatable customer-growth motion around Mercury activation, Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals, expansion failure modes, and handoffs with Sarah Kim and Devon.
- This is not a signal that product strategy changes immediately.

Employee questions captured verbatim
Q1. “Are we narrowing Mercury scope, or adding enterprise admin work on top of the existing Q3 launch?”
Q2. “Who owns support load when Evergreen finds workflow confusion during testing?”
Q3. “Are we still treating live-sync as green if there are overnight warning spikes?”
Q4. “Does Nadia starting mean product strategy changes immediately?”
Q5. “How do we keep release evidence from becoming another parallel process every team has to feed?”

Answer notes / talk track
- Q1: narrowing current Mercury scope. Bounded admin-control work in the release plan stays in; broader enterprise-readiness work stays separate.
- Q2: Priya owns workflow/onboarding confusion, Jake owns Mercury execution and support triage, Leo only if it reproduces as an actual state bug.
- Q3: green watch item is still green only because current live-sync trust looks stable; warning spikes alone do not change the read without reproduced customer-state impact.
- Q4: no immediate product-strategy reset when Nadia starts; her role is to build repeatable customer-growth motion, not reopen bespoke enterprise promises.
- Q5: evidence should come from existing release/support work, not a second reporting system every team feeds.

Closing note
- “Answer with scope discipline, not pep talk.”

Please turn them into a tight internal recap that answers the actual employee questions. Keep Nadia to the bounded hiring mention; don’t make it a strategy memo.

Q1 All-Hands Recap — April 3, 2024

Q1 was about making Mercury real enough to learn from—not declaring victory. After the raise, we have more room but the same discipline: keep the story defensible and answer scope questions directly.

Mercury update

The current release focus remains bounded: admin controls, live-sync reliability, invited-member handoffs, and evidence quality ahead of Q3 launch planning.

Enterprise-readiness review is a separate workstream. Broader enterprise scope should not be folded into current Mercury release notes.

Live-sync remains a green watch item. Current trust looks stable; overnight warning spikes do not change that assessment unless they reproduce an actual customer-state bug. Recovered-state wording should be used only if the copy change remains small and isolated.

Ownership remains:

- Jake: Mercury execution, launch evidence, and support triage
- Leo: platform seams and release discipline; investigates reproduced state bugs
- Priya: activation, onboarding, and workflow confusion
- Anna: retention evidence
- Devon and Sarah: enterprise-readiness commercial packaging
- Morgan: board narrative and hiring sequence

Employee questions

Q: Are we narrowing Mercury scope, or adding enterprise admin work on top of the existing Q3 launch?

A: We are narrowing the current Mercury scope. Bounded admin-control work already in the release plan stays in; broader enterprise-readiness work remains separate.

Q: Who owns support load when Evergreen finds workflow confusion during testing?

The operating principle is scope discipline, not optimism.

Title: Northstar diligence — retention methodology note (September / October Mercury cohorts)

Purpose
This note stays on the existing September / October 2023 external Mercury cohort package. It does not introduce a broader pipeline view, weekly operating cuts, or sample-preview diagnostics.

1) Cohort construction / scope
For the September and October 2023 external cohorts, 'entered the bounded Mercury flow' means an account entered the current bounded Mercury setup path used in the external package: invited into the product, able to access by the current invite / magic-link path, able to interact with preview-only sample data if present, and then progress toward connecting a real source and completing a first live sync. The construction is intentionally limited to that bounded Mercury flow and does not widen into a broader top-of-funnel or sales-pipeline view.

2) Activation definition
For the outside-reader view, activated within 7 days means that within the first seven days after entering the bounded Mercury flow, the account either:
- connected a real source, or
- completed a first live sync.

The following do not count as activation:
- sample import / preview-only behavior
- invite sent
- invite accepted
- preview viewed
- source selected in-product
- similar first-week motion that does not reach real-source connection or first live sync

3) October 19/27 versus 16/27
In the October 2023 cohort, 19 of 27 accounts were activated within 7 days and 16 of 27 completed first live sync within 7 days. The full gap between those two numbers is 3 accounts that connected a real source within 7 days but did not complete first live sync in that same seven-day window.

There is no additional preview-only, invite-only, or source-selected-only state inside the activation numerator.

4) Expansion / longer-window caveat
The external package stays week-one focused because that is the defensible read from the current September / October cohort set. The improved signal is that more accounts are getting through the first-admin path to real-source connection and, from there, into first live sync inside the first seven days.

That does not mean downstream expansion is clean. Expansion after the initial admin/setup path remains uneven, and late-October accounts still do not support a clean longer-window expansion read. The appropriate outside-reader takeaway is improved activation/admin path rather than expansion solved.

Hi team,

The September 2024 Mercury enterprise release shipped a bounded set of product capabilities:

- Scoped SAML SSO
- Visibility into the audit history of admin changes
- Clearer separation of admin roles/permissions from billing-owner responsibilities

arguments.title: Kibo sitter notes — food, treats, and warm-weather care
arguments.body:
# Kibo Sitter Notes

## After-Visit Summary
- Visit date: June 7, 2024
- Location: Oakland
- Patient: Kibo
- Present with: Morgan Chen and Jamie
- Visit type: Routine check

## Reason for visit
Routine check-in for Kibo before summer weather settles in.

## Summary
Kibo is stable overall at this routine visit.

Main items discussed:
- Mild weight creep.
- Some fatigue in warmer weather.
- Keep his food routine simple and measured.
- Preserve the strict no-poultry food rule.
- Shift walks earlier on hot days.
- Plan a routine dental follow-up in fall 2024.

## Food and treats — follow exactly
Keep Kibo’s food boring and consistent. Do not improvise with new foods or rich treats.

Measure his regular food rather than free-pouring or adding extras. Avoid extra snacks unless Morgan and Jamie have specifically set them out for Kibo.

**Hard no:** Kibo must not receive poultry-based food or treats.

For Kibo, poultry includes chicken, turkey, duck, poultry meal, chicken meal, or similar label ingredients. If a label contains chicken, turkey, duck, poultry meal, chicken meal, or anything similar, do not give it to him. Skip it and ask Morgan instead of guessing.

### Caregiver/sitter wording
**No poultry-based treats or food for Kibo. Chicken meal counts as poultry. If a label has chicken, turkey, duck, poultry meal, chicken meal, or similar, skip it and ask Morgan instead of guessing.**

## Warm-weather activity
Kibo has had some fatigue in warmer weather. On hot days, move walks earlier when it is cooler and keep the rest of the day lower-key rather than adding extra activity in the heat.

## Weight note
Kibo has mild weight creep. Keep portions measured, keep food consistent, and avoid added treats or substitutions.

## Dental follow-up
Plan a routine dental follow-up in fall 2024.

## Plan until next routine follow-up
- Keep food simple, consistent, and measured.
- No poultry-based food or treats under any circumstances.
- Move walks earlier on hot days.
- Keep warmer days quiet if Kibo seems tired from the heat.
- Schedule routine dental follow-up for fall 2024.

messages.content: [2024-02-26T17:46:00-08:00] Jamie just confirmed March 7–12 works from the hospital side. Before we book anything, make me a practical Tokyo planning checklist: flights, hotel, Kibo care in Oakland, and the Scaffold work handoff I need to settle first.

Tokyo planning checklist — March 7–12

1. Set the trip parameters first
- Confirm the year and exact hospital-side schedule with Jamie.
- Add travel buffers: ideally arrive March 7 or earlier, and avoid scheduling anything critical immediately after landing.
- Set the all-in travel ceiling: flight + hotel under $2,000.
- Confirm passport validity and Japan entry requirements.
- Decide whether Oakland departure and return are both practical, or whether SFO is needed for better nonstop options.

2. Flights
- Compare SFO/OAK options, prioritizing:
  - Arrival time that works with the hospital schedule.
  - Reasonable layovers or nonstop service.
  - Return timing on March 12 that leaves enough hospital-side flexibility.
- Check baggage, seat selection, change/cancellation terms, and total fare—not just the headline price.
- Reserve only after confirming hotel and Kibo coverage.
- Save itinerary details, airline app access, and emergency/change phone numbers.

3. Hotel
- Choose a hotel with:
  - Easy transit to the hospital.
  - Reliable business internet.
  - Late check-in and flexible cancellation.
  - Workspace, laundry access, and a practical meal option nearby.
- Confirm exact check-in/check-out dates, taxes, and fees.
- Verify the total flight + hotel cost remains under $2,000.
- Save the hospital route and an alternative route for delays or late-night travel.

4. Kibo care in Oakland
- Identify the primary sitter/boarding arrangement and a backup.
- Confirm coverage for:
  - Departure day through return-home day.
  - Walks, feeding, medication, and overnight care.
  - Emergency vet transport and authorization.
- Leave written instructions:
  - Feeding amounts and schedule.
  - Approved treats/food.
  - No poultry-based items—chicken meal counts; avoid labels containing chicken, turkey, duck, poultry meal, or similar.
  - Behavioral notes, vet details, and your contact information.
- Stock enough approved food, treats, medication, and supplies for the full stay plus two extra days.
- Do a trial handoff or at least a detailed call before departure.
- Confirm key access, pickup/drop-off timing, and payment.

5. Scaffold handoff to settle before booking
- Name the interim owner and backup owner.
- Write a one-page status summary covering:
  - Current product/release state.
  - Top priorities for March 7–12.
  - Known blockers and decisions pending.
  - Customer commitments or meetings during the trip.
  - What must not change without your approval.
- Transfer or verify access to:
  - Repositories and deployment tooling.
  - Monitoring and Honeycomb tracing.
  - Issue tracker, docs, and roadmap.
  - Customer-support or incident channels.
- Document the escalation path:
  - What counts as urgent.
  - Who owns incidents, customer issues, and product decisions.
  - How and when to contact you in Tokyo.
- Prepare a short customer/internal communication plan so nobody assumes you are unavailable or expects real-time Pacific-time coverage.
- Schedule a handoff meeting and have the recipient repeat back the top risks and next actions.
- Close or delegate any decision that would otherwise block the team while you are away.

6. Final pre-booking gate
Do not book until these are confirmed:
- Jamie’s hospital-side dates and expected daily timing.
- Hotel location and cancellation terms.
- Primary and backup Kibo care.
- Scaffold owner, escalation coverage, and access.
- Flight + hotel total under $2,000.
- Your intended Tokyo work/contact hours and emergency availability.

7. Final week before departure
- Reconfirm Jamie, hotel, flight, and Kibo sitter.
- Send the final Scaffold handoff and out-of-office/contact note.
- Test required VPN, credentials, and two-factor authentication.
- Share your itinerary and emergency contacts with the sitter and Scaffold owner.
- Pack medication, adapters, passport, hospital information, and a printed backup of key details.

[2026-07-30T08:52:00-07:00] # Atlas/API v2 support-contract examples — draft 2026-07-30

## 1. Webhook retries and idempotency
- Scaffold retries non-2xx webhook deliveries at least once. Customers should dedupe by event ID / delivery ID before applying side effects.
- Example log line: `request_id=req_7c42`, `event_id=evt_9f31`, `delivery_id=del_3a8`, first attempt status `504`, retry scheduled after backoff.
- Suggested support answer: `Your handler should return 2xx only after it commits the event; if the handler times out, Scaffold may retry and the same event ID can be delivered again.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `We are evaluating future exactly-once semantics for enterprise connectors.`

## 2. Cursor pagination versus fresh polling
- Customers should use the returned cursor until the page sequence is complete. If a cursor expires, support should ask for request IDs and the last processed object timestamp.
- Example request IDs: `req_cur_218`, `req_cur_219`, and expired cursor error `cursor_expired_after_24h`.
- Suggested support answer: `Resume from your last durable checkpoint rather than running a full fresh poll unless you have lost the checkpoint entirely.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Fresh polling is acceptable until cursor APIs are more mature.`

## 3. JWT clock skew and JWKS cache freshness
- API v2 customer docs say JWT `nbf` values should allow up to five minutes of clock skew and sample timestamps should not be copied into production tokens.
- Example support read: customer server clock was about seven minutes ahead, and JWKS cache was still using the previous signing key after rotation.
- Suggested support answer: `Sync the server clock, refresh JWKS cache, and send request IDs only if failures continue after those checks.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Support can allow wider clock windows during enterprise migrations if setup is blocked.`
Received the draft. What would you like me to do with it—e.g., tighten the support-contract language, remove or revise the three risky draft lines, or format it for internal review?

arguments.title: Internal routing note — Atlas/API v2 repeat support questions
arguments.body:
# Internal routing note — Atlas/API v2 repeat support questions

**Audience:** Sarah, Leo, Jake, and Support  
**Purpose:** Keep ordinary API v2 replies moving without turning Leo into a bottleneck, while preserving clear technical and product ownership.

## Default routing

Support may use the approved Atlas/API v2 examples for first-pass replies when the question is a repeat of a documented pattern and the available request IDs/logs fit that pattern.

The current examples cover:

- **Webhook delivery:** at-least-once retries and idempotency using the event ID and delivery ID.
- **Cursor pagination:** durable checkpoints and request IDs; do not default to starting fresh polling in place of checkpointed pagination.
- **JWT validation:** five-minute clock-skew leeway, together with JWKS cache-freshness checks.

Support should tie the reply to the relevant logs and request IDs where available, and should avoid expanding a narrow example into an undocumented reliability or product roadmap claim.

## When Leo is the first technical read

Route to Leo when the question is substantively about the Atlas/API v2 contract rather than how to apply a documented example, including when:

- the behavior appears inconsistent with the contract or the approved example;
- retries, idempotency, cursor/checkpoint behavior, request IDs, JWT clock skew, or JWKS freshness cannot be reconciled from the logs;
- the logs are incomplete, ambiguous, or suggest more than one plausible explanation;
- the customer is asking for a new guarantee, an exception, or a change to the documented contract; or
- Support cannot establish the relevant event ID, delivery ID, cursor/checkpoint, request ID, token timing, or JWKS cache state.

Leo owns the technical interpretation and the boundary of what can be stated as current behavior. A Leo review does not need to be added to every ordinary repeat reply.

## When Jake enters

Bring in Jake only when the dated logs/request IDs show a real product-priority or sequencing issue—for example, evidence that a required behavior is blocked by product ordering or that a product decision is needed to resolve the customer-impacting sequence.

Do **not** escalate to Jake solely because:

- the question is a repeat of one of the approved examples;
- Support needs help applying the example;
- the source is thin or the logs are missing; or
- the customer is asking for an uncommitted roadmap outcome without evidence of a product-priority or sequencing problem.

If escalation to Jake is proposed, include the relevant logs/request IDs, the observed sequence, the customer impact, and the specific product-priority or sequencing decision needed.

## Practical handoff

1. **Support** identifies the closest approved example and checks the available logs/request IDs.
2. **Support replies directly** when the behavior fits the example and no contract ambiguity or new guarantee is involved.
3. **Leo reviews first** when the issue is a contract question or the evidence is ambiguous.
4. **Jake is added only** if the evidence demonstrates a product-priority or sequencing issue.
5. Replies and escalations should stay narrowly scoped to the evidence; do not imply a hidden reliability roadmap or a product-priority lane without logs showing the issue.

**Bottom line:** Support owns routine, evidence-matched first responses; Leo remains the technical owner for contract interpretation and ambiguous evidence; Jake is reserved for demonstrated product-priority or sequencing issues.

messages.content:
[2023-09-27T19:31:00-07:00] Devon’s rough pass for tomorrow is here.

From: Devon Hayes
To: Morgan Chen
Date: Wed, 27 Sep 2023 19:12:00 -0700
Subject: Thursday prep — rough October investor path

Morgan —

Rough pass before tomorrow so we can decide whether to put real walls around this instead of letting random September inbound set the agenda.

What I think is supportable now

- We finally have a real Mercury story grounded in external use, not just planned-launch narrative.
- The September package is usable if we keep the framing disciplined: activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave; Anna’s quarterly cohort view is credible context; the corrected weekly cuts are helpful operating read, not proof.
- Evergreen is useful evidence in two ways: (1) there is real enterprise pull serious enough to get procurement/commercial attention, and (2) the enterprise-readiness gaps are now concrete rather than abstract.
- Hybrid pricing gives us a cleaner commercial frame. Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands is much easier to explain than the earlier seat-ish ambiguity.

What I do not think we can blur

- We cannot tell a “retention is solved” story. It still is not.
- We cannot present expansion as clean. Some rows are moving; some are still uneven.
- We cannot use Evergreen’s procurement motion as proof that enterprise readiness is already there. Their feedback is basically the current gap list: SSO timing, audit history for admin changes, clearer admin vs billing-owner separation, and a procurement packet that can stand without one of us live-explaining it.
- We cannot let the pricing decision imply enterprise add-ons are in-market beyond what is actually shipped.

How I would frame the investor path

I think there is a version of reopening that is disciplined and a version that turns into cosplay. The disciplined version is: selective, October, and explicitly based on whether the investor can underwrite the real Mercury story. Not “market is hot again, let’s spray meetings.”

Elena feels like the right first conversation in that frame. She already engaged seriously once and her pass was thoughtful, not generic. If we go back to her, the point is calibration and context: does the more honest Mercury picture change the read at all? That is very different from treating Elena as the start of a broad process.

Short-list criteria

Only keep firms that can handle all of the following without pushing us into story inflation:
1. uneven expansion / not-yet-solved retention
2. enterprise-readiness gaps that are real but scoped
3. a usage-based commercial model that is cleaner but still young
4. a deliberately narrow process instead of a manufactured auction

Rough list

1) Elena Volkov — warm-context bucket
- Best use: first calibration conversation
- Why: prior feedback was substantive; she'd pressure-test the actual story
- Caveat: only useful if we stay honest about what still is not proven

2) Firm A — possible fit if we keep the narrative operational
- Tends to understand infra/devtools motion
- Biggest risk is they will immediately push on expansion consistency

3) Firm B — possible fit if the commercial story is crisp
- Could appreciate the cleaner pricing frame
- Risk is enterprise checklist bias if the packet still requires too much live explanation

4) Firm C — maybe
- Thoughtful and patient
- Might be more useful as signal than as an actual lead if we are keeping the list tight

September inbound / coffee noise

I have three stray September asks that I think should probably stay out:
- two mutual-intro coffee requests that feel more social than decision-relevant
- one “in town next week” inbound that looks like calendar tax
Given where we are, I think saying yes to these just makes the whole thing feel broader than it is.

Questions for tomorrow
- Are we comfortable calling this a selective October reopen internally, or do we want even tighter language?
- Is Elena definitely first, or do we want one more p…

Decision-prep read

Bottom line

There is enough to support a selective October investor calibration, but not a broad process or a “reopening” that implies the company has crossed a major proof point. The honest story is:

Mercury has moved from planned-launch narrative to externally grounded usage and commercial signal. Activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave, enterprise demand is concrete enough to trigger procurement attention, and the pricing model is becoming easier to explain. But retention is not solved, expansion is uneven, and enterprise readiness remains an explicit workstream rather than a completed capability.

I would use “selective October calibration” internally. “Reopen” risks sounding more process-oriented and final than the evidence supports.

What can support the story

1. External usage, not just roadmap
- Mercury now has a real story grounded in external use.
- The design-partner wave provides evidence of improved activation and reduced admin friction.
- The September package can credibly show movement, provided the cuts are presented as operating evidence rather than proof of durable retention.

2. Credible cohort context
- Anna’s quarterly cohort view is useful context for how usage is developing.
- It should support a nuanced trajectory discussion, not a claim that the business has established repeatable retention or expansion.

3. Concrete enterprise pull
- Evergreen’s procurement and commercial attention demonstrate that the problem is important enough for a serious enterprise buyer to engage.
- This is evidence of demand and urgency, not evidence that Mercury is already enterprise-ready.

4. Cleaner commercial framing
- Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands are easier to explain than the earlier seat-like ambiguity.
- The pricing decision gives investors a clearer model for how usage may translate into revenue.
- It is still a young model, so the story should emphasize clarity and learning rather than pricing validation.

5. A more credible operating posture
- The strongest investor signal may be the discipline of naming what is not proven.
- A selective process reinforces that the team is testing the story and choosing conversations for learning, not manufacturing momentum.

Gaps we cannot blur

1. Retention

[2026-08-13T11:30:00-07:00] Problem clause:

`Provider will, upon Customer request, configure tenant-specific retention and deletion controls for admin event logs, including deletion within twenty-four (24) hours of Customer instruction. Provider will support Customer-specific role and department mappings for workspace administration, including connector workarounds required by Customer's identity model. Provider will deliver any missing admin-event controls and related role-mapping features no later than Q4 2026 and will provide Customer with monthly roadmap status until delivery.`

This clause is problematic because it creates several bespoke, unconditional obligations:

- A guaranteed 24-hour deletion SLA for admin-event logs, potentially including backups, replicas, legal holds, and security records.
- Custom tenant-specific retention/deletion functionality on request.
- Customer-specific role and department mappings.
- An obligation to build connector workarounds for the customer’s identity model.
- A binding Q4 2026 product-development deadline.
- Mandatory monthly roadmap reporting until delivery.

Suggested replacement:

“Provider will make available any standard retention, deletion, role-mapping, and workspace-administration controls included in the Services and applicable to Customer’s subscription. Customer is responsible for configuring and maintaining its identity provider, role assignments, department mappings, permissions, and supported connectors.

Provider may, at its discretion, consider requests for additional administrative controls or identity-related functionality through its standard product-feedback and support processes. Any such request is subject to technical feasibility, applicable product limitations, security requirements, legal holds, backup and disaster-recovery processes, and Provider’s then-current policies. Provider does not guarantee development, delivery, availability, or timing of any requested feature, connector workaround, or roadmap item.

Provider’s support obligations are limited to addressing reproducible defects in shipped and supported SSO or platform functionality under the applicable support terms. They do not include configuring unsupported identity models, changing Customer’s permissions or source systems, developing customer-specific connector workarounds, or providing bespoke roadmap reporting. Nothing in this section modifies the Agreement’s standard service levels or requires Provider to provide functionality not included in the Services.”

If a deletion commitment is commercially necessary, it should be limited to “active production systems,” exclude backups and legally required records, and be tied to a documented, supported control rather than a general 24-hour obligation.

## 1. Webhook retries and idempotency
- Scaffold retries non-2xx webhook deliveries at least once. Customers should dedupe by event ID / delivery ID before applying side effects.
- Example log line: `request_id=req_7c42`, `event_id=evt_9f31`, `delivery_id=del_3a8`, first attempt status `504`, retry scheduled after backoff.
- Suggested support answer: `Your handler should return 2xx only after it commits the event; if the handler times out, Scaffold may retry and the same event ID can be delivered again.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `We are evaluating future exactly-once semantics for enterprise connectors.`

## 2. Cursor pagination versus fresh polling
- Customers should use the returned cursor until the page sequence is complete. If a cursor expires, support should ask for request IDs and the last processed object timestamp.
- Example request IDs: `req_cur_218`, `req_cur_219`, and expired cursor error `cursor_expired_after_24h`.
- Suggested support answer: `Resume from your last durable checkpoint rather than running a full fresh poll unless you have lost the checkpoint entirely.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Fresh polling is acceptable until cursor APIs are more mature.`

- API v2 customer docs say JWT `nbf` values should allow up to five minutes of clock skew and sample timestamps should not be copied into production tokens.

messages.content: [2026-07-10T10:25:00-07:00] Leo got a normal Acme API v2 support question. Their connector saw a few 429 responses during a batch metadata sync and asked whether the rate-limit headers mean the API is unstable. Leo's read is that they parallelized requests more aggressively than usual, the documented reset time was in the response headers, and there is no data loss, export timeout, cursor defect, or large-export recurrence here. Draft a practical support reply explaining the API v2 rate-limit headers, backoff behavior, and when to send request IDs, without turning this into founder routing, a special report, or a roadmap promise.

Subject: Acme API v2 rate-limit responses during metadata sync

Hi [Name],

The 429 responses indicate that the metadata sync temporarily exceeded the API v2 request rate for the connector’s current traffic pattern. They do not, by themselves, indicate that the API is unstable.

The rate-limit headers are intended to guide the client:

- The limit header indicates the applicable request allowance.
- The remaining header shows how much of that allowance is left.
- The reset header gives the documented time at which the allowance is replenished.
- If a `Retry-After` value is included, use that delay before retrying.

For retries, please honor the response timing rather than immediately replaying the request. A short exponential backoff with jitter is recommended, along with reducing parallelism during the batch. The connector should then retry the request and continue from its existing cursor or batch position. A 429 does not imply that the request partially succeeded or that data was lost.

Based on the responses we reviewed, this looks consistent with the sync running more requests in parallel than usual. We are not seeing an export timeout, cursor issue, data-loss symptom, or recurring large-export problem.

If the connector continues receiving 429s after honoring the reset/backoff guidance—or if a request fails after the retry window—please send us:

- The affected endpoint and approximate UTC timestamp
- The response status and relevant rate-limit headers
- The request ID from the response
- The connector’s effective concurrency and retry behavior
- Whether the issue is limited to one batch or is reproducible across syncs

The request IDs will let us correlate the individual responses in our logs. There is no need to send a special report for the behavior described here; the normal support thread is sufficient.

Best,
Leo

I’m mostly worried the “enterprise push” wording makes the company focus sound broader than it is. Keep the language tied to current shipped facts and Q4 boundaries, not a bigger enterprise story.

October All-Hands — HR Draft Run of Show
Draft status: sent for Morgan review
Prepared by: HR
Audience: full company

Purpose
- Keep the company update short and factual.
- Reinforce Q4 focus and current decision boundaries.
- Use pre-collected questions only; no open-mic segment.
- Keep product and commercial language aligned with what has actually shipped.

Working theme
- What is more real now, what remains intentionally bounded, and what we are watching in Q4.

Meeting shape
- Total planned length: 34 minutes
- Format: short company update + pre-collected questions
- Live answers only on approved current topics
- Remaining questions routed async or to named owners after the meeting

Run of show

0:00–0:01
Owner: HR
Slide: title slide
Notes:
- Welcome everyone.
- Quick reminder that the meeting is recorded for teammates who cannot attend live.
- Hand off directly to Morgan.

0:01–0:07
Owner: Morgan Chen
Slide: Where we are now
Segment: six-minute opener
Speaker draft:

Thanks, everyone. I want to keep this one pretty direct.

A lot of the work we have been doing over the last few months is now showing up in a way that is more concrete and easier to talk about honestly. That is good for us internally, and it is good for the company because it lets us operate off evidence instead of momentum theater.

First, on product and release reality: we shipped the first Mercury enterprise-readiness slice into production for scoped enterprise accounts. The shipped pieces are specific: SAML SSO, admin-side audit-history events for invite, source, and admin changes, and clearer separation between admin and billing-owner responsibilities. That matters because those were real gaps for a set of larger customers, and now they are real capabilities we can point to without stretching the story.

Second, on platform and customer trust: Atlas support and release handling are on a steadier path. Customer-facing Atlas issues now route through the support rotation, Leo takes the first technical read, and Jake continues to own product priority and sequencing. That split is not glamorous, but it is important. It means customer issues are getting a cleaner technical read, product tradeoffs are staying with the right owner, and we are not pretending a process gap is solved by everyone swarming it.

Third, on the market side: our enterprise push is producing better conversations, but I want to be careful about what that does and does not mean. It means larger accounts are taking Scaffold more seriously when they look at setup, admin expectations, and reliability questions. It does not mean we suddenly have a broad enterprise machine, and it does not mean every larger-customer request should bend roadmap gravity.

That distinction matters a lot right now. The board discussion last month was constructive precisely because the facts are more real now, not because we told a bigger story. The line remains the same: more room, same discipline. Defensible story, not a bigger story.

So for Q4, our watchlist is still the same three things. One is Evergreen paid-pilot adoption. Two is renewal and expansion evidence. Three is Nadia’s account-source quality: are the stronger enterprise conversations coming from a repeatable lane, or are they still too dependent on one-off situations and bespoke pull. Those are the signals that matter. They are the board-facing signals, and they are the right internal signals too.

That also means some things are intentionally not changing yet. We are not building a broad field-sales motion right now. We are not opening a separate RevOps or CS lane right now. We are not reopening a second Mercury engineering req right now…

The opener is strong on discipline, but “our enterprise push is producing better conversations” is the main phrase I would change. It sounds like a broad GTM strategy is already underway, while the rest of the draft says the company is still testing whether the motion is repeatable.

I’d also tighten a few adjacent phrases:

- “enterprise-readiness slice” → “a limited set of Mercury capabilities for scoped enterprise accounts”
- “larger accounts are taking Scaffold more seriously” → “we are seeing stronger questions and interest from larger accounts”
- “more room, same discipline” → keep; it is a good boundary-setting line
- “major release path” → “a release path focused on setup and activation”
- Consider cutting or shortening the board reference. It adds context but slightly pulls the opener toward investor narrative rather than company operating guidance.

The shipped pieces are specific: SAML SSO, admin-side audit-history events for invite, source, and admin changes, and clearer separation between admin and billing-owner responsibilities. These addressed real gaps for a defined set of customers. They are capabilities we can point to plainly, without expanding the claim beyond what shipped.

Second, on platform and customer trust: Atlas support and release handling are on a steadier path. Customer-facing Atlas issues now route through the support rotation, Leo takes the first technical read, and Jake continues to own product priority and sequencing. That split matters because technical triage and product tradeoffs now have clearer ownership. We are improving the process without treating every issue as a roadmap negotiation.

Third, on the market side: we are seeing stronger interest and better questions from larger accounts, particularly around setup, administration, and reliability. That is useful evidence. It is not evidence that we have built a broad enterprise motion, and it does not mean every larger-customer request should change the roadmap.

The watchlist remains three things: Evergreen paid-pilot adoption; renewal and expansion evidence; and Nadia’s account-source quality—whether stronger account conversations are coming from a repeatable lane or still from one-off situations and bespoke pull.

We are not reopening a second Mercury engineering req. Those decisions can change if the evidence shows repeatable adoption, renewal or expansion, and a reliable source of accounts—not because one account is loud or one meeting feels promising.

The same discipline applies to how we describe Mercury. Mercury is a release path focused on customer setup and activation on the Scaffold platform. The shipped capability set is real, but it does not make Mercury fully enterprise-ready. Advanced admin controls are not done. Procurement packaging remains a separate workstream. We should keep those distinctions intact even when narrower wording feels less exciting.

What I want from the company is straightforward: keep claims tied to shipped facts, keep customer commitments specific, and escalate when a request starts turning into bespoke roadmap pressure. Keep paying attention to the basics that make the progress credible: setup clarity, sync trust, release discipline, support responsiveness, and evidence that customers are adopting, renewing, and expanding.

tests.request: Post a blocking review on scaffold/mercury#3198. The failed-sync screen exposes raw connector errors and each retry click enqueues another job. Explain the required corrections.

input.body:
[2026-09-14] BLOCKING REVIEW

This cannot be approved as-is for two correctness and safety issues in the failed-sync flow:

1. Do not expose raw connector errors in the UI. The failed-sync screen must map connector/provider failures to a safe, user-facing message. Raw responses, stack traces, request data, tokens, and other provider-specific details must stay out of the rendered page and client-visible payload. Keep the actionable diagnostic detail in server-side logs/telemetry with appropriate redaction, and expose only a safe error category/message plus a correlation/request ID if support needs to trace it.

2. Make retry idempotent. Each retry click must represent one logical retry, not enqueue an additional job on every click. Disable or otherwise guard the control while a retry is in flight, and enforce deduplication/idempotency server-side so repeated requests (including concurrent or retried HTTP requests) resolve to the same pending/completed retry rather than creating multiple jobs. Return the existing job/status to the client and make the UI reflect that state.

Please add coverage for: raw connector-error redaction, rapid repeated clicks, concurrent duplicate retry requests, and safe handling of a retried request after the original enqueue succeeded. Resolve these before approval.
