messages.content:
September 2024 Cloud Infrastructure Variance Note

September cloud infrastructure spend was $8,642.18, up $452.18, or 5.5%, from August’s $8,190.00. The variance is supported by identifiable usage increases; no unexplained or apparent duplicate charges were found in the supplied detail.

Primary drivers:

- Production Atlas API v2: +$309.10
  - EC2 compute: +$140.22
  - Data transfer: +$88.41
  - Application Load Balancer: +$47.16
  - RDS PostgreSQL: +$23.58
  - ElastiCache Redis: +$9.73
  - The increase is consistent with higher production API request, response, and webhook traffic. RDS notes indicate no one-time restore or failover charge.

- Mercury staging release validation: +$129.62
  - ECS Fargate: +$98.40
  - CloudWatch: +$31.22
  - These costs reflect a one-week increase in staging/test compute and observability during Mercury release validation.

- Other identified changes: +$13.46
  - S3 connector payloads and archives: +$4.16
  - Shared NAT Gateway: +$5.30
  - Route 53/WAF: +$1.82
  - Legacy non-production EC2/EBS baseline: +$2.18

The Support Plan was unchanged at $711.58. The legacy non-production us-west-2 baseline also remained essentially flat, increasing by only $2.18.

Recommendation: The invoice variance is adequately explained by higher production Atlas API v2 usage and a discrete Mercury staging validation event. Subject to normal AP controls and confirmation that the Mercury validation work was authorized, the September invoice appears reasonable for approval.

[2025-01-17T10:42:00-08:00] These are my kickoff notes for Project Compass, the Scaffold product/operating project to make our internal customer-health signals useful in customer-facing and customer-growth work. Please turn them into a tight internal owner-routing note so the team understands Compass without reading it as a new hiring lane or another board-dashboard project.

Project Compass kickoff notes
Date: January 17, 2025
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

Purpose of the meeting
- Name the next operating/product push before the January work turns into separate account threads, Mercury cleanup, and board shorthand.
- Use the signals Scaffold already has from internal operating work, but make them useful to customers and customer-growth follow-up instead of turning them into another internal reporting layer.

Working project name
- Project Compass

Why now
- We already have real signal categories showing up in Mercury/Evergreen work.
- The current-state Evergreen packet exists, so enterprise-readiness can be handled as actual evidence instead of vague sales language.
- The team does not want another board dashboard that looks clean internally but does not change what happens in an account.

Project intent
- Turn internal customer-health signals into customer-facing and customer-success/customer-growth follow-up that changes account behavior.
- The point is not to score accounts for internal consumption only.
- The point is to make the signal lead to a next action, better follow-up, or better customer-facing guidance.

Signals currently available from internal operating use
- Retention
- Activation
- Expansion
- Admin friction
- Enterprise readiness
- Account-note quality

Boundary / what Compass is not
- Do not build another board dashboard.
- Do not treat the first version as investor packaging.
- Do not turn this into a generic health-score project.
- Do not let it become a bespoke Evergreen side track.
- Do not use Compass as a reason to open a new hiring lane.
- Stay with the current lightweight staffing model.

Discussion notes

Morgan
- The framing should stay operational and customer-real, not presentation-ready.
- If Compass becomes a prettier internal dashboard, we missed the point.
- Board narrative matters later, but the first job is to make the signals produce better customer behavior and better follow-up.
- Keep the naming clean now so the work does not fragment into separate Mercury, Evergreen, and customer-growth side conversations.

Anna
- Signal definitions need caveats or they will get over-read immediately.
- “Renewal risk” can easily collapse together very different things: actual product weakness, admin handoff confusion, procurement packaging, or ordinary activation drag.
- Admin friction should not be treated as a churn prediction label by default.
- Every Compass signal needs source evidence attached, plus caveats about what the signal does and does not mean.
- Account-note quality is not separate housekeeping; it changes whether any of the other signals are trustworthy.

Nadia
- Useful only if the signal changes follow-up behavior.
- Customer-growth use cases need owner routing, not just visibility.
- A signal without a next action turns into an FYI bucket and then dies.
- The useful categories still look similar to what worked in the earlier Mercury/Evergreen read: activation friction, admin handoff/role confusion, procurement/security packaging, expansion stalls after first live sync, and true product gaps. Compass should preserve that logic instead of flattening everything into one score.
- Need follow-up that distinguishes evidence from inference so customer-facing outreach does not sound made up.

Jake
- Keep v0.1 narrow enough that it can actually ship or be tested.
- If Compass starts asking for a big new product surface immediately, it will collide with Mercury work and stall.
- Initial product implementation should bias toward lightweight prom…

Project Compass — Internal Owner-Routing Note
Kickoff: January 17, 2025

Purpose

Compass turns existing customer-health signals into better customer-facing guidance and customer-success/growth follow-up. A signal is useful only when it carries evidence, caveats, and a clear next action.

This is an operating/product workflow—not another internal reporting layer.

What Compass is not

- Not a new board dashboard.
- Not investor packaging.
- Not a generic health-score project.
- Not a bespoke Evergreen workstream.
- Not a broad admin-policy or enterprise-controls product.
- Not a reason to open a new hiring lane.

Stay within the current lightweight staffing model: Nadia/Sarah operating support with Jake/Leo implementation support.

v0.1 focus

1. Renewal-risk and admin-friction evidence
   - Show when apparent renewal risk may instead reflect admin friction, setup/control issues, role confusion, procurement packaging, or activation drag.
   - Do not use binary risk labels without context.
   - Attach source evidence and caveats to every signal.

2. Post-first-live-sync expansion prompts
   - Identify the smallest useful prompt or follow-up after an account reaches first live sync and appears ready for broader usage.
   - Optimize for timely, evidence-based action—not generic upsell language.

3. Account-note source quality
   - Make follow-up traceable by distinguishing:
     - Customer statements
     - Observed usage/readout
     - Support-derived facts
     - Internal interpretation
   - Preserve provenance and recency.
   - Treat note quality as foundational to signal trustworthiness, not as separate housekeeping.

Owner routing

- Anna Martinez — Signal definitions and caveats
  - Define retention, activation, expansion, admin friction, enterprise readiness, and account-note quality.
  - Separate evidence from inference.
  - Document what each signal does and does not mean.

- Nadia Singh — Customer-success and customer-growth use cases
  - Define the follow-up behavior each signal should trigger.
  - Own routing, recipient, and next-action design.
  - Ensure customer-facing guidance is grounded in evidence rather than implied certainty.

- Jake — Product implementation and sequencing
  - Keep v0.1 lightweight: prompts, account workflow support, or a contained product assist.
  - Prevent scope from expanding into a broad new product surface or general enterprise-controls work.

- Leo Park — Data/platform seams
  - Reuse existing signals and event paths.
  - Avoid a separate scoring service or platform layer at this stage.
  - Define the minimum evidence bundle that can move from internal read to customer/action use.
  - Keep usage evidence, account-note evidence, and inferred account state distinct.

- Sarah Kim — Account-thread hygiene
  - Improve source quality in account notes.
  - Separate customer quotes, internal interpretation, support follow-up, and procurement context.
  - Make the underlying record trustworthy enough for growth follow-up.

- Morgan Chen — Board/customer narrative
  - Keep the framing operational and customer-real.
  - Do not turn early Compass work into presentation-ready reporting.
  - Board narrative comes later, after the workflow changes account behavior.

Working signal logic

Preserve the distinctions already useful in Mercury/Evergreen work:

- Activation friction
- Admin handoff or role confusion
- Procurement/security packaging
- Expansion stalls after first live sync
- True product gaps

Do not flatten these into a single score or treat admin friction as a churn prediction by default.

v0.1 success test

A Compass signal is working when:

- It triggers a clearer next action.
- The recipient understands why they are seeing it.
- Evidence and caveats travel with the signal.
- Follow-up quality improves—not merely internal visibility.

Immediate next decisions

- Minimum evidence package required for each signal.
- Signals that remain internal versus those suitable for customer-facing use…

messages.content:
Tuesday working session: Compass v0.1 signal decisions

Attendees: Anna, Nadia, Jake, Leo, Sarah  
Goal: Turn each Compass v0.1 signal into a bounded, actionable operating rule.

1. Opening — 5 min
- Confirm v0.1 scope and decision standard.
- Reaffirm boundaries:
  - No board dashboard.
  - No new hiring lane or hiring workflow.
  - Signals should support existing customer, product, and growth motions—not create a parallel operating system.

2. Signal-by-signal review — 10 min each

For every Compass v0.1 signal, decide:

- Trigger: What specific action should this signal prompt?
- Audience: Who sees it—customer team, product, growth, leadership, or only the account owner?
- Evidence: What evidence travels with the signal?
- Caveat: What uncertainty, limitation, or alternative explanation must travel with it?
- Account note: What must be recorded in the account note for the signal to be useful?
- Source quality: What source, freshness, corroboration, or confidence threshold must be true?
- Explicit non-build: What are we deliberately not building for this signal?
- Owner and next step: Who owns the resulting action, and how will we know it happened?

3. Cross-signal consistency check — 10 min
- Are triggers mutually consistent?
- Are any signals duplicative or too noisy to act on?
- Are audiences limited to people who can take the action?
- Are evidence and caveats visible together?
- Does any proposed workflow accidentally become a board dashboard or new hiring lane?

arguments.title: Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist
arguments.body:
# Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist

Working session: January 21, 2025  ·  Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

## v0.1 operating boundary
- **Purpose:** turn a narrow set of defensible signals into named follow-up actions; do not produce labels for their own sake.
- **Boundary:** no board dashboard, no prettier internal dashboard, and no new hiring lane. Jake’s January Mercury activation remains the center of gravity; Compass must not become a dashboard/platform build while that work is active.
- **Visibility rule:** start with the current team only. A signal leaves that team only after Sarah’s source-quality check, Anna’s attached definition/caveat, and Leo’s data/platform-seam check.

## Owner checklist

### 1) Renewal-risk / admin-friction
- [ ] **Signal — Anna (definition):** identify the specific admin friction, setup-control issue, or role confusion causing the apparent risk. Keep true product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag as separate categories; never use “renewal risk” alone.
- [ ] **Trigger — Nadia (action):** trigger a named account-owner follow-up that names the friction and the next customer/account-team step. Do not trigger from a risk label alone.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Nadia:** first: Nadia and the account owner, as an account-team script candidate. Before the gate: Anna, Sarah, and the current team only; no broad customer outreach or external distribution.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Sarah + Anna:** attach the account-thread provenance, separating customer statement, observed/support fact, and internal interpretation; state what is known, inferred, and unresolved. The minimum package remains an open decision; Nadia must approve the bar before it becomes a script rather than an internal FYI.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah:** rate the underlying note reliable, mixed, or too thin. Weak or mixed notes must carry an explicit caveat; too-thin notes stay internal and cannot support outreach.
- [ ] **Not building:** not a generic renewal-risk score, account-risk label, automated escalation, or dashboard of at-risk accounts.

### 2) Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt
- [ ] **Signal — Jake + Leo:** first live sync is actually live, with teammate-invite and admin-role basics visible enough to ground a follow-up. Distinguish observed usage from inferred readiness for broader usage.
- [ ] **Trigger — Nadia:** issue the smallest useful customer-growth/account-team prompt after first real traction: a timely next-action script, not generic upsell language or a metrics view.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Nadia:** first: Nadia and the account owner after the trigger conditions are met. Before release outside the current team: Jake, Leo, Anna, and Sarah review; do not expose it as a broad product or customer surface.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Leo + Anna:** Leo confirms the event path and data/platform seam are defendable; Anna keeps the definition and uncertainty attached. Record the live-sync event, visible invite/admin-role state, and the boundary between observed usage and inferred expansion readiness.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah:** confirm the account note and usage/event evidence are traceable and rate the note reliable, mixed, or too thin. If the source is weak, keep the prompt internal and state the caveat.
- [ ] **Not building:** not an expansion score, recommendation engine, product surface, metrics dashboard, or platform build.

### 3) Account-note source quality
- [ ] **Signal — Sarah:** classify each supporting thread note as reliable, mixed, or too thin, with provenance tags for customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, and internal interpretation.
- [ ] **Trigger — Sarah + Anna:** only permit a signal to feed real follow-up when the note-quality status and caveats are explicit; otherwise keep it as an internal FYI.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Sarah first:** Sarah, Anna, and the current team see the quality assessment first. Nadia sees it for outreach only when the source-quality bar is met; do not pass mushy notes off as customer fact.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Sarah:** preserve the traceable source note and distinguish fact from interpretation; Anna ensures caveats travel with the signal. Define the required note fields/source tags before external-team use.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah (gate):** no reliable/traceable provenance, no outside-current-team use. Mixed requires an explicit caveat and review; too thin stays internal and cannot trigger outreach.
- [ ] **Not building:** not a note-cleanup program, universal CRM taxonomy, automated sentiment/provenance system, or dashboard of source-quality scores.

## Ownership and exit gate
- **Anna:** definitions and caveats remain attached to every signal.
- **Nadia:** owns the customer-growth/account-team script and follow-up logic; no outreach from mushy notes or internal inference presented as customer fact.
- **Jake:** protects the v0.1 boundary while January Mercury activation is active; no dashboard/platform drift.
- **Leo:** completes the data/platform-seam and event-path defensibility check before any signal leaves the current team.
- **Sarah:** owns source hygiene and the reliable/mixed/too-thin classification; source quality is a gating input, not cleanup.
- **Before any signal leaves the current team:** action and first viewer are named; evidence/caveat bundle is attached; Sarah’s source-quality gate, Anna’s caveat check, and Leo’s seam check are complete; Nadia accepts the follow-up use; Jake confirms the scope remains v0.1.
- **Explicitly not building in v0.1:** no board dashboard, no new hiring lane, no prettier internal dashboard, and no broad platform/product surface. First pass stays narrow enough to test whether signals produce action.

arguments.title: Compass v0.1 — First Preview Readout Scaffold
arguments.body:
# Compass v0.1 — First Preview Readout

## Purpose
Assess whether the first preview produced useful account-team action—not whether the experience looked polished or customers said they understood a dashboard.

## Scope and guardrails
- v0.1 remains a narrow preview/discovery read, not a dashboard or platform evaluation.
- Keep **signal legibility** separate from **behavior change**.
- Preserve Acme’s live-only review boundary: discuss only Acme’s own account-health, reliability, and renewal-risk signals with Greg Shipman, Sarah Kim, Nadia Singh, and Jake. Do not circulate written Mercury packets, screenshots, Evergreen examples, or other customer-specific Compass materials to Acme.
- Keep definitions, caveats, confidence, and event provenance attached to every signal.
- Treat account-thread notes as source-quality-specific; do not collapse observation, interpretation, and reported action.

## 1. Legibility: could the intended user interpret the signal?
Capture evidence for:
- Signal definition and status were understood without relying on unstated context.
- The user could identify the relevant account risk or friction and its supporting evidence.
- Caveats and confidence changed or constrained interpretation as intended.
- The user could tell what was observed versus inferred, including event provenance.
- Questions or confusion were about the signal itself, not merely the presentation.

Record separately:
- Who read it and in what review context.
- Signal, definition, caveats, confidence, and provenance shown.
- Exact questions, misreadings, or missing context.
- Source quality of each note: direct observation, account-thread record, participant report, or interpretation.

## 2. Behavior change: did the signal change what someone did next?
Do not count recognition, agreement, or “this is useful” as behavior change. Look for concrete evidence that an account-team script, renewal-risk response, admin-friction follow-up, or customer-growth action changed.

### Concrete next-action evidence
For each red or otherwise actionable signal, look for:
- A named owner who accepted responsibility.
- A specific next action, not a general intention.
- A committed timing or trigger.
- The account/customer context used to tailor the action.
- Evidence attached to the action: source event(s), account-thread note(s), definition, caveat, and confidence.
- A recorded follow-up in the relevant account thread, task, or system of record.
- Subsequent evidence that the action occurred.
- If no action occurred, the stated blocker and whether the signal, evidence, ownership, or workflow was insufficient.

For Greg’s question, explicitly answer: “When the signal is red, who does what next, based on which evidence?”

## 3. Readout table
| Signal / scenario | Legibility evidence | Misread or missing context | Named owner | Specific next action | Timing / trigger | Evidence carried with action | Follow-up observed | Source quality | Confidence / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

## 4. Interpretation rules
- Report legibility and behavior-change findings as separate findings; one does not substitute for the other.
- A clear signal with no changed action is a legibility success but not a behavior-change success.
- A changed action without traceable evidence is not sufficient; assess provenance and source quality.
- Keep “account team changed its script/workflow” distinct from “customer-growth follow-up changed.”
- Do not generalize from Evergreen to Acme. Acme evidence must remain live-only and account-specific.
- Do not use board-proof, GTM-proof, customer-understanding, or dashboard-success language. Use observed behavior, attributable evidence, and bounded preview findings.

## 5. Open questions for the first read
- Which roles should act on renewal-risk versus admin-friction signals?
- What minimum evidence must travel with each signal for the owner to act confidently?
- Which caveats or confidence levels materially change the next action?
- Where is event provenance incomplete or ambiguous?
- What is the smallest workflow change that would make the intended action more likely?

## 6. Bottom line format
- **Legibility:** [what users could/could not interpret, with evidence]
- **Behavior change:** [what action changed, by whom, and what was observed afterward]
- **Evidence quality:** [what traveled with the signal; provenance and caveats]
- **Boundary:** [Evergreen current-state evidence and Acme live-only evidence kept separate]
- **Next narrow test:** [one workflow/action question for v0.1; no dashboard/platform expansion]

bookend_end.content:

It avoids dashboard-success, board-proof, and GTM-proof framing.

# Compass v0.1 — First Working-Session Agenda (Reconstructed)

Working session: Tuesday, January 21, 2025
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

## Purpose

Move Compass v0.1 from abstract “useful signals” to bounded operating rules: when a signal appears, what should happen, who should act, and what evidence makes the action defensible.

Decision standard: a signal is useful only if it produces a named next action with evidence and caveats attached. Visibility, recognition, or dashboard polish is not the outcome.

## Opening — 5 minutes

- Confirm the v0.1 scope and the action-oriented decision standard.
- Reaffirm that January Mercury activation remains the center of gravity: workspace → first source → first live sync, plus teammate-invite and admin-role basics.
- Confirm that Compass gets only enough seam work to test the narrow evidence and follow-up paths below.

## Signal review — 10 minutes per signal

For each signal, answer the same questions:

1. Trigger: What specific action should this signal trigger?
2. Owner: Who is responsible for that action, and how will we know it happened?
3. Audience: Who sees it first—account owner, customer-success/growth, product, leadership, or only the current internal team?
4. Evidence: What source evidence travels with the signal?
5. Caveat: What uncertainty, limitation, or alternative explanation must travel with it?
6. Account note: What must be recorded in the account note for the signal to be useful?
7. Source quality: What provenance, freshness, corroboration, or confidence threshold must be true?
8. Visibility gate: Which uses remain internal, and what must be checked before the signal is used in customer-facing or account-team follow-up?
9. Explicit non-build: What are we deliberately not building for this signal?

### 1. Renewal-risk / admin-friction evidence

Working question: Is the apparent renewal risk actually product weakness, admin friction, setup/control trouble, role confusion, procurement drag, or activation drag—and what should the account owner do next?

Questions for the group:

- What minimum evidence package must be present before Nadia will allow this to become an account-team script rather than an internal FYI?
- What named account-owner follow-up should the signal trigger?
- Who sees it first, and who must not see it before the source-quality and caveat checks are complete?
- How do we keep “renewal risk” from collapsing distinct causes into one blunt label?
- What evidence must be attached from the account thread, support readout, usage, or customer statement?
- How do we separate customer statements, observed/support facts, and internal interpretation?
- What caveat or confidence statement prevents the signal from being over-read?
- What account-note fields or source tags must be true for follow-up?
- What does Sarah classify as reliable, mixed, or too thin, and what happens at each level?
- What are we explicitly not building: a generic renewal-risk score, an account-risk label, an automated escalation, or a dashboard of at-risk accounts?

### 2. Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt

Working question: After first real traction, what is the smallest useful next-action prompt for the account team or customer-growth motion?

Questions for the group:

- What exact event proves that first live sync is actually live?
- Are teammate-invite and admin-role basics visible enough that the follow-up is grounded in real account state?
- What is the smallest prompt that changes behavior without becoming generic upsell language or a metrics view?
- Who sees the prompt first, and who owns the customer/account-team follow-up?
- What observed usage evidence travels with it, and what is only inferred readiness for broader usage?
- Can Leo defend the underlying event path and data/platform seam before anything leaves the current team?
- What caveat is required where readiness is inferred rather than observed?
- What account-note/source-quality condition must be met before this becomes an actionable script?
- What is the timing or trigger for the next action after first live sync?
- What are we explicitly not building: an expansion score, recommendation engine, product surface, metrics dashboard, or platform build?

### 3. Account-note source quality

Working question: What must be true of the underlying account-thread record before any Compass signal can drive real follow-up?

Questions for the group:

- What required note fields or source tags distinguish customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, and internal interpretation?
- Can Sarah classify the note as reliable, mixed, or too thin, and what operational consequence follows from each classification?
- Who sees the source-quality assessment first?
- When does a weak or mixed note stay an internal FYI rather than feed Nadia’s outreach or an account-team script?
- What provenance and freshness must be preserved so the signal can be traced back to its source?
- What caveat must travel with a mixed or incomplete note?
- How do we prevent internal inference from being presented as customer fact?
- What minimum source-quality bar will Nadia accept before a real follow-up is allowed?
- How will Anna keep definitions, caveats, and confidence attached to the signal?
- What are we explicitly not building: a note-cleanup program, universal CRM taxonomy, automated sentiment/provenance system, or dashboard of source-quality scores?

## Cross-signal consistency check — 10 minutes

- Are the triggers mutually consistent and specific enough to produce action?
- Are any signals duplicative or too noisy to act on?
- Are audiences limited to people who can take the named action?
- Do evidence, caveats, confidence, and provenance remain visible together?
- Are observed facts kept distinct from inference across all three signals?
- Does any proposed workflow accidentally become a board dashboard, a prettier internal dashboard, a generic health score, or a new platform layer?
- Does any proposal create a new hiring lane or hiring workflow?

## Decisions and close — 5 minutes

- Confirm the accepted v0.1 operating rule for each signal.
- Record the named owner, first viewer, trigger, next action, evidence bundle, caveat, and source-quality gate.
- Mark any signal that needs more evidence or a tighter threshold before limited discovery.
- Assign owners for unresolved questions: Anna for definitions/caveats; Nadia for scripts, routing, and follow-up; Jake for scope and sequencing; Leo for event provenance and the data/platform seam; Sarah for account-note source quality.
- Capture the explicit “not building” boundary beside every approved signal.

## Hard limits on what Compass v0.1 was building

- No board dashboard.
- No prettier internal dashboard or reporting layer.
- No investor packaging or board narrative as the first deliverable.
- No generic health-score or single account-risk score.
- No broad platform or product surface.
- No separate scoring service or platform layer at this stage.
- No automated escalation or generic upsell engine.
- No bespoke Evergreen side track.
- No new hiring lane, hiring workflow, or staffing expansion.
- No customer-facing use of weakly sourced signals; too-thin notes stay internal.
- No flattening of activation friction, admin handoff/role confusion, procurement/security packaging, expansion stalls after first live sync, and true product gaps into one score.

The first pass stayed narrow: test whether defensible signals changed account-team or customer-growth behavior, using the current lightweight staffing model—not build a new reporting, staffing, or platform system.

messages.content:
[2023-08-01T09:06:00-07:00] Jake’s first-wave shape is finally concrete enough to review with Devon.

Discord group DM — Jake, Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes
2023-08-01 08:47 PT

Jake:
Pulled together a first-pass view on the external Mercury design-partner wave.

My proposal is to use Evergreen Bank as the enterprise-shaped candidate in the first wave.

Why Evergreen:
- They are likely to stress the exact admin/security edges we still care about: admin handoff, role/state clarity, auditability questions, and how trustworthy the early sync/failure path feels.
- That gives us a real test of the standard Mercury path without immediately turning the rollout into bespoke build work.
- Put differently: hard enough to expose whether the product is enterprise-ready on the current path, but still within the boundaries of the product we are actually trying to ship.

I’m keeping the rest of the wave deliberately lighter; the enterprise question is whether Evergreen should be the anchor stress case.

On Acme, I would keep them in the not-now column.
- The NDA scope thread is still muddy enough that sending fresh Mercury material feels like asking for a document fight instead of product signal.
- I do still think their prior feedback is useful internally, especially on admin pain, failure-state legibility, and procurement/security questions.
- I would use that feedback to sharpen blocker rows in MER-1279, but not send Acme new packet/screens/notes unless the NDA thread gets narrowed first.

MER-1279 rows this would pressure-test most directly:
- invited-member/admin handoff confidence
- queued-sync trust / retry confidence
- failed-state legibility and recovery
- admin/security questions that show up before anyone asks for one-off treatment

Not calling any of those closed. This is just the cleanest first-wave shape I can see right now.

If you both agree with the direction, I can turn it into a tighter wave outline before the review.

Give me decision questions for that Devon review, not an announcement. I want them to pressure-test three things: why Evergreen Bank is a good enterprise stress case for admin/security without dragging us into bespoke work, what exactly keeps Acme out while the NDA scope thread is unresolved, and which parts of Acme’s prior feedback can still sharpen internal blocker rows in MER-1279 without sending Acme anything fresh.

Devon review decision questions

Evergreen Bank as the enterprise stress case

1. Does Evergreen test the admin/security risks we care about—admin handoff, role/state clarity, auditability, and sync/failure trust—using the standard Mercury path we intend to ship?

2. What specific evidence would show that Evergreen is exposing a product gap versus simply requesting bespoke treatment?

3. Which Evergreen needs are within the current product boundary, and which requests would be a stop condition for including them in the first wave?

4. What is the minimum first-wave scope that gives us meaningful enterprise signal without committing to custom implementation, integrations, or workflow exceptions?

5. Who decides when an Evergreen request becomes bespoke work, and how will that decision be recorded against MER-1279?

6. If Evergreen surfaces a blocker, what outcome are we looking for: product change before launch, documented limitation, or removal from the wave?

Acme and the unresolved NDA scope

7. What exactly remains unresolved in the NDA scope thread, and what category of Mercury material could that ambiguity put at risk?

8. Is there any fresh material we could send safely under the current scope, or is the correct decision to send nothing until the scope is narrowed in writing?

9. What would constitute sufficient resolution to reconsider Acme—clarified permitted materials, an amended NDA, written confirmation from the relevant parties, or something else?

10. Are we keeping Acme out because of legal exposure, because the ambiguity would distract from product signal, or both?

arguments.body:
# Mercury product offsite — May 12 working agenda

This is an operating offsite, not a launch narrative or deck rehearsal.

## 1. Opening: operating objectives
- Confirm the decisions required in the room.
- Review the highest-impact activation and admin blockers.
- Leave with explicit cuts, owners, evidence, and next checkpoints.

## 2. Activation / onboarding cuts
Decision points:
- Which onboarding work is required for the next release?
- Which requests or polish items are cut from scope?
- What unresolved activation blocker needs an owner today?

Cuts:
- Defer non-blocking UX cleanup and polish that does not affect setup or first value.
- Defer changes that require new measurement before the immediate operating decision.

Blockers:
- Setup friction that prevents users from reaching first value.
- Missing owner or acceptance criteria for any retained onboarding item.

Owner:
- Assign one directly responsible owner per retained item in the room.

## 3. Admin blocker triage
Decision points:
- Which admin issues are rollout blockers versus follow-up bugs?
- What must be fixed for reliable team rollout?
- Which items are explicitly cut from the current cycle?

Blockers to resolve:
- Invite reliability.
- Permission confusion.
- Account-level controls.
- Any admin issue that prevents broader rollout inside a team.

Cuts:
- Defer isolated bugs without a rollout or adoption impact.
- Defer expansion requests that are not needed for the next operating checkpoint.

Owner:
- Assign a directly responsible owner and target checkpoint for each retained blocker.

## 4. Retention instrumentation with Anna
Decision points:
- Which instrumentation or mapping issues block an operating decision?
- Which data-quality work is necessary now, and what can wait?
- What evidence will determine whether the retained activation and admin changes worked?

Blockers:
- Unresolved event mapping or instrumentation gaps.
- Cuts that cannot be evaluated because the evidence path is unclear.
- Conflicting definitions or ownership for the metrics used at the next checkpoint.

Cuts:
- Defer analysis and instrumentation cleanup that does not change a current decision.
- Do not expand the measurement scope beyond the retained work without an owner and checkpoint.

Owner:
- Anna owns the instrumentation readout and documents caveats, required fixes, and the next evidence checkpoint.

## 5. Final decision log
Record on one page:
- What is shipping.
- What is being cut.
- Each blocker and its directly responsible owner.
- Acceptance criteria or evidence for each retained item.
- Next checkpoint and date.

## 6. Close
- Confirm decisions and unresolved escalations.
- Confirm owners and checkpoints aloud.
- Capture only follow-ups that have a named owner and a required decision or deliverable.

arguments.title: Mercury offsite closeout — owners, cuts, launch blockers
arguments.body:
# Mercury offsite closeout

Source: closeout whiteboard transcription, 2023-05-12 late afternoon

## Operating frame
- This is a work-closeout document, not a deck: ship work, owners, cuts, blockers.
- Weekly spine: Jake runs the weekly from this document.
- If discussion turns into narrative polish or a cleaner launch story, cut it.
- Morgan is pulled in only for actual scope calls or unblocking.
- Devon can pressure-test logic, but should not turn it into investor copy.
- Every owner brings: what moved / what slipped / what we cut.
- Customer examples beat opinions.
- Keep the launch-blocker list short and named.

## Launch bar
Launch is ready when:
- Activation works without founder handholding.
- The expansion path is visible in product, not only in slides.
- The top admin pain is reduced enough that calls stop repeating the same three complaints.
- Each blocker has one owner.

## 1. Activation

### Owners
- Priya — path, copy, and screens.
- Jake — implementation, feature flag, and rollout sequence.
- Anna — event definitions and success cut.

### Required by next review
- Set one primary CTA: connect first source.
- Make inviting teammates optional after first value, not before.
- Show sample data only when there is no real event in the first session.
- Define the activation event chain in plain English and as actual events.

### Blockers
- Billing gate timing is unresolved:
  - Before the first real run is probably too much friction.
  - After first value is better, but needs an abuse cap / usage limit.
- Event names are still fuzzy. Anna needs an exact handoff; Jake will not wire to vibes.
- Role-setup copy is too abstract; admins do not know what changes later versus now.
- Feature-flag rollout criteria are not written anywhere.

### Scope cuts
- No template gallery for v1.
- No SSO in the first-run path.
- No advanced permissions setup during activation.
- No logo upload or custom branding in the first run.

### Decision / definition to preserve
- “First value” means connected source plus first successful action; inviting a teammate does not count.
- Stop debating the empty-state illustration.
- Do not reopen the entire settings IA here.

## 2. Expansion

### Owners
- Jake — overall.
- Priya — upgrade moments and UI.
- Anna — usage-threshold sanity check and measurement.

### What stays in
- Expose the upgrade trigger where usage actually hits the limit.
- Provide one clean in-app path from cap hit to plan/owner action.
- Show the admin why the workspace is constrained.
- Keep copy light; no packaging essay.

### Blockers
- Mercury feature-flag rollout remains ambiguous:
  - Who flips it.
  - Merge criteria.
  - Rollback note.
  - Target date.
- The usage-threshold cut is noisy; choose one number the team will actually use.
- Upgrade copy is split between product/admin language and billing language.

### Scope cuts
- No annual-plan flow work for launch.
- No seat-management overhaul.
- No contract-specific enterprise branching in product.
- No pricing-story work in this room.

### Decision / definition to preserve
- The expansion path must exist even if monetization details evolve later.
- If it requires sales explanation every time, it is not launch-ready.

## 3. Admin pain

### Owners
- Jake — backend, account actions, and audit surfaces.
- Priya — admin home and settings grouping.
- Anna — tag incoming issues by severity and frequency.

### Repeated pain to fix
1. Permissions and roles are unclear.
2. Bulk user actions are too manual.
3. There is no clean audit trail for “who changed what.”
4. The wrong person gets admin / billing noise.
5. Settings are scattered across too many places.

### Blockers
- Audit-log scope is unclear: what events are mandatory for launch?
- CSV/import failures still do a poor job explaining what broke to admins.
- The permission-model explanation is too hand-wavy for security-conscious customers.
- Notification-routing rules are not explicit enough.

### Scope cuts
- No full settings redesign.
- No granular notification matrix.
- No admin analytics dashboard.
- No custom role builder.

### Decision / definition to preserve
- Fix repeated pain, not every admin complaint anyone has ever had.
- If a problem only matters after launch scale, write it down and move on.

## Cross-cutting working rules
- Jake runs the weekly from this document, not Morgan.
- Morgan is pulled in only for actual scope calls or unblocking.
- Devon may pressure-test logic, but does not turn it into investor copy.
- Every owner comes to weekly with: what moved / what slipped / what we cut.
- Use customer examples rather than opinions.
- The launch-blocker list stays short and named.

## Open blockers to carry forward
1. Billing gate timing.
2. Activation instrumentation definitions.
3. Mercury feature-flag rollout owner, merge criteria, and rollback criteria.
4. Admin audit-log minimum scope.

## Decisions due
For the next Mercury weekly, close or explicitly assign:
- Billing gate placement relative to first value, including the abuse cap / usage limit.
- Exact activation event names and the plain-English event chain.
- Mercury feature-flag owner, merge criteria, rollback note, and target date.
- One operational usage-threshold number for expansion.
- Minimum launch audit-log event scope.
- Final alignment of upgrade copy between product/admin and billing language.
- Explicit owner for each remaining blocker; no shared-owner ambiguity.

## Compact internal recap for the next Mercury weekly

### Focus
Owners, cuts, blockers, and decisions due. This is not a launch-story or narrative-polish review.

### Owners
- Jake: run the weekly; own implementation/rollout for activation, overall expansion, and backend/account/audit surfaces.
- Priya: activation path/copy/screens, expansion UI/upgrade moments, admin home/settings grouping.
- Anna: activation instrumentation, success cut, usage-threshold measurement, and issue severity/frequency tagging.
- Morgan: scope calls and unblockers only.
- Devon: logic pressure-test only; no investor-copy work.

### Cuts to hold
- Activation: no template gallery, SSO in first run, advanced permissions setup, or branding in first run.
- Expansion: no annual-plan flow, seat-management overhaul, enterprise branching, or pricing-story work.
- Admin: no full settings redesign, granular notification matrix, admin analytics dashboard, or custom role builder.

### Blockers to name in the room
- Billing gate timing and abuse cap / usage limit.
- Exact activation event definitions.
- Mercury feature-flag rollout owner and merge/rollback criteria.
- Admin audit-log minimum scope.

### Decisions due
- Decide billing gate placement relative to first value.
- Lock event names and the activation event chain.
- Assign the feature-flag owner, criteria, rollback note, and target date.
- Pick one usage-threshold number.
- Define mandatory launch audit-log events.
- Reconcile upgrade copy across product/admin and billing language.

### Weekly reporting format
Each owner reports only: what moved / what slipped / what was cut / which decision or unblocker is needed. Do not reopen settings IA, empty-state illustration, pricing story, or the broader launch narrative.

## Guardrail for Monday
Do not let Monday become “can we make this story cleaner.”

# Mercury auth baseline — dogfood follow-up

Source: 2023-06-14 internal dogfood pass on the Monday standard-staging Clerk-backed build (Rishi + 5 internal testers).

## Must-fix before the next dogfood pass

### Clarify org-invite copy
The current org-invite experience is functionally working but is being read as signup rather than joining an existing organization.

- Tighten the invite email subject and body so the recipient clearly understands they are joining an existing organization, not creating a new workspace.
- Update the accept-screen header to make “join existing organization” the explicit primary action/context.
- Re-run the next dogfood pass specifically to confirm that testers distinguish joining an organization from creating a workspace.

Scope boundary: this is copy and comprehension cleanup in the existing invite flow—not a new authentication capability.

## Later-scope items

### SSO shortcut
One tester requested an SSO shortcut instead of the current password / magic-link path.

- Keep this as later scope; do not wedge it into v0.2 or block the next dogfood pass on it.
- Track it separately from the org-invite copy work: SSO changes the authentication options, while the invite issue is clarity in the existing flow.

## Current baseline / no blocker for this round

- Sessions were stable across login, app use, refresh, browser close/reopen, with no surprise logouts.
- Invite accept and revoke worked end to end.
- Magic-link delivery was somewhat slow but did not block internal testers.
- Expired-link handling was understandable enough for this round.

Net: continue dogfooding after the org-invite copy cleanup; treat SSO as later scope.

19:14 — Marcus
Figma keeps marking frames ready while release risks are still unresolved. I am not…

The blur is not really Priya versus Marcus; it is three different decisions being treated as one:

1. Design decision rights
- Priya owns the user-facing activation flow: one primary CTA, live value before invite, no admin detour, and the locked error-state structure.
- These decisions should not be reopened merely because implementation risks exist.

2. Implementation/readiness rights
- Marcus is right to surface credential-state, retry, invite-permission, and SSO/admin-fallback risks.
- But those are release/checklist issues unless they require different user-visible behavior. They need owners, severity, and disposition—not an open-ended Figma debate.

3. Ship-gate authority
- “Frame ready,” “implementation ready,” and “safe for dogfood” are being used interchangeably.
- A resolved frame can still be blocked from dogfood. The missing piece is an explicit release decision-maker/process for accepting or stopping on those blockers.

- Frame 15: one CTA and error layout are design decisions; backend failure mapping, exact states, and retry instrumentation are implementation/readiness decisions.
- Frames 18/21: live sync before invite is a design decision; invite permissions and an SSO/admin fallback are release-risk decisions unless they change the agreed flow.
- Frame 24: the structure is locked; copy and instrumentation still need owners.
- “Ready for dogfood” should not be a Figma status unless it explicitly means design-ready rather than ship-ready.

In-room framing:

“I want to separate the user-flow decision from the dogfood release decision. Priya owns the activation behavior, so today we should treat the one-CTA path, live value before invite, and no admin detour as the design baseline. Marcus should absolutely raise technical blockers, but we’ll record them in the release checklist with an owner and disposition. A blocker can stop dogfood without reopening a resolved frame; we only reopen the flow if the implementation constraint changes user-visible behavior. Before we leave, let’s decide the remaining copy and reminder behavior, name owners for retry and invite-permission risks, and identify who makes the final dogfood go/no-go call.”

Evergreen Bank’s admin/security review is demanding enough to pressure-test the current Mercury path under real enterprise scrutiny, without turning wave 1 into a bespoke build. Evergreen is useful because it tests the enterprise edge without forcing a special-case rollout.

[Tab: Devon_notes]
- Evergreen is the clearest live case: 14 invited users are in now, but Sarah Kim's expected real footprint is 45–60 active developers with the second admin group and 110–130 only if the security/procurement expansion happens. Full directory size is much bigger than any honest current-usage number.
- The two anonymized design-partner rows show the same shape at a smaller scale: first month starts in the 9–24 range, and month 3 can plausibly land anywhere from the mid-30s to around 90 if rollout sticks.
- Pure MAU answers the usage question cleanly, but it creates too little floor for procurement.
- Pure seat gives a stronger floor, but it prices theoretical access more than real adoption.
- My bias is some kind of floor + usage-ramp model, but I am not calling the number structure yet. Tuesday's discussion should be about what floor we actually need without pretending every directory seat is live.

Give me a decision-prep read, not a final decision record yet. Compare pure MAU, pure seat/directory, and a hybrid platform-minimum plus active-developer-band model. Frame it around the tradeoff I actually need to settle with Devon: honest usage-ramp logic versus a procurement floor he can forecast against.

Decision-prep read: Mercury pricing check

Core tradeoff

Devon’s export points to a consistent pattern:

- Real usage starts narrow: 9–24 active developers in month 1, or 14 invited users at Evergreen today.
- Usage can expand materially: roughly 35–90 active developers by month 3 for the design partners, and potentially 45–60 at Evergreen before any larger security/procurement expansion.
- Directory or enterprise seat counts are substantially larger than the group actually using Mercury.

The decision is therefore not “usage or seats” in the abstract. It is:

“How do we preserve an honest usage-ramp story while giving procurement and forecasting a minimum commercial commitment?”

1. Pure MAU / active-developer pricing

What it gets right

- Closely tracks actual adoption.
- Makes the ramp visible and defensible.
- Avoids charging for inactive directory access.
- Fits Evergreen especially well: 14 current users is clearly different from the possible 45–60 and 110–130 expansion cases.

Main downside

- Month-1 pricing may look too small or volatile for enterprise procurement.
- Forecasting becomes dependent on rollout timing and adoption behavior.
- A customer can have meaningful implementation, support, security, and platform costs before usage reaches a commercially useful level.
- “Active” needs a precise definition or the model will create counting disputes.

Implication

Pure MAU is the most honest measurement model, but probably provides too little procurement floor in the first live phase.

2. Pure seat / directory pricing

What it gets right

- Simple PO and budget framing.
- Produces a predictable contract value.
- Gives Mercury a floor that is easier to forecast.
- May align with how enterprise buyers already think about software access.

Main downside

- It prices theoretical access rather than actual rollout.
- Evergreen demonstrates the problem directly: the full enterprise directory is not a credible proxy for the 14 users live today or even the expected 45–60 active developers.
- It could make early adoption look artificially expensive and create resistance before value is demonstrated.
- It weakens the credibility of the pricing story if the customer knows that most seats are inactive.

Implication

Pure seat pricing solves procurement predictability by sacrificing the usage logic Devon’s data is trying to preserve. It risks charging the org chart rather than the deployment.

3. Hybrid: platform minimum plus active-developer bands

What it gets right

- Establishes a predictable platform floor for procurement and forecasting.
- Preserves a connection between price and actual rollout.
- Handles the difference between current usage, likely expansion, and speculative expansion.
- Avoids treating Evergreen’s entire directory as immediately billable.
- Gives customers a clearer path from initial deployment to broader adoption.

Main downside

- Requires two simple rules:
  1. What the platform minimum covers.
  2. How active-developer bands are counted and priced.
- Can become confusing if there are too many bands, exceptions, or reconciliation mechanics.
- The floor could quietly become a disguised seat minimum if set too high.
- The model needs a clear treatment of temporary spikes, inactive users, and expansion timing.

Implication

This appears closest to the deployment pattern in the export, but only if the minimum is genuinely a platform/procurement floor and not a proxy for full directory size.

Side-by-side

| Model | Usage honesty | Procurement predictability | Early-phase fit | Main risk |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Pure MAU | Highest | Low | Good for proving adoption | Too little commercial floor |
| Pure seat/directory | Low | Highest | Weak where rollout is narrow | Overpricing theoretical access |
| Hybrid floor + active bands | High if designed carefully | Medium-high | Strongest overall fit | Complexity or an oversized floor |

# September Mercury metrics package — board and H2 prep bounds

**Prepared from:** Anna Martinez’s September Mercury metrics package
**Date of source package:** Sep 6, 2023
**Audience:** Morgan, Devon, Jake
**Status:** Internal prep document

## Purpose and reporting bounds

Keep Mercury reporting in two distinct layers:

1. **Board-operating layer:** appropriate for leadership/board operating alignment and selective H2 prep context.
2. **Internal weekly diagnostics layer:** for operating decisions only; not for board notes, board charts, investor materials, or external/customer communication.

This document preserves the useful operating signal without turning the package into outside proof.

## What the board-operating layer supports

Board-operating alignment and selective H2 prep are supported because:

- Real-source/live-sync activation is cleaner than the repaired May comparable baseline under the current 7-day definition.
- Admin setup friction is down for the current design-partner cohort.
- Evergreen Bank adds meaningful enterprise substance through real admin/user handoff, real-source connections, and repeated live-sync usage rather than preview-only activity.

### Comparable activation view

**Definition:** Activated within 7 days means the account reached either `real_source_connected` or `first_live_sync_completed` within 7 days of workspace creation. Sample-preview-only accounts are excluded from the denominator.

| Cohort / cut | Eligible accounts | Activated within 7 days | Rate | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Repaired May comparable design-partner cut | 10 | 4 | 40% | Corrected May definition; useful baseline only, not for patching older external charts |
| Current design-partner cohort (workspaces created Jul 31–Aug 27) | 11 | 8 | 73% | Current Mercury test flow with real-source/live-sync evidence |

### Admin-friction view

| Metric | Repaired May comparable cut | Current design-partner cohort | Direction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Median days from workspace creation to first invited member accepted | 5.4 | 2.3 | better |
| Accounts needing manual admin intervention after initial setup | 6 / 10 | 2 / 11 | better |
| Accounts reaching first non-owner user within 7 days | 3 / 10 | 7 / 11 | better |

### Evergreen Bank evidence

- Evergreen is the first account in this set that looks like a real admin + user handoff rather than a single champion walking preview data.
- Through Sep 4, Evergreen shows 4 admin users touching setup/settings, 12 invited members, 3 real sources connected, and successful live-sync activity on 8 distinct days.
- The account shows repeated usage after setup rather than a one-day spike.
- This is meaningful enterprise-pattern evidence for internal/board operating context, but it is still one account—not a blanket enterprise-validation claim.

## What remains unresolved

**Expansion is still uneven.** The 30-day account-level read is mixed: Evergreen is the strongest positive signal; several accounts are flat; and others are choppy, fragile, or down. The roll-up is 3 accounts meaningfully up, 3 mostly flat, and 2 choppy or down. Do not present expansion as solved.

**Weekly activation movement is internal-only.** The weekly diagnostics layer has small samples and is sensitive to account mix. It is useful for debugging admin/setup friction and sample-preview exclusions, but it must not appear in board notes, board charts, investor materials, or external/customer communication.

## Explicit non-claims

This package:

- Does **not** prove retention is solved.
- Does **not** solve or prove expansion.
- Does **not** make the Mercury story external-ready or constitute outside proof.

Safe framing: September is materially better than the May operating read on cleaner activation and admin handoff; Evergreen contributes meaningful enterprise-pattern evidence; expansion remains uneven; and weekly activation movement stays internal-only.

## Internal weekly diagnostics layer — operating use only

| Workspace-creation week | Eligible accounts with full 7-day window elapsed | Activated within 7 days | 7-day rate | Sample-preview-only exclusions | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Jul 31 week | 3 | 2 | 67% | 1 | first cleaner post-preview split |
| Aug 7 week | 3 | 2 | 67% | 1 | invited-member handoff improved |
| Aug 14 week | 3 | 2 | 67% | 0 | steady but still small-n |
| Aug 21 week | 2 | 2 | 100% | 1 | strongest week so far |
| Aug 28 week | 0 | pending | pending | 0 | full 7-day window not complete at cutoff |

**Handling rule:** Keep this layer explicitly internal-only and use it only for operating decisions.

arguments.title: Mercury / Evergreen Procurement Packet — Final
arguments.body:
# Mercury / Evergreen Procurement Packet

**Status:** Final procurement-ready packet  
**Prepared for:** Evergreen Bank  
**Product:** Mercury  
**Commercial/procurement owner:** Devon Hayes

## 1. Purpose

This packet summarizes the current Mercury design-partner deployment for procurement and security review. It covers the current commercial model, login and setup experience, current admin/security posture for the bounded launch experience, and known enterprise-readiness gaps that are outside current launch scope.

## 2. Commercial model

Mercury is priced on monthly active developer usage, not purchased seats or directory size.

- **Pilot:** $2,500 per month platform minimum, including up to 50 monthly active developers
- **Growth:** $7,500 per month platform minimum, including up to 200 monthly active developers
- **Overage:** $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers

Monthly active developer usage is the pricing driver. Scaffold internal and test users do not count toward usage. Preview/sample-only behavior is separate from activation reporting and is not usage proof by itself.

This is the standard commercial baseline for the current bounded evaluation and may support expansion if usage widens. It is not a custom Evergreen carveout.

## 3. Current Mercury scope

Evergreen is in the first external design-partner wave, and the current live experience includes:

- Clerk-backed sessions
- Magic-link sign-in
- Organization invites
- A setup flow oriented around connecting a real source
- Preview/sample data available only as preview behavior
- The first live sync path in the product

Preview/sample-only behavior does not activate an account and must not be treated as equivalent to a real source connection or live sync completion.

For operating review, activation is defined as either:

- `real_source_connected` within 7 days; or
- `first_live_sync_completed` within 7 days

## 4. Current login and setup experience

The current Mercury flow is:

1. An invited user enters through the magic-link or organization-invite flow.
2. The user lands in the Mercury workspace context.
3. The user connects a real source.
4. The user reaches the first live sync.

Session handling is Clerk-backed. The current flow is intentionally bounded to the design-partner experience.

## 5. Current admin and security posture

The current product facts are:

- Access is handled through the current magic-link and organization-invite flow.
- Organization-level invitation is available in the current Mercury experience.
- The launch experience is bounded and narrower than a full enterprise admin/security package.
- Product and security review should be based on the current scope described here.

The current launch scope does not include SSO, deeper admin controls, or audit history for admin changes. This packet does not represent Mercury as having a complete enterprise-ready login, administration, or audit-control package.

## 6. Known enterprise-readiness gaps

The following are open enterprise-readiness gaps identified through review:

- SSO
- Audit history for admin changes
- Clearer separation between admin permissions and billing-owner controls
- Procurement materials that can stand on their own without live explanation

These items are not part of the current launch scope.

## 7. Later-scope controls and commercial treatment

SSO, audit history, and deeper admin controls are roadmap-dependent add-ons, not included in the current launch package. They are not committed features or part of the current Mercury scope. If and when any of these controls ship, the applicable scope and commercial terms will be reviewed and quoted at that time.

No bespoke Evergreen roadmap, delivery timing, or procurement commitment is implied by this packet.

## 8. Appendix A — product facts

- Evergreen is in the first external design-partner wave already live.
- The live flow uses Clerk for sessions, magic links, and organization invites.
- Sample data remains preview-only and non-activating.
- Activation is measured as `real_source_connected` or `first_live_sync_completed` within 7 days.
- Current product scope excludes SSO and deeper admin controls.

[2023-09-27T19:31:00-07:00] Devon’s rough pass for tomorrow is here.

From: Devon Hayes
To: Morgan Chen
Date: Wed, 27 Sep 2023 19:12:00 -0700
Subject: Thursday prep — rough October investor path

Morgan —

Rough pass before tomorrow so we can decide whether to put real walls around this instead of letting random September inbound set the agenda.

What I think is supportable now

- We finally have a real Mercury story grounded in external use, not just planned-launch narrative.
- The September package is usable if we keep the framing disciplined: activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave; Anna’s quarterly cohort view is credible context; the corrected weekly cuts are helpful operating read, not proof.
- Evergreen is useful evidence in two ways: (1) there is real enterprise pull serious enough to get procurement/commercial attention, and (2) the enterprise-readiness gaps are now concrete rather than abstract.
- Hybrid pricing gives us a cleaner commercial frame. Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands is much easier to explain than the earlier seat-ish ambiguity.

What I do not think we can blur

- We cannot tell a “retention is solved” story. It still is not.
- We cannot present expansion as clean. Some rows are moving; some are still uneven.
- We cannot use Evergreen’s procurement motion as proof that enterprise readiness is already there. Their feedback is basically the current gap list: SSO timing, audit history for admin changes, clearer admin vs billing-owner separation, and a procurement packet that can stand without one of us live-explaining it.
- We cannot let the pricing decision imply enterprise add-ons are in-market beyond what is actually shipped.

How I would frame the investor path

I think there is a version of reopening that is disciplined and a version that turns into cosplay. The disciplined version is: selective, October, and explicitly based on whether the investor can underwrite the real Mercury story. Not “market is hot again, let’s spray meetings.”

Elena feels like the right first conversation in that frame. She already engaged seriously once and her pass was thoughtful, not generic. If we go back to her, the point is calibration and context: does the more honest Mercury picture change the read at all? That is very different from treating Elena as the start of a broad process.

Short-list criteria

Only keep firms that can handle all of the following without pushing us into story inflation:
1. uneven expansion / not-yet-solved retention
2. enterprise-readiness gaps that are real but scoped
3. a usage-based commercial model that is cleaner but still young
4. a deliberately narrow process instead of a manufactured auction

Rough list

1) Elena Volkov — warm-context bucket
- Best use: first calibration conversation
- Why: prior feedback was substantive; she'd pressure-test the actual story
- Caveat: only useful if we stay honest about what still is not proven

2) Firm A — possible fit if we keep the narrative operational
- Tends to understand infra/devtools motion
- Biggest risk is they will immediately push on expansion consistency

3) Firm B — possible fit if the commercial story is crisp
- Could appreciate the cleaner pricing frame
- Risk is enterprise checklist bias if the packet still requires too much live explanation

4) Firm C — maybe
- Thoughtful and patient
- Might be more useful as signal than as an actual lead if we are keeping the list tight

September inbound / coffee noise

I have three stray September asks that I think should probably stay out:
- two mutual-intro coffee requests that feel more social than decision-relevant
- one “in town next week” inbound that looks like calendar tax
Given where we are, I think saying yes to these just makes the whole thing feel broader than it is.

Questions for tomorrow
- Are we comfortable calling this a selective October reopen internally, or do we want even tighter language?
- Is Elena definitely first, or do we want one more p…

Decision-prep read

Bottom line

There is enough to support a selective October investor calibration, but not a broad process or a “reopening” that implies the company has crossed a major proof point. The honest story is:

Mercury has moved from planned-launch narrative to externally grounded usage and commercial signal. Activation and admin friction improved in the design-partner wave, enterprise demand is concrete enough to trigger procurement attention, and the pricing model is becoming easier to explain. But retention is not solved, expansion is uneven, and enterprise readiness remains an explicit workstream rather than a completed capability.

I would use “selective October calibration” internally. “Reopen” risks sounding more process-oriented and final than the evidence supports.

What can support the story

1. External usage, not just roadmap
- Mercury now has a real story grounded in external use.
- The design-partner wave provides evidence of improved activation and reduced admin friction.
- The September package can credibly show movement, provided the cuts are presented as operating evidence rather than proof of durable retention.

2. Credible cohort context
- Anna’s quarterly cohort view is useful context for how usage is developing.
- It should support a nuanced trajectory discussion, not a claim that the business has established repeatable retention or expansion.

3. Concrete enterprise pull
- Evergreen’s procurement and commercial attention demonstrate that the problem is important enough for a serious enterprise buyer to engage.
- This is evidence of demand and urgency, not evidence that Mercury is already enterprise-ready.

4. Cleaner commercial framing
- Pilot/Growth as MAU-based platform bands are easier to explain than the earlier seat-like ambiguity.
- The pricing decision gives investors a clearer model for how usage may translate into revenue.
- It is still a young model, so the story should emphasize clarity and learning rather than pricing validation.

5. A more credible operating posture
- The strongest investor signal may be the discipline of naming what is not proven.
- A selective process reinforces that the team is testing the story and choosing conversations for learning, not manufacturing momentum.

Gaps we cannot blur

1. Retention
Do not say or imply that retention is solved. The correct framing is that activation and early operating friction improved, while durable retention remains under validation.

2. Expansion
Expansion is uneven. Avoid aggregate or anecdotal examples that make the pattern look cleaner than the underlying rows. Show the distribution or explicitly label the evidence as mixed.

3. Enterprise readiness
Evergreen’s procurement motion should not become a proxy for readiness. The gaps are specific:
- SSO timing
- audit history for administrative changes
- clearer separation between administrators and billing owners
- a procurement packet that stands without live explanation

The positive point is that the gaps are now scoped and actionable. The negative point is that they are still gaps.

4. Pricing maturity
The hybrid/MAU-based model is cleaner, but enterprise add-ons must not be presented as in-market unless they are actually shipped. Pricing clarity is not the same as commercial validation.

5. September inbound
Do not let stray coffees or “in town next week” meetings create the appearance of a wider process. They are not decision-relevant enough to justify expanding the calendar or the narrative.

Short-list criteria

Keep only investors who can underwrite the actual version of the company, without requiring story inflation:

- Comfortable with uneven expansion and unresolved retention.
- Able to distinguish enterprise demand from enterprise readiness.
- Understand usage-based or MAU-based commercial models that are still being proven.
- Willing to evaluate a narrow, founder-led calibration process rather than demand a manufactured auction.

Title: Northstar diligence — retention methodology note (September / October Mercury cohorts)

Purpose
This note stays on the existing September / October 2023 external Mercury cohort package. It does not introduce a broader pipeline view, weekly operating cuts, or sample-preview diagnostics.

1) Cohort construction / scope
For the September and October 2023 external cohorts, 'entered the bounded Mercury flow' means an account entered the current bounded Mercury setup path used in the external package: invited into the product, able to access by the current invite / magic-link path, able to interact with preview-only sample data if present, and then progress toward connecting a real source and completing a first live sync. The construction is intentionally limited to that bounded Mercury flow and does not widen into a broader top-of-funnel or sales-pipeline view.

2) Activation definition
For the outside-reader view, activated within 7 days means that within the first seven days after entering the bounded Mercury flow, the account either:
- connected a real source, or
- completed a first live sync.

The following do not count as activation:
- sample import / preview-only behavior
- invite sent
- invite accepted
- preview viewed
- source selected in-product
- similar first-week motion that does not reach real-source connection or first live sync

3) October 19/27 versus 16/27
In the October 2023 cohort, 19 of 27 accounts were activated within 7 days and 16 of 27 completed first live sync within 7 days. The full gap between those two numbers is 3 accounts that connected a real source within 7 days but did not complete first live sync in that same seven-day window.

There is no additional preview-only, invite-only, or source-selected-only state inside the activation numerator.

4) Expansion / longer-window caveat
The external package stays week-one focused because that is the defensible read from the current September / October cohort set. The improved signal is that more accounts are getting through the first-admin path to real-source connection and, from there, into first live sync inside the first seven days.

That does not mean downstream expansion is clean. Expansion after the initial admin/setup path remains uneven, and late-October accounts still do not support a clean longer-window expansion read. The appropriate outside-reader takeaway is improved activation/admin path rather than expansion solved.

Weekly cuts, sample-preview diagnostics, and similar operating views remain internal only. They are not the board / investor view and are not being added to this confirmatory package.

arguments.title: Leadership Recap — Mercury Reset (February 26, 2024)
arguments.body:
# Leadership Recap — Mercury Reset

**Date:** February 26, 2024  
**Attendees:** Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes, Jake, Leo Park, Priya, Anna Martinez  
**Opening handoff and enterprise-packaging section:** Sarah Kim

## Operating line

**More room, same discipline. Defensible story, not a bigger story.**

The close is not permission to describe Mercury as enterprise-ready today or to reopen every deferred initiative. We will use shipped and current product facts, keep the next phase bounded, and avoid turning customer interest into bespoke commitments or roadmap negotiation.

## Ownership and operating decisions

- **Jake — Mercury execution and launch evidence.** Jake owns Mercury execution and the weekly launch-evidence path. **MER-1279 remains the internal operating ledger for launch-relevant evidence**, with links back to source evidence rather than summary theater.
- **Leo Park — platform seams and release discipline.** Leo owns platform seams, release discipline, and cases where sync trust or system behavior crosses from cleanup into architecture or system-risk work.
- **Priya — activation and onboarding UX.** Priya owns activation/onboarding UX, admin/setup clarity, and failure-state legibility. Settled design decisions stay settled unless new evidence changes the conclusion.
- **Anna Martinez — retention evidence.** Anna owns retention evidence, cohort-definition discipline, and the board-consistent outside-reader package.
- **Devon Hayes + Sarah Kim — enterprise-readiness commercial packaging.** Devon owns enterprise-readiness commercial framing and procurement packaging, working with Sarah on the customer/external coordination lane. Current-state material must use shipped or current product facts only. Jake and Leo provide product facts and seam-risk input; they do not backdoor roadmap promises into customer material.
- **Morgan Chen — board follow-through and sequencing.** Morgan owns board follow-through, sequencing, dates and promises, explicit not-yet lines, and the hiring sequence.

The close-thread handoff is explicit: Sarah keeps the customer coordination lane, while the operating owners take back their respective lanes.

## Bounded enterprise-readiness sequence

The next-phase list is limited to:

1. SSO timing
2. Admin-change audit history
3. Clearer separation between the admin owner and billing owner
4. A standalone procurement packet

There are **no Evergreen-specific commitments, no feature dates, and no enterprise add-on quoting before the relevant work ships**. Evergreen Bank remains a useful stress case for the current path—not a reason to convert wave-1 learning into bespoke-build behavior.

Enterprise-readiness review remains a separate lane from current Mercury release work so it does not contaminate every release note.

## Board and investor follow-through

The first post-close board framing will stay focused on defensible retention evidence and repeatable enterprise expansion learned through Mercury/Evergreen—not a rush to spin a Series C story.

MER-1279 and Leo Park’s risk readout are internal operating evidence, not board or investor proof claims. Anna Martinez and Morgan Chen will keep the board pack tight:

- retention truth,
- expansion truth, and
- bounded enterprise-readiness next steps.

## Hiring decision

**The second Mercury engineering requisition is not being reopened.**

The **first new search to scope is a customer-growth / GTM leader**, not an immediate Mercury engineering search. The role is intended to build a repeatable customer-growth motion from Mercury/Evergreen-like pull without turning accounts into bespoke commitments or product-roadmap negotiating sessions.

Devon Hayes and HR will draft the initial role description. Morgan Chen will review it before it goes beyond the small reset group.

If Mercury engineering hiring is reconsidered later, the existing evidence rule remains in force:

- senior hire for repeated platform/architecture seam failures requiring independent ownership;
- implementation-heavy mid-level hire for hardening/throughput constraints; or
- no requisition if the current split can close the remaining work.

## Near-term cadence

- The short weekly Mercury truth check stays focused on support edges, live-sync trust, admin friction, and what is materially changing in product.
- Enterprise-readiness review remains a separate lane from current Mercury release work.
- Owners have now taken back their operating lanes from the close-thread handoff.

Scaffold is moving from founder-led customer development toward a repeatable customer-growth motion.
