arguments.title: Mercury offsite closeout — owners, cuts, launch blockers
arguments.body:
# Mercury offsite closeout

Source: closeout whiteboard transcription, 2023-05-12 late afternoon

## Operating frame
- This is a work-closeout document, not a deck: ship work, owners, cuts, blockers.
- Weekly spine: Jake runs the weekly from this document.
- If discussion turns into narrative polish or a cleaner launch story, cut it.
- Morgan is pulled in only for actual scope calls or unblocking.
- Devon can pressure-test logic, but should not turn it into investor copy.
- Every owner brings: what moved / what slipped / what we cut.
- Customer examples beat opinions.
- Keep the launch-blocker list short and named.

## Launch bar
Launch is ready when:
- Activation works without founder handholding.
- The expansion path is visible in product, not only in slides.
- The top admin pain is reduced enough that calls stop repeating the same three complaints.
- Each blocker has one owner.

## 1. Activation

### Owners
- Priya — path, copy, and screens.
- Jake — implementation, feature flag, and rollout sequence.
- Anna — event definitions and success cut.

### Required by next review
- Set one primary CTA: connect first source.
- Make inviting teammates optional after first value, not before.
- Show sample data only when there is no real event in the first session.
- Define the activation event chain in plain English and as actual events.

### Blockers
- Billing gate timing is unresolved:
  - Before the first real run is probably too much friction.
  - After first value is better, but needs an abuse cap / usage limit.
- Event names are still fuzzy. Anna needs an exact handoff; Jake will not wire to vibes.
- Role-setup copy is too abstract; admins do not know what changes later versus now.
- Feature-flag rollout criteria are not written anywhere.

### Scope cuts
- No template gallery for v1.
- No SSO in the first-run path.
- No advanced permissions setup during activation.
- No logo upload or custom branding in the first run.

### Decision / definition to preserve
- “First value” means connected source plus first successful action; inviting a teammate does not count.
- Stop debating the empty-state illustration.
- Do not reopen the entire settings IA here.

## 2. Expansion

### Owners
- Jake — overall.
- Priya — upgrade moments and UI.
- Anna — usage-threshold sanity check and measurement.

### What stays in
- Expose the upgrade trigger where usage actually hits the limit.
- Provide one clean in-app path from cap hit to plan/owner action.
- Show the admin why the workspace is constrained.
- Keep copy light; no packaging essay.

### Blockers
- Mercury feature-flag rollout remains ambiguous:
  - Who flips it.
  - Merge criteria.
  - Rollback note.
  - Target date.
- The usage-threshold cut is noisy; choose one number the team will actually use.
- Upgrade copy is split between product/admin language and billing language.

### Scope cuts
- No annual-plan flow work for launch.
- No seat-management overhaul.
- No contract-specific enterprise branching in product.
- No pricing-story work in this room.

### Decision / definition to preserve
- The expansion path must exist even if monetization details evolve later.
- If it requires sales explanation every time, it is not launch-ready.

## 3. Admin pain

### Owners
- Jake — backend, account actions, and audit surfaces.
- Priya — admin home and settings grouping.
- Anna — tag incoming issues by severity and frequency.

### Repeated pain to fix
1. Permissions and roles are unclear.
2. Bulk user actions are too manual.
3. There is no clean audit trail for “who changed what.”
4. The wrong person gets admin / billing noise.
5. Settings are scattered across too many places.

### Blockers
- Audit-log scope is unclear: what events are mandatory for launch?
- CSV/import failures still do a poor job explaining what broke to admins.
- The permission-model explanation is too hand-wavy for security-conscious customers.
- Notification-routing rules are not explicit enough.

### Scope cuts
- No full settings redesign.
- No granular notification matrix.
- No admin analytics dashboard.
- No custom role builder.

### Decision / definition to preserve
- Fix repeated pain, not every admin complaint anyone has ever had.
- If a problem only matters after launch scale, write it down and move on.

## Cross-cutting working rules
- Jake runs the weekly from this document, not Morgan.
- Morgan is pulled in only for actual scope calls or unblocking.
- Devon may pressure-test logic, but does not turn it into investor copy.
- Every owner comes to weekly with: what moved / what slipped / what we cut.
- Use customer examples rather than opinions.
- The launch-blocker list stays short and named.

## Open blockers to carry forward
1. Billing gate timing.
2. Activation instrumentation definitions.
3. Mercury feature-flag rollout owner, merge criteria, and rollback criteria.
4. Admin audit-log minimum scope.

## Decisions due
For the next Mercury weekly, close or explicitly assign:
- Billing gate placement relative to first value, including the abuse cap / usage limit.
- Exact activation event names and the plain-English event chain.
- Mercury feature-flag owner, merge criteria, rollback note, and target date.
- One operational usage-threshold number for expansion.
- Minimum launch audit-log event scope.
- Final alignment of upgrade copy between product/admin and billing language.
- Explicit owner for each remaining blocker; no shared-owner ambiguity.

## Compact internal recap for the next Mercury weekly

### Focus
Owners, cuts, blockers, and decisions due. This is not a launch-story or narrative-polish review.

### Owners
- Jake: run the weekly; own implementation/rollout for activation, overall expansion, and backend/account/audit surfaces.
- Priya: activation path/copy/screens, expansion UI/upgrade moments, admin home/settings grouping.
- Anna: activation instrumentation, success cut, usage-threshold measurement, and issue severity/frequency tagging.
- Morgan: scope calls and unblockers only.
- Devon: logic pressure-test only; no investor-copy work.

### Cuts to hold
- Activation: no template gallery, SSO in first run, advanced permissions setup, or branding in first run.
- Expansion: no annual-plan flow, seat-management overhaul, enterprise branching, or pricing-story work.
- Admin: no full settings redesign, granular notification matrix, admin analytics dashboard, or custom role builder.

### Blockers to name in the room
- Billing gate timing and abuse cap / usage limit.
- Exact activation event definitions.
- Mercury feature-flag rollout owner and merge/rollback criteria.
- Admin audit-log minimum scope.

### Decisions due
- Decide billing gate placement relative to first value.
- Lock event names and the activation event chain.
- Assign the feature-flag owner, criteria, rollback note, and target date.
- Pick one usage-threshold number.
- Define mandatory launch audit-log events.
- Reconcile upgrade copy across product/admin and billing language.

### Weekly reporting format
Each owner reports only: what moved / what slipped / what was cut / which decision or unblocker is needed. Do not reopen settings IA, empty-state illustration, pricing story, or the broader launch narrative.

## Guardrail for Monday
Do not let Monday become “can we make this story cleaner.”

messages.content:
Monday ask list

Jake drives the weekly
- Run one visible operating list: blocker → owner → next decision.
- Bring the implementation/rollout status for:
  - Activation: feature flag, rollout sequence, and exact event handoff from Anna.
  - Expansion: cap-hit path, one operational usage threshold, and upgrade trigger.
  - Admin: backend/account actions, permission dependencies, audit-log minimum scope.
- Force a disposition on each open blocker: ship, cut, assign an owner/date, or escalate.
- Report only: what moved, what slipped, what was cut, and what decision/unblocker is needed.
- Keep the blocker list short and named; use customer examples over opinions.

Stays with Priya
- Activation path, copy, and screens:
  - Connect-first CTA.
  - Optional teammate invite after first value.
  - Clear fallback when connection is skipped or fails.
  - Role/setup clarity.
- Expansion UI and upgrade moments.
- Admin home and settings grouping.
- She should identify UX confusion, but not absorb backend or permissions defects as “copy work.”

Stays with Anna
- Exact activation event definitions and the plain-English event chain.
- Success cut and instrumentation quality/freshness.
- Usage-threshold sanity check for expansion.
- Severity/frequency tagging for incoming admin issues.
- Explicitly separate fresh signal from backfill or noise.

Specific cutoffs for narrative polish
- If someone proposes a “why Mercury / why now” opening, a cleaner launch story, or investor framing: “Not a Monday decision. What changes in scope, behavior, or ownership?”
- If Devon suggests slides, charts, retention framing, or packaging language: let him pressure-test the logic, then stop the conversion into investor copy.
- If discussion turns to pricing-story work, annual-plan flow, enterprise branching, or a packaging essay: park it.
- If anyone reopens the empty-state illustration, full settings IA, broad redesign, or every possible admin complaint: point to the existing cuts and ask whether it blocks launch.
- If a topic has no concrete decision, owner, acceptance criterion, or checkpoint: cut it from the weekly.

The Monday test: if it does not move activation, expansion-in-product, repeated admin pain, or a named launch blocker, it belongs in the parking lot—not the weekly.

Status: Open
Author: Marcus
Time: 2023-06-06 18:19 PT
Comment:
For the recovery path, do we want retry-in-place, back-to-provider-list, or a support CTA?

This is less about visuals and more about whether the design is claiming a recovery path we can actually support in the first cut.
Replies:

Give me a neutral read on which comments are product decisions I need to make versus implementation…

Product decisions for you

1. C-223 — Activation promise
   - Decide whether the headline is:
     - “Connect your first source” — literal, lower-risk promise, or
     - “Get your first live sync” — stronger activation framing, dependent on sync reliability.
   - This is a product positioning and success-definition decision.

2. C-231 — “Skip for now”
   - Decide whether skipping source connection is allowed in the Mercury launch flow.
   - The implications are product scope, activation-state definition, support workflow, and reporting—not just UI.

3. C-241 — Teammate invite timing and scope
   - Decide whether invite is:
     - Part of launch-day activation,
     - Visible but explicitly secondary, or
     - Deferred until after first live sync.
   - This determines what counts as initial success and whether invite-related states need to ship in the first handoff.

4. C-244 — Recovery policy
   - Decide what recovery experience Mercury is willing to support initially:
     - Retry in place,
     - Return to provider list,
     - Support escalation, or
     - A constrained combination.
   - The key decision is whether the first cut promises self-serve recovery or acknowledges operational intervention.

Implementation-readiness concerns

1. C-219 — Missing provider error states
   - Define and provide states for:
     - Provider timeout,
     - Expired magic link,
     - Permission denied after OAuth.
   - These are required before engineering handoff, even if the primary flow is otherwise stable.

2. C-227 — Loading-state protections

3. C-241 — Invite-state coverage

4. C-244 — Recovery-state implementation

Already-resolved design work

- C-214 — Primary versus secondary action hierarchy.
- C-236 — Reduced supporting copy.
- C-227 — Loading and CTA lock behavior.

Mercury activation surface handoff review
Date: Wed, Jul 5, 2023
Attendees: Morgan Chen, Priya, Marcus, Anna Martinez
Purpose: lock the handoff between Figma source-of-truth and implementation ship gates before the next internal dogfood

Notes

1. Surface / state ownership
- Priya said the Figma v0.2 activation surface is still the design source of truth.
- No new state exploration in this pass; the user-facing surface stays at the reviewed four branches:
  1) no source connected
  2) invited member waiting on admin / first source
  3) first sync queued
  4) sync failed
- Locked CTA labels remain:
  - no source: “Connect a data source”
  - invited member: “View setup guide”
  - queued: no primary CTA
  - failed: “Try again”

2. What moved out of design debate and into implementation gates
- Marcus said the blocker list is being translated into Linear checklist gates rather than kept as open design discussion.
- Checklist / gate items Marcus read back:
  - sample data stays visually separate / preview-only and must not create an activated-looking path
  - sample data must be excluded from activation eventing
  - invited-member rendering must use server role plus source state
  - queued sync must show honest status only; no fake percent and no ETA / countdown
  - failed sync must use normalized buckets: auth / permissions, source unavailable / timeout, unknown / retry
  - retry must be idempotent
  - no raw vendor strings in UI
- Marcus said if implementation finds a mismatch, he will name it in review with Priya instead of routing around it in chat.

3. Anna’s data / definition check
- Anna asked for final proof before the next dogfood gate is treated as clear:
  - eventing excludes `sample_import_completed` and any sample-data path from activation
  - activation still maps only to `real_source_connected` or `first_live_sync_completed` within 7 days
- She does not want a “looks activated” UI path to leak into the metric definition.

4. Quick read on Priya / Marcus split
- Morgan asked whether any of the same blocker items are still being argued twice, once as design and again as release-readiness.
- Priya said no: the surface and states live in Figma; implementation gates belong in the checklist.
- Marcus agreed and said he is not looking to reopen the state map, only to gate the implementation against it.

5. Parked as follow-up / polish, not launch blockers
- setup-guide copy tightening
- small-width preview-card spacing cleanup
- failed-state icon polish; neutral warning circle direction still holds, not broken-link

Follow-ups
- Priya to send the final Figma frame reference for the four-state surface.
- Marcus to post the translated Linear checklist gates.
- Anna to review once the proof on eventing / definition alignment is posted.

Turn this into a tight decision table for me only: release gates, design source-of-truth, implementation checklist work, and polish. I especially want the table to make clear whether Priya and Marcus have stopped treating the same blockers as a design debate.

Mercury activation-surface handoff — decision table

| Area | Decision / requirement | Owner / source of truth | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Release gates | Four reviewed branches only: no source, invited member awaiting admin/first source, first sync queued, sync failed. | Priya’s reviewed Figma surface; Marcus gates implementation against it. | Locked |
| Release gates | Locked CTAs: “Connect a data source,” “View setup guide,” no primary CTA for queued, and “Try again.” | Figma + implementation checklist | Locked |
| Release gates | Sample data must remain preview-only, visually separate, and must not create an activated-looking path. | Marcus / Linear checklist | Required before dogfood |
| Release gates | Sample data is excluded from activation eventing. Activation maps only to `real_source_connected` or `first_live_sync_completed` within 7 days. | Anna’s eventing/definition review | Proof still required |
| Release gates | Invited-member rendering uses server role plus source state. | Marcus / Linear checklist | Required |
| Release gates | Queued sync shows honest status only—no fake percentage, ETA, or countdown. | Marcus / Linear checklist | Required |
| Release gates | Failed sync uses normalized buckets: auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, unknown/retry. No raw vendor strings in UI. | Marcus / Linear checklist | Required |
| Release gates | Retry is idempotent. | Marcus / Linear checklist | Required |
| Design source-of-truth | Figma v0.2 is authoritative for the activation surface and state map. No new state exploration in this pass. | Priya | Locked; final frame reference pending |
| Implementation checklist work | Open blocker items are being translated into Linear implementation gates, not kept as design discussion. | Marcus | In progress; checklist post pending |
| Implementation checklist work | Any implementation/design mismatch is raised in review with Priya rather than handled informally in chat. | Marcus + Priya | Agreed working process |
| Design vs. release-readiness split | Priya owns the surface and states in Figma; Marcus owns implementation and ship-gate verification in the checklist. They are no longer treating the same blockers as two separate debates. | Priya + Marcus | Explicitly aligned |
| Polish | Setup-guide copy, narrow-width preview-card spacing, and failed-state icon polish are deferred. Neutral warning-circle direction remains. | Priya / implementation follow-up | Not launch blockers |

Bottom line: the design-vs.-implementation overlap has been resolved. Priya’s Figma defines what the surface and states are; Marcus’s checklist defines whether implementation is safe to ship. The remaining pre-dogfood item needing explicit proof is eventing/activation-definition alignment.

arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp
arguments.body:
# Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp

## Purpose and first-month center of gravity

Leo’s first month is intentionally narrow and practical: Mercury release discipline, platform seams, and launch readiness. This is not a broad architecture-tour onboarding or a rewrite exercise.

Leo should work in the real product states immediately, especially activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams that can fail in dogfood. The first useful output is a release-risk readout grounded in evidence: where launch risk is hiding, where evidence is thin, and what needs direct verification before wider dogfood or launch decisions.

Use the existing operating cadence rather than creating a parallel process. Jake’s Mercury weekly is where launch-critical work is surfaced and forced to closure. Internal working docs, blockers, and owners matter more than investor-style packaging.

## Jake walkthrough — Mercury weekly and blockers

Mercury weekly is the operating spine. Its agenda is blockers, evidence, decisions, and owner gaps. Work belongs there when it is tied to launch readiness.

The current blocker shape is primarily seam risk across activation, auth edges, and proof that real product states behave as the design specifies—not a single large missing feature.

Auth v0.2 currently uses Clerk for sessions, magic links, and org invites in internal builds. SSO and deeper admin controls are later scope. There is no production conversation until the standard staging path is clean on:

- session path
- magic-link flow
- org-invite flow

Org-invite / invited-member behavior remains a watch area because rendering depends on the correct server-role and source-state combination.

Retention and activation reporting have two audiences:

- directional internal weekly cuts for operating decisions
- sturdier quarterly cohort views for board/investor use

Do not mix these audiences or their evidence standards. Leo should use the weekly to identify risk and missing evidence, not to reopen settled product/design calls unless there is real launch impact.

## Priya handoff — Figma and activation/onboarding source of truth

Figma is the source of truth for activation/onboarding decisions. Quick discussion can happen elsewhere, but design calls live in review against the file. Leo should point to the exact state/frame and user consequence when raising a risk, rather than making a general taste argument.

Internalize this initial state map:

- no source connected
- invited member waiting on admin / first source
- first sync queued
- sync failed

Locked design logic and non-negotiables:

- Sample data is preview-only and must remain visually separate from anything that looks activated.
- Invited-member rendering keys off server role + source state.
- Queued sync does not show fake percent or ETA.
- Failed sync uses normalized buckets and clean UI language, not raw vendor strings.

Locked CTA labels:

- no source: “Connect a data source”
- invited member: “View setup guide”
- queued: no primary CTA
- failed: “Try again”

## Marcus handoff — release readiness and thin evidence

Marcus’s scope is release-readiness constraints, implementation checklist feedback, and evidence quality—not reopening design ownership.

Some paths look reasonable in review but still lack enough real dogfood evidence, especially edge states rather than the happy path. Leo’s readout should distinguish among:

1. behavior with repeated evidence
2. behavior that only looks correct in demos or screenshots
3. behavior that is technically implemented but still under-proven for launch

For each meaningful risk, call out:

- the seam or state involved
- severity and launch consequence
- evidence that exists now
- the one more direct check still needed, if applicable

Separate real blockers from later cleanup or polish. Do not turn every rough edge into launch drama, but do not wave through anything that creates a regression or makes the state misleading.

## First-month expected output

A concise, evidence-backed Mercury release-risk readout covering activation/onboarding, auth-adjacent seams, and launch-critical dogfood evidence. It should identify what is known, what is only demonstrated, what remains under-proven, and which direct checks are needed before wider dogfood or launch decisions.

arguments.message: Leo’s first useful output should be a Mercury release-risk readout grounded in evidence: where seam risk is hiding, what is repeatedly verified vs. only demoed, and what still needs a direct check before wider dogfood or launch decisions—not abstract platform recommendations.

arguments.title: Mercury — Weekly Operating Note (June 12, 2023)
arguments.body:
# Mercury — Weekly Operating Note

**Week of June 12, 2023 · Working team only**

## Top blockers

1. **Org-invite copy cleanup** — The flow works, but the copy needs a final pass before widening dogfood.
2. **Single release-readiness checklist** — Consolidate design and implementation readiness into one owner-managed checklist. It currently spans Figma, review comments, and implementation tracking.
3. **Keep admin/settings scope contained** — Prevent admin/org-settings work from reopening SSO or deeper admin-control scope ahead of the next dogfood cut.

## Owner questions

- Who owns the final org-invite copy pass?
- Who owns the release-readiness checklist end to end, including copy/UX/empty states and gating/logging/fallback behavior?
- Do admin/org-settings changes stay fully out until after the next dogfood cut, or is there a narrowly defined subset worth including?

## Current operating position

- Continue this week's build on the Clerk baseline; sessions, magic links, and org invites are sufficient for internal use.
- Treat SSO and deeper admin controls as later scope. Do not mix them into the current Mercury release story.
- Widen dogfood only after the invite-copy decision and a unified readiness checklist are resolved.

## Keep out of investor framing

- The unresolved split between design-side and implementation-side readiness tracking.
- Invite-copy cleanup, empty-state polish, and other internal quality work as standalone narrative points.
- SSO, deeper admin controls, and broad admin/org-settings expansion; these are later-scope noise for this week's story.

This note is for execution and owner assignment, not external or investor distribution.

arguments.title: Mercury activation surface — release-readiness checklist
arguments.body:
# Mercury activation surface — release-readiness checklist

> **INTERNAL IMPLEMENTATION MATERIAL — NOT INVESTOR-FACING NARRATIVE**
>
> This document is for product, engineering, release, and QA execution. It is not a launch story, customer-facing explanation, or investor narrative.

## Purpose and source split

This checklist translates the June 19 Figma review into release-readiness work for the Mercury activation surface.

- **Priya — product-owner decisions / product source of truth:** the reviewed activation branches, the intended primary CTA for the no-source state, the product behavior for invited members, and the copy/design decisions represented in the canonical Figma frames.
- **Marcus — release / QA constraints:** the implementation gates, state-transition and invitation-edge coverage, retry/idempotency checks, activation-event review, responsive QA, and the rule to remove unavailable secondary links.
- **Canonical product source:** Priya’s June 19 Figma decisions.
- **Canonical implementation/release source:** this checklist, for release and QA execution.

## Release gates

- [ ] Keep the v0.2 state map limited to the four reviewed branches:
  - no source connected
  - invited member waiting on admin / first source
  - first sync queued
  - sync failed
- [ ] Do not provide an activated-looking path from sample data.
- [ ] If sample data appears anywhere, keep it visually separate, label it **preview-only**, and exclude it from activation events.
- [ ] Preserve Priya’s primary CTA in the **no source connected** state: **Connect a data source**.
- [ ] Render the invited-member branch from server role plus source state; do not infer it from client token guesses.
- [ ] Pass the following organization-invite edges on staging:
  - expired invite
  - double accept
  - existing user already in another organization
  - member lands before the first source exists
- [ ] Ensure the queued-sync state shows neither a fake percentage nor an ETA countdown.
- [ ] Normalize failed-sync errors into approved buckets; do not expose raw vendor strings in the UI.
- [ ] Make retry idempotent.
- [ ] Complete one final activation-event naming pass with Anna and Devon before merge, so sample-import behavior does not leak into the activation metric.

## QA constraints and test matrix

### Required matrix

Test each combination of:

- [ ] Role: admin vs invited member
- [ ] Source: exists vs no source yet
- [ ] First live sync: succeeds vs stalls vs fails

### Behavioral checks

- [ ] Confirm retry creates exactly one job.
- [ ] Confirm double-clicking retry does not fan out duplicate work.
- [ ] Confirm refreshing during retry does not fan out duplicate work.
- [ ] Confirm the UI state transition after a real source is connected.
- [ ] Confirm the UI state transition after the first live sync completes.
- [ ] Confirm mobile-width behavior for the invited-member state after Priya shortens the copy.
- [ ] Confirm mobile-width behavior for the failure state after Priya shortens the copy.
- [ ] If documentation or help links are not live at release time, remove the secondary CTA rather than shipping a dead link.

## Open product decisions before release

These remain unresolved from the June 19 review and must be decided before the related implementation is treated as final:

- [ ] Decide whether sample data appears anywhere in v0.2 or is cut entirely.
- [ ] Set the threshold for changing queued-sync copy to **taking longer than usual**.
- [ ] Finalize invited-member copy for the case where the organization exists but the admin has not connected the first source.
- [ ] Finalize the exact user-facing failure buckets; determine what remains collapsed behind the scenes.

Until these decisions are closed, implementation should remain aligned to Priya’s Figma source and should not introduce additional activation branches or narrative copy.

## Release review record

- Product source: Priya’s June 19 Figma review
- Implementation checklist owner/source: Marcus, posted June 21, 2023
- Activation-event naming pass: Anna / Devon
- Environment explicitly called out for invite-edge validation: staging
- Audience: internal product, engineering, release, and QA teams only

arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp
arguments.body:
# Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp

## Purpose and first-month center of gravity

Leo’s first month is intentionally narrow and practical: Mercury release discipline, platform seams, and launch readiness. This is not a broad architecture-tour onboarding or a rewrite exercise.

Leo should work in the real product states immediately, especially activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams that can fail in dogfood. The first useful output is a release-risk readout grounded in evidence: where launch risk is hiding, where evidence is thin, and what needs direct verification before wider dogfood or launch decisions.

Use the existing operating cadence rather than creating a parallel process. Jake’s Mercury weekly is where launch-critical work is surfaced and forced to closure. Internal working docs, blockers, and owners matter more than investor-style packaging.

## Jake walkthrough — Mercury weekly and blockers

Mercury weekly is the operating spine. Its agenda is blockers, evidence, decisions, and owner gaps. Work belongs there when it is tied to launch readiness.

The current blocker shape is primarily seam risk across activation, auth edges, and proof that real product states behave as the design specifies—not a single large missing feature.

Auth v0.2 currently uses Clerk for sessions, magic links, and org invites in internal builds. SSO and deeper admin controls are later scope. There is no production conversation until the standard staging path is clean on:

- session path
- magic-link flow
- org-invite flow

Org-invite / invited-member behavior remains a watch area because rendering depends on the correct server-role and source-state combination.

Retention and activation reporting have two audiences:

- directional internal weekly cuts for operating decisions
- sturdier quarterly cohort views for board/investor use

Do not mix these audiences or their evidence standards. Leo should use the weekly to identify risk and missing evidence, not to reopen settled product/design calls unless there is real launch impact.

## Priya handoff — Figma and activation/onboarding source of truth

Figma is the source of truth for activation/onboarding decisions. Quick discussion can happen elsewhere, but design calls live in review against the file. Leo should point to the exact state/frame and user consequence when raising a risk, rather than making a general taste argument.

Internalize this initial state map:

- no source connected
- invited member waiting on admin / first source
- first sync queued
- sync failed

Locked design logic and non-negotiables:

- Sample data is preview-only and must remain visually separate from anything that looks activated.
- Invited-member rendering keys off server role + source state.
- Queued sync does not show fake percent or ETA.
- Failed sync uses normalized buckets and clean UI language, not raw vendor strings.

Locked CTA labels:

- no source: “Connect a data source”
- invited member: “View setup guide”
- queued: no primary CTA
- failed: “Try again”

## Marcus handoff — release readiness and thin evidence

Marcus’s scope is release-readiness constraints, implementation checklist feedback, and evidence quality—not reopening design ownership.

Some paths look reasonable in review but still lack enough real dogfood evidence, especially edge states rather than the happy path. Leo’s readout should distinguish among:

1. behavior with repeated evidence
2. behavior that only looks correct in demos or screenshots
3. behavior that is technically implemented but still under-proven for launch

For each meaningful risk, call out:

- the seam or state involved
- severity and launch consequence
- evidence that exists now
- the one more direct check still needed, if applicable

Separate real blockers from later cleanup or polish. Do not turn every rough edge into launch drama, but do not wave through anything that creates a regression or makes the state misleading.

## First-month expected output

A concise, evidence-backed Mercury release-risk readout covering activation/onboarding, auth-adjacent seams, and launch-critical dogfood evidence. It should identify what is known, what is only demonstrated, what remains under-proven, and which direct checks are needed before wider dogfood or launch decisions.

# Mercury release-risk readout — 2023-07-14

Attendees: Morgan Chen, Leo Park, Jake, Priya, Marcus

## Scope
Leo kept this readout to release risk and evidence—not a platform roadmap and not an owner-split launch ledger. The focus was where Mercury can still surprise us at the seams, especially where activation depends on auth/org state and where dogfood evidence is thin.

## Risk areas and evidence

### 1. Org-invite roles vs activation-state seam
**Risk:** Invited-member rendering depends on server role and source state, which may not settle at the same time. After invite acceptance, a user can briefly land in the wrong branch or see the wrong CTA.

**Evidence:**
- Only 2 real dogfood invited-member accounts have been tested end to end.
- One bug-bash pass required refresh/re-entry before the expected UI branch settled.
- Confidence still comes more from happy-path staging than repeated real dogfood coverage.

**Severity / confidence:** High severity, medium confidence.

**Verification needed:**
- Exercise more real invited-member accounts across admin-first and invitee-first orderings.
- Verify no path creates an activated-looking state without a real source or first live sync.
- Confirm sample data remains visually separate/preview-only and cannot shift the branch into something that looks activated.
- Watch CTA selection on first load after invite acceptance.

**Room context:** Priya reaffirmed the four-branch design intent with no pseudo-activated middle state. Jake classified this as a release risk because it crosses auth/org state. Marcus wants to distinguish wrong-CTA rendering defects from stale-state timing.

### 2. Release-readiness evidence gaps
**Risk:** Some paths may be close in code but are not proven ready; thin proof is itself material launch risk.

**Evidence:**
- Invited-member branch has only 2 real dogfood accounts.
- Queued-sync retry logs remain sparse after removing fake progress/countdown behavior.
- Failed-sync screenshots are cleaner, but sample depth remains shallow.

**Verification needed:**
- Retest every failed bucket with captured UI.
- Confirm no raw vendor strings leak.
- Confirm retry remains idempotent and bucket text/UI stay normalized on every branch.

- No SSO/admin-depth wishlist.

- Senior profile is still his default because he thinks the remaining risk is more about independent judgment through ugly edge cases than raw ticket throughput.

- Agrees the risk is real, but the pipeline does not support a reflex reopen.
- Reopening now means starting a fresh search from zero, not converting an active pipeline.
- Wants a decision rule tied to product-readiness evidence, not another calendar reminder.

- July's actual signal is that Leo is finding the right seams.

# Historical Mercury UI handoff note

Recorded: 2026-09-14
Historical decision path: June–July 2023
Audience: internal product, design, engineering, release, and QA teams

## Purpose

This note records the historical Mercury activation/onboarding handoff so ownership and decision paths are not reconstructed from old chat threads.

The central operating rule was to separate the UX decision from the question of whether the implementation was safe and sufficiently evidenced to ship. The separation clarified the workflow; it did not mean that every underlying design/implementation tension disappeared.

## Owner and source-of-truth map

| Area | Owner | Where the decision or evidence belonged | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mercury activation/onboarding UX | Priya | Canonical Figma file and design review, including the reviewed state map and copy decisions | Own the user-facing flow, states, hierarchy, CTA behavior, and wording. |
| Release readiness and dogfood gating | Marcus | Implementation checklist / Linear release-readiness view and release review | Own implementation gates, QA constraints, dogfood blockers, state-transition checks, retry/idempotency checks, and ship-gate verification. |
| Cross-service/platform-seam risk and missing evidence | Leo | Mercury launch-readiness ledger, row-level evidence, and weekly risk readout | Identify seam risk and distinguish repeated evidence from demos, screenshots, or under-proven behavior. |
| Activation definitions and instrumentation | Anna | Eventing/definition review, with evidence attached to the readiness record | Confirm that the UI state does not redefine activation; activation was tied to `real_source_connected` or `first_live_sync_completed` within 7 days, while sample-import-only activity was excluded. |
| Mercury operating cadence | Jake | MER-1279 weekly-decision column and Mercury weekly | Run the weekly from the ledger, forcing blockers, evidence, owners, and decisions to closure rather than collecting separate status narratives. |
| Scope calls and unblocking | Morgan | The existing Mercury operating cadence | Enter for actual scope calls or unblockers, not to become the default owner of design or implementation detail. |

## What belonged in design

Priya’s Figma source of truth defined the reviewed activation surface and its user-facing behavior. The locked v0.2 state map was:

- no source connected
- invited member waiting on admin / first source
- first sync queued
- sync failed

The locked CTA labels were:

- no source: “Connect a data source”
- invited member: “View setup guide”
- queued: no primary CTA
- failed: “Try again”

Design-owned decisions included:

- the activation branches and their intended user experience
- primary versus secondary action hierarchy
- user-facing copy and state meaning
- whether the product promised a self-serve recovery path or acknowledged operational intervention
- whether “Skip for now,” teammate invite, or a particular headline belonged in the launch flow
- the approved failure-language treatment and visual direction

A design review should point to the exact Figma frame and the user consequence. General taste arguments were not a substitute for a frame-level decision.

## What belonged in release readiness

Marcus’s implementation checklist and release review were the canonical home for whether the approved UX was implemented safely and had sufficient evidence for dogfood or release. The checklist covered, among other things:

- rendering invited members from server role plus source state
- keeping sample data visually separate and preview-only, without an activated-looking path
- excluding sample-data paths from activation eventing
- keeping queued-sync status honest, with no fake percentage, ETA, or countdown
- normalizing failed-sync buckets and keeping raw vendor strings out of the UI
- making retry idempotent and preventing duplicate work on double click or refresh
- validating invite edges, state transitions, responsive behavior, and rollback steps
- distinguishing “implemented” from “proven” through real dogfood evidence

A checklist item was not automatically a new design debate. If it exposed a genuine UX problem or required changing the approved behavior, it had to link the exact Figma frame and reopen only that design decision with Priya. Otherwise, it remained an implementation, QA, or evidence gate owned in the checklist.

## How disagreements should be resolved

1. Classify the disagreement first.
   - UX intent, state meaning, hierarchy, or copy: design decision.
   - Correctness, edge-state behavior, instrumentation, rollback, or evidence sufficiency: release-readiness decision.
   - Cross-service timing or auth/org-state seam: release risk; Leo documents the risk and missing evidence, while Marcus carries the implementation gate.
   - Activation definition or measurement integrity: Anna’s definition review.

2. Put the issue in its canonical place.
   - Design questions go to the relevant Figma frame/comment and design review.
   - Implementation and ship-risk questions go to the Linear checklist or MER-1279 ledger row.
   - Discord or chat may point people to the record, but should not become a third source of truth.

3. Require a concrete disagreement record.
   State the exact frame or checklist row, the user or release consequence, the evidence available, the proposed change, the owner, and the verification needed. Replace “this feels wrong” or “it looks ready” with a testable claim.

4. Reopen only the affected decision.
   If Marcus’s gate identifies a mismatch that truly changes user-facing behavior, Marcus raises it in review with Priya and links the exact frame. Priya decides the UX change; Marcus then updates or verifies the corresponding implementation gate. Do not reopen the whole state map or broader settings IA for a local issue.

5. Resolve evidence disputes with direct checks.
   Leo’s distinction was: repeated evidence, demo/screenshot evidence, or technically implemented but under-proven behavior. When the disagreement is about readiness, run the smallest targeted dogfood or staging check that can separate “unproven” from “broken,” and attach the result to the ledger.

6. Use the weekly for closure.
   Jake’s Mercury weekly should force each open item to a named owner, decision, acceptance criterion, and checkpoint. Report what moved, what slipped, what was cut, and which decision or unblocker is needed. Morgan is brought in for actual scope calls or unresolved unblockers—not for routine arbitration of Priya’s or Marcus’s lanes.

## Historical outcome

By the July 5 handoff review, Priya and Marcus explicitly agreed that the same blocker should not be argued twice: Figma defined the surface and states, while Marcus’s checklist defined implementation gates. Any mismatch was to be named in review with Priya rather than routed around in chat.

The July 24 MER-1279 operating model made the split durable:

- Marcus: implementation gates and dogfood blockers
- Priya: Figma design source of truth
- Leo: cross-service platform-seam risks and missing-evidence callouts
- Jake: Mercury weekly driven from the ledger

Polish such as setup-guide copy tightening, small-width spacing cleanup, and icon refinement was kept separate from launch gates unless it caused actual user confusion, clipping, overlap, or misleading state meaning.

## Short handoff rule

Priya decides what Mercury should feel and say. Marcus decides whether the approved behavior is correctly implemented and safe to gate. Leo identifies seam risk and thin evidence. Anna protects the activation definition. Jake drives closure from the ledger. When a release concern requires a design change, link the exact evidence to the exact Figma decision, resolve that narrow question with Priya, and return the resulting implementation gate to Marcus—without creating a parallel debate in chat.

- keeping sample data visually separate and preview-only, without an activated-looking path
- excluding sample-data paths from activation eventing
- keeping queued-sync status honest, with no fake percentage, ETA, or countdown
- normalizing failed-sync buckets and keeping raw vendor strings out of the UI
- making retry idempotent and preventing duplicate work on double click or refresh
- validating invite edges, state transitions, responsive behavior, and rollback steps
- distinguishing “implemented” from “proven” through real dogfood evidence

A checklist item was not automatically a new design debate. If it exposed a genuine UX problem or required changing the approved behavior, it had to link the exact Figma frame and reopen only that design decision with Priya. Otherwise, it remained an implementation, QA, or evidence gate owned in the checklist.

## How disagreements should be resolved

1. Classify the disagreement first.
   - UX intent, state meaning, hierarchy, or copy: design decision.
   - Correctness, edge-state behavior, instrumentation, rollback, or evidence sufficiency: release-readiness decision.
   - Cross-service timing or auth/org-state seam: release risk; Leo documents the risk and missing evidence, while Marcus carries the implementation gate.
   - Activation definition or measurement integrity: Anna’s definition review.

2. Put the issue in its canonical place.
   - Design questions go to the relevant Figma frame/comment and design review.
   - Implementation and ship-risk questions go to the Linear checklist or MER-1279 ledger row.
   - Discord or chat may point people to the record, but should not become a third source of truth.

3. Require a concrete disagreement record.
   State the exact frame or checklist row, the user or release consequence, the evidence available, the proposed change, the owner, and the verification needed. Replace “this feels wrong” or “it looks ready” with a testable claim.

4. Reopen only the affected decision.
   If Marcus’s gate identifies a mismatch that truly changes user-facing behavior, Marcus raises it in review with Priya and links the exact frame. Priya decides the UX change; Marcus then updates or verifies the corresponding implementation gate. Do not reopen the whole state map or broader settings IA for a local issue.

5. Resolve evidence disputes with direct checks.
   Leo’s distinction was: repeated evidence, demo/screenshot evidence, or technically implemented but under-proven behavior. When the disagreement is about readiness, run the smallest targeted dogfood or staging check that can separate “unproven” from “broken,” and attach the result to the ledger.

6. Use the weekly for closure.
   Jake’s Mercury weekly should force each open item to a named owner, decision, acceptance criterion, and checkpoint. Report what moved, what slipped, what was cut, and which decision or unblocker is needed. Morgan is brought in for actual scope calls or unresolved unblockers—not for routine arbitration of Priya’s or Marcus’s lanes.

## Historical outcome

By the July 5 handoff review, Priya and Marcus explicitly agreed that the same blocker should not be argued twice: Figma defined the surface and states, while Marcus’s checklist defined implementation gates. Any mismatch was to be named in review with Priya rather than routed around in chat.

The July 24 MER-1279 operating model made the split durable:

- Marcus: implementation gates and dogfood blockers
- Priya: Figma design source of truth
- Leo: cross-service platform-seam risks and missing-evidence callouts
- Jake: Mercury weekly driven from the ledger

Polish such as setup-guide copy tightening, small-width spacing cleanup, and icon refinement was kept separate from launch gates unless it caused actual user confusion, clipping, overlap, or misleading state meaning.

## Short handoff rule

Priya decides what Mercury should feel and say. Marcus decides whether the approved behavior is correctly implemented and safe to gate. Leo identifies seam risk and thin evidence. Anna protects the activation definition. Jake drives closure from the ledger. When a release concern requires a design change, link the exact evidence to the exact Figma decision, resolve that narrow question with Priya, and return the resulting implementation gate to Marcus—without creating a parallel debate in chat.

Goal: Turn each Compass v0.1 signal into a bounded, actionable operating rule.

- Are evidence and caveats visible together?
- Does any proposed workflow accidentally become a board dashboard or new hiring lane?

4. Decisions and close — 5 min
- Confirm accepted v0.1 rules.
- Mark signals needing more evidence or a tighter source-quality requirement.
- Assign owners for unresolved questions.
- Capture the explicit “not building” boundary beside each approved signal.

arguments.title: Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist
arguments.body:
# Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist

Working session: January 21, 2025  ·  Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

## v0.1 operating boundary
- **Purpose:** turn a narrow set of defensible signals into named follow-up actions; do not produce labels for their own sake.
- **Boundary:** no board dashboard, no prettier internal dashboard, and no new hiring lane. Jake’s January Mercury activation remains the center of gravity; Compass must not become a dashboard/platform build while that work is active.
- **Visibility rule:** start with the current team only. A signal leaves that team only after Sarah’s source-quality check, Anna’s attached definition/caveat, and Leo’s data/platform-seam check.

## Owner checklist

### 1) Renewal-risk / admin-friction
- [ ] **Signal — Anna (definition):** identify the specific admin friction, setup-control issue, or role confusion causing the apparent risk. Keep true product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag as separate categories; never use “renewal risk” alone.
- [ ] **Trigger — Nadia (action):** trigger a named account-owner follow-up that names the friction and the next customer/account-team step. Do not trigger from a risk label alone.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Nadia:** first: Nadia and the account owner, as an account-team script candidate. Before the gate: Anna, Sarah, and the current team only; no broad customer outreach or external distribution.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Sarah + Anna:** attach the account-thread provenance, separating customer statement, observed/support fact, and internal interpretation; state what is known, inferred, and unresolved. The minimum package remains an open decision; Nadia must approve the bar before it becomes a script rather than an internal FYI.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah:** rate the underlying note reliable, mixed, or too thin. Weak or mixed notes must carry an explicit caveat; too-thin notes stay internal and cannot support outreach.
- [ ] **Not building:** not a generic renewal-risk score, account-risk label, automated escalation, or dashboard of at-risk accounts.

### 2) Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt
- [ ] **Signal — Jake + Leo:** first live sync is actually live, with teammate-invite and admin-role basics visible enough to ground a follow-up. Distinguish observed usage from inferred readiness for broader usage.
- [ ] **Trigger — Nadia:** issue the smallest useful customer-growth/account-team prompt after first real traction: a timely next-action script, not generic upsell language or a metrics view.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Nadia:** first: Nadia and the account owner after the trigger conditions are met. Before release outside the current team: Jake, Leo, Anna, and Sarah review; do not expose it as a broad product or customer surface.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Leo + Anna:** Leo confirms the event path and data/platform seam are defendable; Anna keeps the definition and uncertainty attached. Record the live-sync event, visible invite/admin-role state, and the boundary between observed usage and inferred expansion readiness.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah:** confirm the account note and usage/event evidence are traceable and rate the note reliable, mixed, or too thin. If the source is weak, keep the prompt internal and state the caveat.
- [ ] **Not building:** not an expansion score, recommendation engine, product surface, metrics dashboard, or platform build.

### 3) Account-note source quality
- [ ] **Signal — Sarah:** classify each supporting thread note as reliable, mixed, or too thin, with provenance tags for customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, and internal interpretation.
- [ ] **Trigger — Sarah + Anna:** only permit a signal to feed real follow-up when the note-quality status and caveats are explicit; otherwise keep it as an internal FYI.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Sarah first:** Sarah, Anna, and the current team see the quality assessment first. Nadia sees it for outreach only when the source-quality bar is met; do not pass mushy notes off as customer fact.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Sarah:** preserve the traceable source note and distinguish fact from interpretation; Anna ensures caveats travel with the signal. Define the required note fields/source tags before external-team use.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah (gate):** no reliable/traceable provenance, no outside-current-team use. Mixed requires an explicit caveat and review; too thin stays internal and cannot trigger outreach.
- [ ] **Not building:** not a note-cleanup program, universal CRM taxonomy, automated sentiment/provenance system, or dashboard of source-quality scores.

## Ownership and exit gate
- **Anna:** definitions and caveats remain attached to every signal.
- **Nadia:** owns the customer-growth/account-team script and follow-up logic; no outreach from mushy notes or internal inference presented as customer fact.
- **Jake:** protects the v0.1 boundary while January Mercury activation is active; no dashboard/platform drift.
- **Leo:** completes the data/platform-seam and event-path defensibility check before any signal leaves the current team.
- **Sarah:** owns source hygiene and the reliable/mixed/too-thin classification; source quality is a gating input, not cleanup.
- **Before any signal leaves the current team:** action and first viewer are named; evidence/caveat bundle is attached; Sarah’s source-quality gate, Anna’s caveat check, and Leo’s seam check are complete; Nadia accepts the follow-up use; Jake confirms the scope remains v0.1.
- **Explicitly not building in v0.1:** no board dashboard, no new hiring lane, no prettier internal dashboard, and no broad platform/product surface. First pass stays narrow enough to test whether signals produce action.

[2025-02-04T15:48:00-08:00] Compass owner fill-in is more concrete, but dashboard drift is trying to sneak back in. Give me a concise gap/risk read: what’s ready enough for owner follow-up, what still looks like dashboard drift, and what has to be settled before any limited discovery pass.

Owner fill-in notes:
Anna Martinez proposes that renewal-risk/admin-friction signals carry definitions, caveats, and confidence, and must not collapse true product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag into one bucket. Nadia Singh proposes that renewal/admin-friction follow-up should point to a named account-owner action and that the post-first-live-sync expansion prompt should produce a customer-growth or account-team script, not a generic upsell view. Jake says Compass v0.1 must remain narrow while January Mercury activation is active and must not become a dashboard or platform build. Leo Park says the data/platform seam can be checked for the renewal/admin-friction evidence path and the first-live-sync trigger, but anything shown outside the current team needs defendable event provenance first. Sarah Kim says account-thread notes need source tags that separate customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, and internal interpretation, and she can mark notes as reliable, mixed, or too thin. Open gaps are the minimum evidence bundle Nadia will accept before a script is used, who sees each signal first, which signals stay internal, and the exact not-building line for each v0.1 prompt.

Gap/risk read

Ready enough for owner follow-up
- Signal definitions: renewal risk/admin friction should carry definitions, caveats, and confidence—and stay split across product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag.
- Actionability: each follow-up should name an account-owner action; post-first-live-sync output should be a customer-growth/account-team script, not an upsell dashboard.
- Evidence discipline: account-thread notes can be tagged by source—customer statement, observed usage, support fact, or internal interpretation—and rated reliable, mixed, or too thin.
- Technical seam: Leo can validate the evidence path and first-live-sync trigger, provided provenance is defensible.
- Scope guardrail: Compass v0.1 remains narrow and does not become a dashboard or platform build.

Dashboard-drift risks still present
- Aggregating distinct causes into a single “renewal risk” or “admin friction” score.
- Producing signals without a named owner action or script.
- Showing generic upsell/expansion views instead of a post-sync prompt.
- Exposing weakly sourced signals outside the current team.
- Expanding from a few prompts into monitoring, reporting, or platform infrastructure.

Must be settled before a limited discovery pass
1. Nadia’s minimum evidence bundle for allowing a script to be used.
2. First-view routing: who receives each signal, in what order, and with what escalation.
3. Which signals remain internal versus may be shared externally.
4. Required provenance/source tags and the threshold for “reliable” versus “too thin.”
5. The exact not-building line for every v0.1 prompt, including no dashboard, generic upsell view, or platform layer.
6. A pass/fail check for both the renewal/admin-friction evidence path and the first-live-sync trigger.

Bottom line: the owner logic is concrete enough to prepare follow-up, but discovery should not start until evidence acceptance, routing/visibility, and explicit scope exclusions are written as operating rules.

arguments.title: Compass v0.1 — First Preview Readout Scaffold
arguments.body:
# Compass v0.1 — First Preview Readout

## Purpose
Assess whether the first preview produced useful account-team action—not whether the experience looked polished or customers said they understood a dashboard.

## Scope and guardrails
- v0.1 remains a narrow preview/discovery read, not a dashboard or platform evaluation.
- Keep **signal legibility** separate from **behavior change**.
- Preserve Acme’s live-only review boundary: discuss only Acme’s own account-health, reliability, and renewal-risk signals with Greg Shipman, Sarah Kim, Nadia Singh, and Jake. Do not circulate written Mercury packets, screenshots, Evergreen examples, or other customer-specific Compass materials to Acme.
- Keep definitions, caveats, confidence, and event provenance attached to every signal.
- Treat account-thread notes as source-quality-specific; do not collapse observation, interpretation, and reported action.

## 1. Legibility: could the intended user interpret the signal?
Capture evidence for:
- Signal definition and status were understood without relying on unstated context.
- The user could identify the relevant account risk or friction and its supporting evidence.
- Caveats and confidence changed or constrained interpretation as intended.
- The user could tell what was observed versus inferred, including event provenance.
- Questions or confusion were about the signal itself, not merely the presentation.

Record separately:
- Who read it and in what review context.
- Signal, definition, caveats, confidence, and provenance shown.
- Exact questions, misreadings, or missing context.
- Source quality of each note: direct observation, account-thread record, participant report, or interpretation.

## 2. Behavior change: did the signal change what someone did next?
Do not count recognition, agreement, or “this is useful” as behavior change. Look for concrete evidence that an account-team script, renewal-risk response, admin-friction follow-up, or customer-growth action changed.

### Concrete next-action evidence
For each red or otherwise actionable signal, look for:
- A named owner who accepted responsibility.
- A specific next action, not a general intention.
- A committed timing or trigger.
- The account/customer context used to tailor the action.
- Evidence attached to the action: source event(s), account-thread note(s), definition, caveat, and confidence.
- A recorded follow-up in the relevant account thread, task, or system of record.
- Subsequent evidence that the action occurred.
- If no action occurred, the stated blocker and whether the signal, evidence, ownership, or workflow was insufficient.

For Greg’s question, explicitly answer: “When the signal is red, who does what next, based on which evidence?”

## 3. Readout table
| Signal / scenario | Legibility evidence | Misread or missing context | Named owner | Specific next action | Timing / trigger | Evidence carried with action | Follow-up observed | Source quality | Confidence / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

## 4. Interpretation rules
- Report legibility and behavior-change findings as separate findings; one does not substitute for the other.
- A clear signal with no changed action is a legibility success but not a behavior-change success.
- A changed action without traceable evidence is not sufficient; assess provenance and source quality.
- Keep “account team changed its script/workflow” distinct from “customer-growth follow-up changed.”
- Do not generalize from Evergreen to Acme. Acme evidence must remain live-only and account-specific.
- Do not use board-proof, GTM-proof, customer-understanding, or dashboard-success language. Use observed behavior, attributable evidence, and bounded preview findings.

## 5. Open questions for the first read
- Which roles should act on renewal-risk versus admin-friction signals?
- What minimum evidence must travel with each signal for the owner to act confidently?
- Which caveats or confidence levels materially change the next action?
- Where is event provenance incomplete or ambiguous?
- What is the smallest workflow change that would make the intended action more likely?

## 6. Bottom line format
- **Legibility:** [what users could/could not interpret, with evidence]
- **Behavior change:** [what action changed, by whom, and what was observed afterward]
- **Evidence quality:** [what traveled with the signal; provenance and caveats]
- **Boundary:** [Evergreen current-state evidence and Acme live-only evidence kept separate]
- **Next narrow test:** [one workflow/action question for v0.1; no dashboard/platform expansion]

Project Compass — Internal Owner-Routing Note
Kickoff: January 17, 2025

Purpose

Compass turns existing customer-health signals into better customer-facing guidance and customer-success/growth follow-up. A signal is useful only when it carries evidence, caveats, and a clear next action.

This is an operating/product workflow—not another internal reporting layer.

What Compass is not

- Not a new board dashboard.
- Not investor packaging.
- Not a generic health-score project.
- Not a bespoke Evergreen workstream.
- Not a broad admin-policy or enterprise-controls product.
- Not a reason to open a new hiring lane.

Stay within the current lightweight staffing model: Nadia/Sarah operating support with Jake/Leo implementation support.

v0.1 focus

1. Renewal-risk and admin-friction evidence
   - Show when apparent renewal risk may instead reflect admin friction, setup/control issues, role confusion, procurement packaging, or activation drag.
   - Do not use binary risk labels without context.
   - Attach source evidence and caveats to every signal.

2. Post-first-live-sync expansion prompts
   - Identify the smallest useful prompt or follow-up after an account reaches first live sync and appears ready for broader usage.
   - Optimize for timely, evidence-based action—not generic upsell language.

3. Account-note source quality
   - Make follow-up traceable by distinguishing:
     - Customer statements
     - Observed usage/readout
     - Support-derived facts
     - Internal interpretation
   - Preserve provenance and recency.
   - Treat note quality as foundational to signal trustworthiness, not as separate housekeeping.

Owner routing

- Anna Martinez — Signal definitions and caveats
  - Define retention, activation, expansion, admin friction, enterprise readiness, and account-note quality.
  - Separate evidence from inference.
  - Document what each signal does and does not mean.

- Nadia Singh — Customer-success and customer-growth use cases
  - Define the follow-up behavior each signal should trigger.
  - Own routing, recipient, and next-action design.
  - Ensure customer-facing guidance is grounded in evidence rather than implied certainty.

- Jake — Product implementation and sequencing
  - Keep v0.1 lightweight: prompts, account workflow support, or a contained product assist.
  - Prevent scope from expanding into a broad new product surface or general enterprise-controls work.

- Leo Park — Data/platform seams
  - Reuse existing signals and event paths.
  - Avoid a separate scoring service or platform layer at this stage.
  - Define the minimum evidence bundle that can move from internal read to customer/action use.
  - Keep usage evidence, account-note evidence, and inferred account state distinct.

- Sarah Kim — Account-thread hygiene
  - Improve source quality in account notes.
  - Separate customer quotes, internal interpretation, support follow-up, and procurement context.
  - Make the underlying record trustworthy enough for growth follow-up.

- Morgan Chen — Board/customer narrative
  - Keep the framing operational and customer-real.
  - Do not turn early Compass work into presentation-ready reporting.
  - Board narrative comes later, after the workflow changes account behavior.

Working signal logic

Preserve the distinctions already useful in Mercury/Evergreen work:

- Activation friction
- Admin handoff or role confusion
- Procurement/security packaging
- Expansion stalls after first live sync
- True product gaps

Do not flatten these into a single score or treat admin friction as a churn prediction by default.

A Compass signal is working when:

- It triggers a clearer next action.
- The recipient understands why they are seeing it.
- Evidence and caveats travel with the signal.
- Follow-up quality improves—not merely internal visibility.

Immediate next decisions

- Minimum evidence package required for each signal.
- Signals that remain internal versus those suitable for customer-facing use…

arguments.body:
# Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist

Working session: January 21, 2025  ·  Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

## v0.1 operating boundary
- **Purpose:** turn a narrow set of defensible signals into named follow-up actions; do not produce labels for their own sake.
- **Boundary:** no board dashboard, no prettier internal dashboard, and no new hiring lane. Jake’s January Mercury activation remains the center of gravity; Compass must not become a dashboard/platform build while that work is active.
- **Visibility rule:** start with the current team only. A signal leaves that team only after Sarah’s source-quality check, Anna’s attached definition/caveat, and Leo’s data/platform-seam check.

## Owner checklist

### 1) Renewal-risk / admin-friction
- [ ] **Signal — Anna (definition):** identify the specific admin friction, setup-control issue, or role confusion causing the apparent risk. Keep true product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag as separate categories; never use “renewal risk” alone.
- [ ] **Trigger — Nadia (action):** trigger a named account-owner follow-up that names the friction and the next customer/account-team step. Do not trigger from a risk label alone.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Nadia:** first: Nadia and the account owner, as an account-team script candidate. Before the gate: Anna, Sarah, and the current team only; no broad customer outreach or external distribution.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Sarah + Anna:** attach the account-thread provenance, separating customer statement, observed/support fact, and internal interpretation; state what is known, inferred, and unresolved. The minimum package remains an open decision; Nadia must approve the bar before it becomes a script rather than an internal FYI.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah:** rate the underlying note reliable, mixed, or too thin. Weak or mixed notes must carry an explicit caveat; too-thin notes stay internal and cannot support outreach.
- [ ] **Not building:** not a generic renewal-risk score, account-risk label, automated escalation, or dashboard of at-risk accounts.

### 2) Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt
- [ ] **Signal — Jake + Leo:** first live sync is actually live, with teammate-invite and admin-role basics visible enough to ground a follow-up. Distinguish observed usage from inferred readiness for broader usage.
- [ ] **Trigger — Nadia:** issue the smallest useful customer-growth/account-team prompt after first real traction: a timely next-action script, not generic upsell language or a metrics view.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Nadia:** first: Nadia and the account owner after the trigger conditions are met. Before release outside the current team: Jake, Leo, Anna, and Sarah review; do not expose it as a broad product or customer surface.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Leo + Anna:** Leo confirms the event path and data/platform seam are defendable; Anna keeps the definition and uncertainty attached. Record the live-sync event, visible invite/admin-role state, and the boundary between observed usage and inferred expansion readiness.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah:** confirm the account note and usage/event evidence are traceable and rate the note reliable, mixed, or too thin. If the source is weak, keep the prompt internal and state the caveat.
- [ ] **Not building:** not an expansion score, recommendation engine, product surface, metrics dashboard, or platform build.

### 3) Account-note source quality
- [ ] **Signal — Sarah:** classify each supporting thread note as reliable, mixed, or too thin, with provenance tags for customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, and internal interpretation.
- [ ] **Trigger — Sarah + Anna:** only permit a signal to feed real follow-up when the note-quality status and caveats are explicit; otherwise keep it as an internal FYI.
- [ ] **Who sees it — Sarah first:** Sarah, Anna, and the current team see the quality assessment first. Nadia sees it for outreach only when the source-quality bar is met; do not pass mushy notes off as customer fact.
- [ ] **Evidence/caveat — Sarah:** preserve the traceable source note and distinguish fact from interpretation; Anna ensures caveats travel with the signal. Define the required note fields/source tags before external-team use.
- [ ] **Source-quality requirement — Sarah (gate):** no reliable/traceable provenance, no outside-current-team use. Mixed requires an explicit caveat and review; too thin stays internal and cannot trigger outreach.
- [ ] **Not building:** not a note-cleanup program, universal CRM taxonomy, automated sentiment/provenance system, or dashboard of source-quality scores.

## Ownership and exit gate
- **Anna:** definitions and caveats remain attached to every signal.
- **Nadia:** owns the customer-growth/account-team script and follow-up logic; no outreach from mushy notes or internal inference presented as customer fact.
- **Jake:** protects the v0.1 boundary while January Mercury activation is active; no dashboard/platform drift.
- **Leo:** completes the data/platform-seam and event-path defensibility check before any signal leaves the current team.
- **Sarah:** owns source hygiene and the reliable/mixed/too-thin classification; source quality is a gating input, not cleanup.
- **Before any signal leaves the current team:** action and first viewer are named; evidence/caveat bundle is attached; Sarah’s source-quality gate, Anna’s caveat check, and Leo’s seam check are complete; Nadia accepts the follow-up use; Jake confirms the scope remains v0.1.
- **Explicitly not building in v0.1:** no board dashboard, no new hiring lane, no prettier internal dashboard, and no broad platform/product surface. First pass stays narrow enough to test whether signals produce action.

Archive date: September 14, 2026
Source period: January 17–22, 2025
Project: Compass v0.1

Purpose
Record the approved boundary for Leo Park’s involvement in the January 2025 Compass v0.1 work, and the condition under which scope had to return to Morgan Chen for review.

Leo’s approved involvement
Leo was approved for lightweight data/platform-seam support—not a new Compass platform build. His work was limited to:

- Reusing existing signals and event paths.
- Checking the evidence path for the renewal-risk/admin-friction work.
- Checking the first-live-sync trigger and the minimum event-path support for the post-first-live-sync expansion prompt.
- Defining the minimum evidence bundle that could move from an internal read toward customer/account-action use.
- Keeping usage evidence, account-note evidence, and inferred account state distinct.
- Confirming that event provenance and the underlying data/platform seam were defensible before a signal moved beyond the current team.

The approved implementation shape was lightweight prompts, account-workflow support, or a contained product assist. Leo was not approved to create a separate scoring service, platform layer, broad monitoring/reporting system, dashboard, or general enterprise-controls surface.

January operating center of gravity
January work remained focused on Mercury activation: workspace → first source → first live sync, plus teammate-invite and admin-role basics. Compass v0.1 received only enough Leo seam work to test:

- Renewal-risk/admin-friction evidence.
- A post-first-live-sync expansion prompt grounded in actual account state.

The work had to distinguish observed usage from inferred readiness and could not become generic upsell language or a metrics view.

When scope had to return to Morgan for review
Morgan’s January 17 direction was explicit: a lightweight first read from Leo on Compass seams was acceptable, but if Compass began looking like a dashboard/platform build, the scope had to be brought back to Morgan for review. This review trigger also applied to any drift from the narrow v0.1 test into a broader product surface or a shift of the January center of gravity away from Mercury activation.

This was a scope-control trigger, not approval for Leo to expand the work and seek review afterward. The safe default was to stop the expansion and return the proposed scope to Morgan before proceeding.

Separate release gate
Scope review by Morgan was distinct from the operational release gate. Before any signal left the current team, Leo still had to complete the data/platform-seam and event-path defensibility check, alongside Sarah’s source-quality check, Anna’s definition/caveat check, Nadia’s follow-up-use acceptance, and Jake’s confirmation that the work remained within v0.1.

Archive conclusion
Leo’s approved role in January 2025 was bounded seam validation and evidence-path definition in support of two narrow Compass v0.1 tests. Any dashboard/platform drift, broad productization, separate scoring or platform infrastructure, or displacement of January Mercury activation required the work to stop and return to Morgan for scope review.
